Grokking Finite-Dimensional Algebra

Pascal Jr Tikeng Notsawo Affiliation:  Université de Montréal Affiliation: Mila, Montréal Correspondence to: pascalnotsawo@gmail.com    Guillaume Dumas Affiliation:  Université de Montréal Affiliation: Mila, Montréal Affiliation: CHU Sainte-Justine Research Center, Montréal    Guillaume Rabusseau Affiliation:  Université de Montréal Affiliation: Mila, Montréal Affiliation: CIFAR AI Chair
Abstract

This paper investigates the grokking phenomenon, which refers to the sudden transition from a long memorization to generalization observed during neural networks training, in the context of learning multiplication in finite-dimensional algebras (FDA). While prior work on grokking has focused mainly on group operations, we extend the analysis to more general algebraic structures, including non-associative, non-commutative, and non-unital algebras. We show that learning group operations is a special case of learning FDA, and that learning multiplication in FDA amounts to learning a bilinear product specified by the algebra’s structure tensor. For algebras over the reals, we connect the learning problem to matrix factorization with an implicit low-rank bias, and for algebras over finite fields, we show that grokking emerges naturally as models must learn discrete representations of algebraic elements. This leads us to experimentally investigate the following core questions: (i) how do algebraic properties such as commutativity, associativity, and unitality influence both the emergence and timing of grokking, (ii) how structural properties of the structure tensor of the FDA, such as sparsity and rank, influence generalization, and (iii) to what extent generalization correlates with the model learning latent embeddings aligned with the algebra’s representation. Our work provides a unified framework for grokking across algebraic structures and new insights into how mathematical structure governs neural network generalization dynamics.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

One of the primary objectives of machine learning is generalization, which refers to the ability of models to perform well on data they have not encountered during training. Even if these models perform exceptionally well in different domains today, the underlying reason for their good generalization ability remains an open question. By introducing the grokking phenomenon, Power et al. 2022 recently provides a new lens to view the generalization capabilities of overparametrized neural networks, challenging previous notions that such networks merely memorize training data.

The grokking phenomenon has been studied mainly on algorithmic tasks, which consist of predicting z=x∘yz=x\circ y given (x,y)∈𝒮2(x,y)\in\mathcal{S}^{2}, with ∘\circ a binary mathematical operator and 𝒮\mathcal{S} a finite set of discrete symbols with no internal structure; for instance, finite cyclic groups of order 11 with its binary operation ∘\circ (such as addition in 𝒮=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathcal{S}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} for some prime integer pp). In such settings, it is now established that models like Transformers generalize by recovering the representation of the group itself (Gromov 2023; Nanda et al. 2023; Chughtai et al. 2023; Stander et al. 2024). In this work, we investigate how grokking extends beyond these well-understood settings in terms of algebraic complexity, i.e, moving from groups to more general algebras. Our goal is to understand how specific algebraic or structural properties of the task influence the emergence and timing of the grokking phenomenon.

Motivations

While group operations provide a basic structure, algebras encompass a richer and more complex set of operations, including non-unital, non-commutative, and non-associative behaviors. For example, many systems (in physics, robotics, control, etc) evolve according to infinitesimal transformations whose interaction is governed by a Lie bracket [⋅,⋅][\cdot,\cdot], a bilinear, non-commutative, non-associative, and non-unital operation. Predicting such infinitesimal updates corresponds to learning a FDA.

In drug discovery, predicting how molecules interact with biological targets is crucial for identifying potential drug candidates. This involves understanding the complex relationships and transformations between different molecular structures. An example of a task is chemical reaction prediction (Fooshee et al. 2018), where given two molecules xx and yy, the task is to predict the product x​yxy when these molecules undergo a chemical reaction (and the reaction pathway). If a third molecule zz is involved, the reaction sequence (x​y)​z(xy)z might yield a different product than x⁡(y​z)x(yz). Also, chemical reactions often involve complex mechanisms that cannot be simply reversed or do not have a natural identity element (a molecule that would leave another unchanged in a reaction).

In natural language processing, understanding how the meanings of smaller units (words or phrases) combine to form the meanings of larger units (sentences or documents) is a fundamental challenge. This process is inherently compositional, similar to operations in an algebraic structure where the operation combines elements to produce another element within the same set, and for which the order in which the elements are taken is very important. Consider the semantic composition and decomposition tasks (Turney 2014) as a concrete example. The first task involves understanding the meaning of a text by composing the meanings of the individual words in this text, and the second involves understanding the meaning of an individual word by decomposing it into various aspects that are latent in the word’s meaning. For example, given a noun-modifier bigram ‘x y’, with ‘x’ the head noun and ‘y’ the noun or adjective, the semantic composition task can be to find a noun unigram ‘z’ in the vocabulary which is a synonym of ‘x y’. Conversely, the semantic decomposition can be to find a bigram ‘x y’ synonym to a given ‘z’ from the vocabulary. Examples of (x y, z) are (presidential term, presidency), (electrical power, wattage), (milk sugar, lactose), (bass fiddle, contrabass), etc. This kind of problem is often solved by optimizing arg​max𝐳⁡g​(f⁡(𝐱,𝐲),𝐳)\argmax_{\mathbf{z}}g(f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}),\mathbf{z}), where 𝐱\mathbf{x}, 𝐲\mathbf{y} and 𝐳\mathbf{z} are vectors representing the words ‘x’, ‘y’ and ‘z’; ff a function representing ‘x y’ from 𝐱\mathbf{x} and 𝐲\mathbf{y}; and gg a measure of similarity. Using a symmetric ff is common, such as f⁡(𝐱,𝐲)=𝐱+𝐲f(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y}, but they are order independent and gives the same representation to ‘x y’ and ‘y x’, so that, for example, “good morning” == “morning good” under ff. Landauer 2002 estimates that 80%80\% of the meaning of English text comes from word choice, and the remaining 20%20\% comes from word order. Therefore, methods like vector addition, which do not account for word order, potentially overlook at least 20%20\% of the meaning in a bigram (Turney 2014). So, the order of words affects the meaning; “good morning” conveys a different sentiment and usage than “morning good”. For associativity, when combining more than two words, the order in which they are combined can affect the resulting meaning. For example, combining words in the phrase “old country house” can yield different interpretations based on which words are combined first.

Contributions

Our contributions are fourfold:

  • •

    Leveraging the fact that any tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} defines an nn-dimensional algebra over a field 𝔽\mathbb{F} (n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA), with associativity, commutativity, and unitality encoded as tensor identities, and matrix representations characterized by explicit tensor constraints; we establishe the equivalence between 𝔽n×n×n\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} and all n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA, allowing us to focus on structure tensors rather than abstract algebras.

  • •

    We show that prior work on grokking in groups (e.g., (Nanda et al. 2023), (Chughtai et al. 2023)) is a special case of our tensorial framework, which naturally extends to non-associative, non-commutative, and non-unital algebras.

  • •

    We connect FDA learning over ℝ\mathbb{R} to matrix factorization, while over finite fields grokking emerges when models learn explicit embeddings of FDA elements.

  • •

    We provide the first systematic study of grokking beyond groups, showing that algebraic constraints (associativity, commutativity, unitality) and structural features of the structure tensor (sparsity, rank) significantly affect grokking delay and sample complexity, and that generalization coincides with the emergence of algebra-consistent representations in model layers11 1 The code to reproduce all figures is available at https://github.com/Tikquuss/grokking_fda..

Related Work

On finite groups like ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} and SnS_{n}, it has been shown that models like Transformers grok by recovering the representation of the group itself (Gromov 2023; Nanda et al. 2023; Chughtai et al. 2023; Stander et al. 2024). On the algorithmic task (Power et al. 2022), Liu et al. 2022 shows representation learning to be the main underlying factor of the existence of generalizing solutions for modular arithmetic, supporting Power et al. 2022’s preliminary observations. Gromov 2023 write out the exact-form expression of the weights of a 2-layer MLP (with activation function x↦x2x\mapsto x^{2}) that yield 100%100\% accuracy on modular addition. Nanda et al. 2023 write out the closed-form solution of final trained weights in the case of a one-layer transformer trained on the same task, which is also made of sinusoids as in (Gromov 2023). Chughtai et al. 2023 reverse engineer (small) neural networks learning finite group composition via mathematical representation theory. Stander et al. 2024 do the same, with the focus on composition in the symmetric group S5S_{5}.

To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study grokking in the general setting of FDAs. Prior work on grokking studies algorithmic tasks almost exclusively through group operations. These structures enforce a rigid bundle of properties (associativity, unitality, etc), making it impossible to isolate which algebraic traits influence grokking and whether these properties generalize beyond groups. Our FDA framework provides the first setting in which all previously studied group tasks embed naturally, and non-unital and non-associative operations become accessible. Our experiments show, for instance, that associativity, commutativity, and unitality each induce distinct grokking delays and generalization patterns, and that these patterns persist across all the algebras sampled from each regime.

Structure of the document

Section 2 introduces the structure-tensor view of FDA, characterizes algebraic properties as tensor identities, and provides a criterion for matrix representations. Section 3 shows how the framework subsumes groups, and Section 4 presents the learning formulation together with its theoretical motivation. Experimental results and discussion are given in Section 5 and Section 6, respectively, before concluding in Section 7.

Notations

For n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, [n]:={1,…,n}[n]:=\{1,\dots,n\}. For 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, vec⁡(𝐀)∈ℝm​n\vect(\mathbf{A})\in\mathbb{R}^{mn} denotes the vector obtained by stacking the columns of 𝐀\mathbf{A}. The iith row and column of 𝐀\mathbf{A} are denoted by 𝐀i,:\mathbf{A}_{i,:} (or 𝐀i\mathbf{A}_{i}) and 𝐀:,i\mathbf{A}_{:,i}, respectively. This notation extends naturally to tensor slices. We denote by ⊙\odot the Hadamard product, ⊗\otimes the Kronecker product, ⋆\star the Khatri–Rao product, ∙\bullet the face-splitting product, and ×n\times_{n} the mode-nn tensor–vector product (Kolda & Bader 2009).

2 Finite Dimensional Algebra

In this section, we work with standard notions from FDA and adopt a concrete tensorial viewpoint. Fixing a basis, any nn-dimensional algebra is identified with a structure tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n}. This formulation provides a unified and operational description of algebraic structure that is directly compatible with our setting. In particular, it allows us to treat 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} as a concrete object that can be compared with learned representations, forming the basis for the alignment perspective developed later in the paper.

2.1 Definitions

An algebra 𝔄\mathfrak{A} over a field (𝔽,+,∗)(\mathbb{F},+,*) is a vector space equipped with a 𝔽\mathbb{F}-bilinear product ⋅:𝔄×𝔄→𝔄\cdot:\mathfrak{A}\times\mathfrak{A}\to\mathfrak{A} such that (𝐮+𝐯)⋅𝐰=𝐮⋅𝐰+𝐯⋅𝐰(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w} (right distributivity), 𝐰⋅(𝐮+𝐯)=𝐰⋅𝐮+𝐰⋅𝐯\mathbf{w}\cdot(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{v} (left distributivity) and (α​𝐮)⋅(β​𝐯)=(α∗β)​(𝐮⋅𝐯)(\alpha\mathbf{u})\cdot(\beta\mathbf{v})=(\alpha*\beta)(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) (compatibility with scalars) for all 𝐮,𝐯,𝐰∈𝔄\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{A} and α,β∈𝔽\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}. When ⋅\cdot is associative (resp. commutative), 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is said to be associative (resp. commutative). When there exists an element 1𝔄∈𝔄1_{\mathfrak{A}}\in\mathfrak{A} such that 1𝔄⋅𝐮=𝐮⋅1𝔄=𝐮​∀𝐮∈𝔄1_{\mathfrak{A}}\cdot\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}\cdot 1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathbf{u}\ \forall\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A}, 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is said to be unital. The dimension of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is its dimension as a 𝔽\mathbb{F}-vector space, denoted by dim𝔽​𝔄\text{dim}_{\mathbb{F}}\mathfrak{A}. We say that 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is finite-dimensional if n=dim𝔽​𝔄n=\text{dim}_{\mathbb{F}}\mathfrak{A} is finite. This means that there exists a finite basis {𝐚(i)}i∈[n]\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} (as a vector space over 𝔽\mathbb{F}) such that for every 𝐮∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A}, 𝐮=∑i=1nαi​𝐚(i)\mathbf{u}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)} with αi∈𝔽\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{F}.

Let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) and (𝔅,×)(\mathfrak{B},\times) be two 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebras. A homomorphism of 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebras ϕ:𝔄→𝔅\phi:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathfrak{B} is a 𝔽\mathbb{F}-linear map satisfying ϕ⁡(𝐮⋅𝐯)=ϕ⁡(𝐮)×ϕ⁡(𝐯)\phi(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})=\phi(\mathbf{u})\times\phi(\mathbf{v}) for all 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔄\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{A}; and ϕ⁡(1𝔄)=1𝔅\phi(1_{\mathfrak{A}})=1_{\mathfrak{B}} when 𝔄\mathfrak{A} and 𝔅\mathfrak{B} are unitals. This homomorphism ϕ\phi is called an isomorphism if it is bijective. Two 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebras 𝔄\mathfrak{A} and 𝔅\mathfrak{B} are isomorphic if there exists an algebra isomorphism ϕ:𝔄→𝔅\phi:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathfrak{B} between them. In other words, 𝔄\mathfrak{A} and 𝔅\mathfrak{B} may look different at the level of their elements or chosen bases, but they share exactly the same algebraic structure.

In the following, 𝔽\mathbb{F}-FDA means FDA over the field 𝔽\mathbb{F}, and n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA means 𝔽\mathbb{F}-FDA of dimension nn.

2.2 Structure Constants of FDA

Let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) be an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA and B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} a basis of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}. The structure of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in BB is entirely captured by the tensor 𝓒(B)∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} defined by 𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j)=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k(B)​𝐚(k)\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}^{(B)}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}. The entries of 𝓒(B)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)} are called structure coefficients/constants of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in BB. We will call the tensor 𝓒(B)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)} the structure tensor of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in the basis BB, and when the context is clear, we will omit BB from the notation. That said, we have for all 𝐮=∑i=1n𝐮i​𝐚(i)\mathbf{u}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)} and 𝐯=∑i=1n𝐯i​𝐚(i)\mathbf{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{v}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)} in 𝔄\mathfrak{A}, 𝐮⋅𝐯=∑k=1n(𝓒×1𝐮×2𝐯)k𝐚(k)\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}\right)_{k}\mathbf{a}^{(k)} with

𝓒×1𝐮×2𝐯:=[𝐮⊤𝓒:,:,k𝐯]k∈[n]⊤=𝓒(3)(𝐯⊗𝐮)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}:=\left[\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{:,:,k}\mathbf{v}\right]_{k\in[n]}^{\top}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(3)}\left(\mathbf{v}\otimes\mathbf{u}\right) (1)

In this equation, 𝓒(3)∈𝔽n×n2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(3)}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n^{2}} is the mode-3 unfolding of 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}: (𝓒(3))k,:=vec(𝓒:,:,k)∈𝔽n2∀k∈[n]\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(3)}\right)_{k,:}=\vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{:,:,k})\in\mathbb{F}^{n^{2}}\ \forall k\in[n].

Example 2.1.

The complex numbers ℂ=(ℝ2,⋅)\mathbb{C}=\left(\mathbb{R}^{2},\cdot\right) can be seen as a 2​ℝ2\mathbb{R}-FDA, with the product ⋅\cdot defined as (a+b​𝐢)⋅(c+d​𝐢)=(a​c−b​d)+(a​d+b​c)​𝐢(a+b\mathbf{i})\cdot(c+d\mathbf{i})=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)\mathbf{i}, where 𝐢2=−1\mathbf{i}^{2}=-1. The structure tensor of ℂ\mathbb{C} in (𝐚(1),𝐚(2))≡(1,𝐢)(\mathbf{a}^{(1)},\mathbf{a}^{(2)})\equiv(1,\mathbf{i}) is

[𝓒111𝓒112𝓒121𝓒122],[𝓒211𝓒212𝓒221𝓒222]=[1001],[01−10]\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{111}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{112}\\ \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{121}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{122}\\ \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{211}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{212}\\ \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{221}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{222}\\ \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\\ \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\\ \end{bmatrix} (2)

In the field 𝔽=𝔽p:=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_{p}:=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} for pp prime (or power of prime), we have 𝐢2=(−1)modp=p−1\mathbf{i}^{2}=(-1)\mod p=p-1 instead, so 𝓒221=p−1\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{221}=p-1 (the other coefficients remain unchanged).

One may ask whether every tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} defines an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA. If this holds, then one could in principle sample the entries of 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} over 𝔽\mathbb{F} and study the resulting algebra through the properties of its structure tensor. The following proposition shows that analyzing the space 𝔽n×n×n\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} is equivalent to studying all n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA. What remains open, however, is how to sample 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} in a principled way so as to obtain meaningful and general insights about the phenomena of interest. We return to this issue in Section 4.

Proposition 2.1.

For all 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n}, there exists an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA whose structure tensor is 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} in some basis. Moreover, all algebras that have 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} as a structure tensor in one of their bases are isomorphic to each other.

The proof of this proposition is constructive. We define on the vector space 𝔽n\mathbb{F}^{n} the bilinear map 𝐮×𝐯=𝓒×1𝐮×2𝐯\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}, and show that (𝔽n,×)(\mathbb{F}^{n},\times) is an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA with structure tensor 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} in the canonical basis {𝐞(i)}i∈[n]\{\mathbf{e}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}, 𝐞j(i)=δi​j\mathbf{e}^{(i)}_{j}=\delta_{ij} (Lemma B.1). We call this algebra the algebra generated by 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}, and denote it 𝔽⁡[𝓒]\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}]. We then show that 𝔽⁡[𝓒]\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}] is isomorphic to any n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA whose structure tensor is 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} in some basis (Lemma B.2). Although any 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} defines an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA, a key question is how the algebraic properties of (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) are reflected in 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}. The following proposition makes this connection explicit by characterizing associativity, commutativity, and unitality in terms of tensor equations.

An n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) with structure tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} in the basis B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} is

    associative if and only if ∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓒k​l​m=∑k=1n𝓒i​k​m​𝓒j​l​k​∀i,j,l,m∈[n]\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{klm}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ikm}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{jlk}\ \forall i,j,l,m\in[n];

In that case, λ\lambda is unique and 1𝔄=∑i=1nλi​𝐚(i)1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}.

2.3 Representations of FDA

For m∈ℕ∗m\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, let ℳm​(𝔽)\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) denote the set of all m×mm\times m matrices over 𝔽\mathbb{F}, which is an m2​𝔽m^{2}\mathbb{F}-FDA under standard matrix multiplication. A representation of dimension mm of a 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebra (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) involves a homomorphism ρ:𝔄→ℳm​(𝔽)\rho:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) such that ρ⁡(α​𝐮+β​𝐯)=α​ρ​(𝐮)+β​ρ​(𝐯)\rho(\alpha\mathbf{u}+\beta\mathbf{v})=\alpha\rho(\mathbf{u})+\beta\rho(\mathbf{v}) and ρ⁡(𝐮⋅𝐯)=ρ⁡(𝐮)​ρ​(𝐯)\rho(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})=\rho(\mathbf{u})\rho(\mathbf{v}) for all 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔄\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{A} and α,β∈𝔽\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}. If 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is unital, it is further required that ρ⁡(1𝔄)=𝕀m\rho(1_{\mathfrak{A}})=\mathbb{I}_{m}. The following proposition characterizes when such a representation exists in terms of the structure tensor.

Proposition 2.3.

Let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) be an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA with structure tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} in B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}. Fix m∈ℕ∗m\in\mathbb{N}^{*} and 𝓡∈𝔽n×m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times m\times m}. Set 𝓡k=𝓡k,:,:∈𝔽m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k,:,:}\in\mathbb{F}^{m\times m} for all k∈[n]k\in[n]. The linear map ρ:𝔄→ℳm​(𝔽)\rho:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) defined by ρ⁡(∑k=1nαk​𝐚(k)):=∑k=1nαk​𝓡k​∀α∈𝔽n\rho\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right):=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\ \forall\alpha\in\mathbb{F}^{n} is a representation of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} if and only if

𝓡i​𝓡j=∑k𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k∀i,j∈[n]\begin{array}[]{ll}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\sum_{k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\quad\forall i,j\in[n]\end{array} (3)

and, if 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is unital with 1𝔄=∑iλi​𝐚(i)1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}, ∑iλi​𝓡i=𝕀m\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{m}.

See Proposition B.16. ∎

Example 2.2.

With the algebra of complex numbers in 𝔽=ℝ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}, the defining relations for (𝐚(1),𝐚(2))=(1,𝐢)(\mathbf{a}^{(1)},\mathbf{a}^{(2)})=(1,\mathbf{i}) are 𝓡12=𝓡1,𝓡1​𝓡2=𝓡2​𝓡1=𝓡2,𝓡22=−𝓡1\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}^{2}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1},\ \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2},\ \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}^{2}=-\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}; together with 𝓡1=𝕀m​ since ​1𝔄=𝐚(1)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}=\mathbb{I}_{m}\text{ since }1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathbf{a}^{(1)}. Hence 𝓡22=−𝕀m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}^{2}=-\mathbb{I}_{m}, which forces mm to be even. Writing m=2​km=2k, the general solution is 𝓡2=𝐒⁡(𝕀k⊗𝓒2⊤)​𝐒−1​∀𝐒∈GLm​(ℝ)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}=\mathbf{S}(\mathbb{I}_{k}\otimes\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}^{\top})\mathbf{S}^{-1}\ \forall\mathbf{S}\in\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{R}), with GLm​(ℝ)\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{R}) the general linear group, and 𝓒2⊤=[[0−1],[10]]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}\end{bmatrix} (the standard real representation of multiplication by 𝐢\mathbf{i}). In 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, 𝓡22=−𝕀m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}^{2}=-\mathbb{I}_{m} becomes 𝓡22=(p−1)​𝕀m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}^{2}=(p-1)\mathbb{I}_{m}. There is no parity restriction on mm, and a convenient normal form is 𝓡2=(p−1)1/2​𝐒​diag⁡(ϵ)​𝐒−1​∀𝐒∈GLm​(ℝ),ϵ∈{±1}m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}=(p-1)^{1/2}\mathbf{S}\diag\big(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\big)\mathbf{S}^{-1}\ \forall\mathbf{S}\in\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{R}),\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\in\{\pm 1\}^{m}.

It is worth asking, for a given 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n}, what is the smallest mm (or the values of mm) for which the system of equations (3) admits a non-trivial solution. This question amounts to determining the minimal dimension of a faithful representation of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}, which is a classical but non-trivial problem in representation theory. For associatives n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA, this smallest mm is less than or equal to nn (Proposition B.18). Since our goal in Section 5 is to investigate whether neural networks trained on data from 𝔄=𝔽⁡[𝓒]\mathfrak{A}=\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}] implicitly learn such representations, we do not attempt to solve the minimality problem here. Instead, we will assume a sufficiently large mm so that the system can be solvable and concentrate on analyzing how the learned embedding dimension relates to the properties of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} and its structure tensor.

3 From Groups to FDA

We show in this section that group learning is a special case of FDA learning. In fact, the study of grokking in groups naturally extends to algebras through their structure tensors. To see this, consider a finite group (G,∘)(G,\circ) with nn elements {gi}i∈[n]\{g_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}. One can construct the Cayley table of the group as a matrix 𝐀∈Gn×n\mathbf{A}\in G^{n\times n}, where each entry is given by 𝐀i​j=gi∘gj,∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{A}_{ij}=g_{i}\circ g_{j},\ \forall i,j\in[n]. This table contains n2n^{2} operations, which are then randomly partitioned into two disjoint non-empty subsets, a training set and a test set (Power et al. 2022). More precisely, the model is trained to predict Ψ⁡(gi∘gj)\Psi(g_{i}\circ g_{j}) given Ψ⁡(gi)\Psi(g_{i}) and Ψ⁡(gj)\Psi(g_{j}), with Ψ:G→{0,1}n\Psi:G\to\{0,1\}^{n} the one-hot encoding defined on GG, Ψ⁡(gi):=[𝟙⁡(gk=gi)]k∈[n]∈{0,1}n​∀i∈[n]\Psi(g_{i}):=\left[\mathbb{1}(g_{k}=g_{i})\right]_{k\in[n]}\in\{0,1\}^{n}\ \forall i\in[n], 𝟙\mathbb{1} the indicator function.

Now, for a field 𝔽\mathbb{F}, define the set 𝔽⁡[G]:={∑i=1nαi​𝐚(i)∣α∈𝔽n}\mathbb{F}[G]:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\ \mid\ \alpha\in\mathbb{F}^{n}\right\}, where 𝐚(i)=Ψ⁡(gi)∈{0𝔽,1𝔽}n​∀i∈[n]\mathbf{a}^{(i)}=\Psi(g_{i})\in\{0_{\mathbb{F}},1_{\mathbb{F}}\}^{n}\ \forall i\in[n]. For all 𝐮=∑i𝐮i​𝐚(i)\mathbf{u}=\sum_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)} and 𝐯=∑j𝐯j​𝐚(j)\mathbf{v}=\sum_{j}\mathbf{v}_{j}\mathbf{a}^{(j)} in 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G], let 𝐮⋅𝐯:=∑i,j𝐮i​𝐯j​Ψ​(gi∘gj)=∑k(∑i,j𝐮i​𝐯j​𝟙​(gi∘gj=gk))​𝐚(k)\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}:=\sum_{i,j}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\Psi\left(g_{i}\circ g_{j}\right)=\sum_{k}\left(\sum_{i,j}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\mathbb{1}(g_{i}\circ g_{j}=g_{k})\right)\mathbf{a}^{(k)}. The following proposition shows that (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot) is an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA, and that training a model on the group (G,∘)(G,\circ) is equivalent to training it on the multiplication in (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot). In fact, applying the encoding Ψ\Psi to each entry of the Cayley table 𝐀\mathbf{A} of GG directly yields the structure tensor 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} of (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot) in B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}. Therefore, any framework developed for algebras already subsumes the case of groups. In particular, by investigating grokking in algebras, we not only extend the scope of previous studies but also recover them as a special case.

Proposition 3.1.

For a finite group (G,∘)(G,\circ) with nn elements {gi}i∈[n]\{g_{i}\}_{i\in[n]} and identity ee, (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot) is an nn-dimensional associative and unital 𝔽\mathbb{F}-FDA with 1𝔽⁡[G]=Ψ⁡(e)1_{\mathbb{F}[G]}=\Psi(e). Also, (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot) is commutative if and only if GG is commutative. Moreover, the structure tensor of 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G] in B={Ψ⁡(gi)}i∈[n]B=\{\Psi(g_{i})\}_{i\in[n]} is given by 𝓒i​j​k=𝟙𝔽​(gi∘gj=gk)​∀i,j,k∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb{F}}(g_{i}\circ g_{j}=g_{k})\ \forall i,j,k\in[n]; and we have Ψ(gi∘gj)=𝓒×1Ψ(gi)×2Ψ(gj)∀i,j∈[n]\Psi(g_{i}\circ g_{j})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\Psi(g_{i})\times_{2}\Psi(g_{j})\ \forall i,j\in[n].

Proof.

See Proposition B.10. ∎

4 Learning Finite Dimensional Algebra

In this section, we study supervised learning of multiplication in a finite-dimensional algebra (FDA). We show in the previous section that any nn-dimensional FDA 𝔄\mathfrak{A} over a field 𝔽\mathbb{F} with structure tensor 𝓒∗∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} is isomorphic to 𝔽n\mathbb{F}^{n} endowed with the bilinear product (𝐮,𝐯)↦𝓒∗×1𝐮×2𝐯∈𝔽n(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\mapsto\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{F}^{n} (Proposition 2.1). Given inputs 𝐱=(𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔽n×𝔽n\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathbb{F}^{n}\times\mathbb{F}^{n}, the supervised target is 𝐲∗(𝐱)=𝓒∗×1𝐮×2𝐯\mathbf{y}^{*}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}. The structure of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} (e.g., rank, sparsity pattern) is inherited from 𝔄\mathfrak{A} and can shape both sample complexity and the dynamics of generalization. We propose to investigate how these properties impact generalization and the underlying mechanism by which they do so.

4.1 Grokking Regimes in FDAs

Liu et al. 2023 argue that grokking arises when task performance hinges on learning a useful representation. For algorithmic data (Power et al. 2022), representation quality typically determines all-or-nothing accuracy (random guess vs. 100%100\%), while on natural data (e.g., MNIST) representation quality may separate 95%95\% from 100%100\% accuracy. In our setting, this viewpoint yields a concrete mechanism: for a finite-field FDA (𝔽=𝔽p=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_{p}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}, pp prime), treat 𝔄\mathfrak{A} as a vocabulary, index each element 𝐮∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A} by ⟨𝐮⟩∈[q]\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle\in[q] with q=|𝔄|q=|\mathfrak{A}|, and learn an embedding matrix 𝐄∈ℝq×d\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times d} so that 𝐄⟨𝐮⟩\mathbf{E}_{\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle} is the trainable vector attached to 𝐮\mathbf{u}. Grokking corresponds to the point at which 𝐄\mathbf{E} and the downstream layers collectively represent the algebra, so a simple linear readout recovers the correct output token.

By contrast, for 𝔽=ℝ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}, a model that operates directly on (𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔽n×𝔽n(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathbb{F}^{n}\times\mathbb{F}^{n} and parameterizes a (bi)linear map can often fit without a prolonged representation-formation phase; grokking (in the strict “delayed generalization after memorization” sense) typically requires being induced via, e.g., large-scale initialization with small weight decay (Liu et al. 2023; Lyu et al. 2024) or by strongly misaligning the Neural Tangent Kernel with the target (Kumar et al. 2024). Moreover, Levi et al. 2024 and Notsawo et al. 2025 document cases of “grokking without understanding”: a sharp decrease in the test error during training, driven by changes in the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm of the model parameters, but that does not result in convergence to an optimal solution.

From this analysis, we distinguish ℝ\mathbb{R} from 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}. The present paper focuses on the finite-field setting, where representation learning is intrinsic and grokking phenomena are most salient (Figure 1). We include a concise treatment of the real case below, where learning reduces to a linear inverse problem where explicit or implicit low-rank bias governs recovery, and defer rank/coherence details to the supplement.

4.2 A Linear Inverse View for 𝔽=ℝ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}

Let 𝐔,𝐕,𝐘∈𝔽N×n\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathbf{Y}\in\mathbb{F}^{N\times n} be such that for each s∈[N]s\in[N], 𝐘s=𝓒∗×1𝐔s×2𝐕s=𝓒(3)∗(𝐕s⊗𝐔s)\mathbf{Y}_{s}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{s}\times_{2}\mathbf{V}_{s}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}_{(3)}\!\left(\mathbf{V}_{s}\otimes\mathbf{U}_{s}\right). Stacking gives 𝐘=𝐗​𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)} with design 𝐗:=𝐕∙𝐔∈ℝN×n2\mathbf{X}:=\mathbf{V}\bullet\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times n^{2}}, where ∙\bullet is the face-splitting product (𝐗s=𝐕s⊗𝐔s\mathbf{X}_{s}=\mathbf{V}_{s}\otimes\mathbf{U}_{s}). We recall that 𝐘s\mathbf{Y}_{s} is the ssth row of 𝐘\mathbf{Y} treated as a column vector, same thing for 𝐔s\mathbf{U}_{s} and 𝐕s\mathbf{V}_{s}. Finding another structure tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} such that 𝐘s=𝓒×1𝐔s×2𝐕s∀s∈[N]\mathbf{Y}_{s}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{s}\times_{2}\mathbf{V}_{s}\ \forall s\in[N] is equivalent to solving the following linear equation in 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}};

𝐗​𝓒(3)⊤=𝐘=𝐗​𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤⟺𝐌𝐛=vec⁡(𝐘)=𝐌𝐛∗\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{\top}_{(3)}=\mathbf{Y}=\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)}\Longleftrightarrow\mathbf{M}\mathbf{b}=\vect(\mathbf{Y})=\mathbf{M}\mathbf{b}^{*} (4)

with 𝐌:=𝕀n⊗𝐗∈𝔽N​n×n3\mathbf{M}:=\mathbb{I}_{n}\otimes\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{F}^{Nn\times n^{3}} and 𝐛:=vec⁡(𝓒(3)⊤)∈𝔽n3\mathbf{b}:=\vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{\top}_{(3)})\in\mathbb{F}^{n^{3}}, similarly for 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*}. This problem can be viewed as a matrix factorization problem with matrix 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤∈𝔽n2×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)}\in\mathbb{F}^{n^{2}\times n} and measurement (𝐔,𝐕)(\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}), or a compressed sensing problem with signal 𝐛∗\mathbf{b}^{*} and measurement 𝐌\mathbf{M}. Thus, learning 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} from (𝐔,𝐕,𝐘)(\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V},\mathbf{Y}) is a linear inverse problem whose identifiability and sample complexity are governed by the conditioning of 𝐗=𝐕∙𝐔\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{V}\bullet\mathbf{U} vis-à-vis the signal 𝓒(3)∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}_{(3)}, and the effective low-rank structure of 𝓒(3)∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}_{(3)}. A convenient parameterization is a linear network 𝓒⊤(3)=𝐖(L)⋯𝐖(1)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{\top}_{(3)}=\mathbf{W}^{(L)}\cdots\mathbf{W}^{(1)} with 𝐖(L)∈ℝn2×d\mathbf{W}^{(L)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}\times d}, 𝐖(i)∈ℝd×d\mathbf{W}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} (1<i<L1<i<L), and 𝐖(1)∈ℝd×n\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}. For L=1L=1, explicit low-rank regularization (e.g., nuclear norm) or appropriate sparsity penalties may be necessary when NN is sufficiently large (Candès & Tao 2010; Notsawo et al. 2025). For L≥2L\geq 2, gradient descent exhibits an implicit bias toward low-rank solutions, enabling accurate recovery without explicit regularization in many regimes (Gunasekar et al. 2017; Arora et al. 2018; Arora et al. 2019; Gidel et al. 2019; Gissin et al. 2019; Razin & Cohen 2020; Li et al. 2020). Beyond rank, recovery depends on coherence of the left/right singular subspaces of 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)} with the measurement matrix 𝐗\mathbf{X} (Candès & Tao 2010; Candes & Recht 2012; Chen et al. 2014). We summarize these implications for Equation  (4) in Section C.1.

While Equation (4) makes it straightforward to study recovery as a function of properties of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}, the same is not true for the induced algebra ℝ⁡[𝓒∗]=(ℝn,×)\mathbb{R}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}]=(\mathbb{R}^{n},\times). Associativity, commutativity, and unitality correspond to polynomial constraints of measure zero in ℝn3\mathbb{R}^{n^{3}} (Proposition 2.2). Thus, a randomly sampled 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} almost surely defines a degenerate non-associative, non-commutative, non-unital product. This makes principled empirical study over ℝ\mathbb{R} difficult22 2 This limitation is a property of the algebraic landscape over ℝ\mathbb{R}, not our tensorial framework, which simply makes it explicit. Structured (e.g., unital) n​ℝn\mathbb{R}-FDA form a measure-zero subset among the set of all possible n​ℝn\mathbb{R}-FDA. Thus, random sampling yields almost always degenerate algebras. and motivates our focus on finite fields, where structured algebras occur with non-negligible probability.

4.3 Finite Fields 𝔽=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}

Over 𝔽=𝔽p\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_{p}, algebraic properties have positive density. For moderate (n,p)(n,p), the space of possibilities (pn3p^{n^{3}} tensors) is finite and can be systematically explored and stratified by properties such as associativity, commutativity, and unitality. Our experimental program is thus: (i) vary algebraic properties of 𝔽p​[𝓒∗]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}] and measure their effect on grokking delay and generalization; (ii) study how structural features of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} shape learning dynamics; and (iii) probe whether models learn algebraic representations during training.

5 Experiments and Results

5.1 Experiment Setup

From now on, we work over the finite field 𝔽=𝔽p\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_{p} (prime pp). Identify 𝔄≡𝔽n\mathfrak{A}\equiv\mathbb{F}^{n} and set q:=|𝔄|=pnq:=|\mathfrak{A}|=p^{n}. Each element 𝐮∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A} is treated as a vocabulary symbol with index ⟨𝐮⟩∈[q]\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle\in[q]. The models we use will associate to each of these symbols a trainable vector 𝐄⟨𝐮⟩∈ℝd\mathbf{E}_{\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, with 𝐄∈ℝV×d\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}, V=q+2V=q+2 the vocabulary size, 22 for the special tokens 𝒮={×,=}\mathcal{S}=\left\{\times,\texttt{=}\right\}.

We train the model using a classification approach. The logits for 𝐱=(𝐮,×,𝐯,=)\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{u},\times,\mathbf{v},\texttt{=}) with (𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔄2(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathfrak{A}^{2} are given by yθ​(𝐱)=φ⁡(ϕ⁡(𝐄⟨𝐮⟩⊕𝐄⟨×⟩⊕𝐄⟨𝐯⟩⊕𝐄⟨=⟩))∈ℝqy_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\varphi\left(\phi\left(\mathbf{E}_{\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle}\oplus\mathbf{E}_{\langle\times\rangle}\oplus\mathbf{E}_{\langle\mathbf{v}\rangle}\oplus\mathbf{E}_{\langle\texttt{=}\rangle}\right)\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{q}, where ⊕\oplus is the vector concatenation, ϕ\phi the encoder and φ\varphi the classifier33 3 The tokens ×\times and = are not strictly necessary. Training the classifier on the simpler input pair (𝐮,𝐯)(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) yields qualitatively identical conclusions. We included for consistency with the formulation in (Power et al. 2022), but the results do not rely on them.. The dataset 𝒟={((𝐮,×,𝐯,=),𝐲∗(𝐮,𝐯)∣(𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔄2}\mathcal{D}=\{((\mathbf{u},\times,\mathbf{v},\texttt{=}),\mathbf{y}^{*}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\mid(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathfrak{A}^{2}\} is randomly partitioned into two disjoint and non-empty sets 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}} and 𝒟test\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}, the training and the validation dataset respectively, following a ratio r:=|𝒟train|/|𝒟|∈(0,1]r:=|\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}|/|\mathcal{D}|\in(0,1], which allows us to interpolate between different data-availability regimes. The models are trained to minimize the average cross-entropy loss ℒtrain​(θ)=∑(𝐱,𝐲∗)∈𝒟trainℓ⁡(yθ​(𝐱),⟨𝐲∗⟩)\mathcal{L}_{\text{train}}(\theta)=\sum_{(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}^{*})\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}}\ell\left(y_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}),\langle\mathbf{y}^{*}\rangle\right), with ℓ⁡(𝐲,i)=−𝐲i+log⁡(∑jexp⁡(𝐲j))​∀𝐲∈ℝq,i∈[q]\ell\left(\mathbf{y},i\right)=-\mathbf{y}_{i}+\log\left(\sum_{j}\exp\left(\mathbf{y}_{j}\right)\right)\ \forall\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{q},i\in[q]. We denoted by 𝒜train\mathcal{A}_{\text{train}} the corresponding accuracy (ℒtest\mathcal{L}_{\text{test}} and 𝒜test\mathcal{A}_{\text{test}} on 𝒟test\mathcal{D}_{\text{test}}).

We use a linear classifier φ⁡(𝐳)=𝐛+𝐖𝐳∈ℝq\varphi(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}. The learnable parameters θ\theta consist of 𝐄,𝐖,𝐛{\mathbf{E},\mathbf{W},\mathbf{b}} together with those of the encoder ϕ\phi. We consider three architectures for ϕ\phi: an MLP, an LSTM, and a Transformer (full details are provided in Appendix D). For clarity, we present mainly the MLP results and some Transformer results in the following section. Additional results, along with experimental details, are deferred to Appendix E.

5.2 Representation Learning

Over a finite alphabet, the model must construct a representation in which all q2q^{2} algebra products are linearly separable by the classifier head, q:=|𝔄|q:=|\mathfrak{A}|. Early training can memorize subsets of products via brittle lookup-like features; only after the embedding geometry aligns with the algebraic structure does linear decoding succeed on the full combinatorial support, producing the characteristic delayed generalization of grokking (Liu et al. 2023). To see this, assume that (𝔄,×)(\mathfrak{A},\times) has a group structure and let ρ:𝔄→ℝm×m\rho:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} be a faithful representation of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}. If the model 𝐱→𝐖​ϕ​(𝐱)\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{W}\phi(\mathbf{x}) encodes a pair 𝐱=(𝐮,𝐯)\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) as ϕ⁡(𝐱)=ρ⁡(𝐮×𝐯)\phi(\mathbf{x})=\rho(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}) and the linear classifier head stores the inverses ρ​(𝐰)−1​∀𝐰∈𝔄\rho(\mathbf{w})^{-1}\ \forall\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{A} in its weights, then the decoding rule recovers the correct product 𝐮×𝐯\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}. In other words, under these assumptions, the model is able to generalize to all inputs.

Proposition 5.1.

Assume that (𝔄,×)(\mathfrak{A},\times) has a group structure, and let ρ:𝔄→ℝm×m\rho:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} be a faithful matrix representation of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}. Suppose a model yθ​(𝐱)=𝐖​ϕ​(𝐱)∈ℝqy_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{W}\phi(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{q} encodes pairs 𝐱=(𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔄2\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathfrak{A}^{2} as ϕ⁡(𝐮,𝐯)=ρ⁡(𝐮×𝐯)\phi(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=\rho(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}) and decodes with a linear classifier parameterized by weights 𝐖∈ℝq×m2\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times m^{2}} containing ρ​(𝐰)−1\rho(\mathbf{w})^{-1} for each 𝐰∈𝔄\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{A}. Then the predicted label satisfies arg​maxi∈[q]⁡yθ​(𝐱)​[i]=𝐮×𝐯\argmax_{i\in[q]}y_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})[i]=\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}. As a consequence, the classifier linearly separates all qq outputs.

Proof.

See Proposition D.1. ∎

Thus, the classifier achieves exact decoding of the group product for all pairs (𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔄2(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathfrak{A}^{2} once the embedding geometry aligns with the group structure. Unfortunately, algebras do not have a group structure. However, in Proposition 2.3 we established a necessary and sufficient condition for verifying that a set of matrices represents an algebra, namely 𝓡i​𝓡j=∑k𝓒i​j​k∗​𝓡k​∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\sum_{k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\ \forall i,j\in[n]. By setting 𝐫(i)=vec⁡(𝓡i)∈𝔽m2​∀i∈[n]\mathbf{r}^{(i)}=\vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i})\in\mathbb{F}^{m^{2}}\ \forall i\in[n] and defining 𝐫(i)⋅𝐫(j):=vec⁡(𝓡i​𝓡j)=∑k𝓒i​j​k∗​𝐫(k)​∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{r}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{r}^{(j)}:=\vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j})=\sum_{k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}_{ijk}\mathbf{r}^{(k)}\ \forall i,j\in[n] in 𝔅:={∑i=1nαi​𝐫(i)∣α∈𝔽n}\mathfrak{B}:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}\mathbf{r}^{(i)}\mid\alpha\in\mathbb{F}^{n}\right\}, we obtain 𝐮⋅𝐯=𝔅𝓒∗×1𝐮×2𝐯∀𝐮,𝐯∈𝔅\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=_{\mathfrak{B}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}\ \forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{B}, where =𝔅=_{\mathfrak{B}} is the equality when expressed in basis. We performed linear probing to check whether such a structure emerges in the features learned by the models.

More precisely, let 𝐟(ℓ)​(𝐮)∈ℝm2\mathbf{f}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{u})\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}} and 𝐟(r)​(𝐮)∈ℝm2\mathbf{f}^{(r)}(\mathbf{u})\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}} denote the feature vectors produced by the model for 𝐮∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A} when 𝐮\mathbf{u} appears on the left and on the right of an equation (i.e. when appearing as the left/right operand), respectively; and let 𝐟⁡(𝐮)∈ℝm2\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}} denote the feature vector of 𝐮\mathbf{u} produced by the unembedding layer (the classifier). We want to determine whether there exists 𝓦∈ℝm2×m2×m2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}\times m^{2}\times m^{2}} such that 𝐟⁡(𝐮×𝐯)=𝐟^𝓦​(𝐮,𝐯)\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})=\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) for all 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔄\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{A}, where 𝐟^𝓦(𝐮,𝐯):=𝓦×1𝐟(ℓ)(𝐮)×2𝐟(r)(𝐯)\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}):=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{f}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{u})\times_{2}\mathbf{f}^{(r)}(\mathbf{v}) is a bilinear model parameterized by 𝓦\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}. We use the cosine similarity 𝒜rep=1|𝔄2|​∑(𝐮,𝐯)⟨𝐟⁡(𝐮×𝐯),𝐟^𝓦​(𝐮,𝐯)⟩/‖𝐟⁡(𝐮×𝐯)‖​‖𝐟^𝓦​(𝐮,𝐯)‖\mathcal{A}_{\text{rep}}=\frac{1}{|\mathfrak{A}^{2}|}\sum_{(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})}{\langle\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}),\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\rangle}/{\|\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\|\,\|\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\|} associated with solving this problem (i.e., finding 𝓦\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}) as a measure of how algebra-like structure emerges in the model’s feature space. The tensor 𝓦\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}} is obtained by minimizing a squared reconstruction error ∑(𝐮,𝐯)‖𝐟⁡(𝐮×𝐯)−𝐟^𝓦​(𝐮,𝐯)‖22\sum_{(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})}\left\|\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})-\hat{\mathbf{f}}_{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\right\|_{2}^{2}. This is solved using ordinary least squares with ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization (more details in Sections D.2.2 and E of the Appendix).

As shown in Figure 2, before grokking 𝒜rep\mathcal{A}_{\text{rep}} remains relatively low and then sharply increases as the model groks. Figure 3 plots 𝒜test\mathcal{A}_{\text{test}} as a function of 𝒜rep\mathcal{A}_{\text{rep}} across different model layers, training steps, and training dataset sizes. Each point is (𝒜rep(ℓ),𝒜test)(\mathcal{A}_{\text{rep}}^{(\ell)},\mathcal{A}_{\text{test}}) for a certain layer ℓ\ell. We observe that 𝒜test\mathcal{A}_{\text{test}} increases with 𝒜rep(ℓ)\mathcal{A}_{\text{rep}}^{(\ell)} in a low-data regime, showing that the emergence of algebra-consistent features directly facilitates generalization when data are scarce. For Figures 2 and  3, the algebra being learned is the algebra of complex numbers over 𝔽7\mathbb{F}_{7}.

5.3 The Properties of the FDA on Generalization

We demonstrate in this section how algebraic structure (e.g., associativity) influences sample complexity, memorization time, and learning dynamics. For now on, we denote by t2t_{2} (resp. t4t_{4}) the step at which the training (resp. test) accuracy first reaches ≈99%\approx 99\%.

With the structure tensor 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} of complex numbers in 𝔽=ℤ/7​ℤ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Z}/7\mathbb{Z} (Example 2.1), we observed that the model exhibits grokking (Figure 1), but in a manner highly sensitive to the specific entries of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}. A single random perturbation of one entry in 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} can dramatically reduce/increase the grokking delay (Figure 1). These observations suggest that the internal algebraic structure encoded by 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} exerts a direct influence on generalization.

Using (n,p)=(2,7)(n,p)=(2,7), we generate 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} in 𝔽pn×n×n\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n\times n\times n}. We have pn3=78=5764801p^{n^{3}}=7^{8}=5764801 possibilities for such 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}. Let aa=a​s​s​o​c​i​a​t​i​v​eassociative, cc=c​o​m​m​u​t​a​t​i​v​ecommutative, uu=u​n​i​t​a​lunital. We have the following 232^{3} possible categories : a​c​uacu, a​c​u¯ac\bar{u}, a​c¯​ua\bar{c}u, a¯​c​u\bar{a}cu, a​c¯​u¯a\bar{c}\bar{u}, a¯​c​u¯\bar{a}c\bar{u}, a¯​c¯​u\bar{a}\bar{c}u and a¯​c¯​u¯\bar{a}\bar{c}\bar{u}. The bar on top of the s​y​m​b​o​l​s¯\bar{symbols} represents negation, and the concatenation is the Boolean conjunction. For example, a​c​u¯ac\bar{u} represents the tensor algebras that are associative and commutative but non-unital. We obtain 996​(0.017%)​a​c​u996\ (0.017\%)\ acu, 1741​(0.03%)​a​c​u¯1741(0.03\%)\ ac\bar{u}, 0​(0.0%)​a​c¯​u0\ (0.0\%)\ a\bar{c}u, 0​(0.0%)​a¯​c​u0\ (0.0\%)\ \bar{a}cu, 96​(0.002%)​a​c¯​u¯96\ (0.002\%)\ a\bar{c}\bar{u}, 114912​(1.99%)​a¯​c​u¯114912\ (1.99\%)\ \bar{a}c\bar{u}, 0​(0.0%)​a¯​c¯​u0\ (0.0\%)\ \bar{a}\bar{c}u and 5647056​(97.958%)​a¯​c¯​u¯5647056\ (97.958\%)\ \bar{a}\bar{c}\bar{u}. We sampled 1010 tensors in each case (category). We varied r=|𝒟train|/|𝒟|r=|\mathcal{D}_{\text{train}}|/|\mathcal{D}| in {0.2,0.3,…,0.9}\{0.2,0.3,\dots,0.9\}. For each triplet (category,𝓒∗,r)(\texttt{category},\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*},r), we repeated the experiment twice.

Our results are summarized in Figures 4 (for the other values of rr, see Figure 14) and 5. We varied rr to show that algebra-dependent effects persist across regimes. Small rr leads to memorization; intermediate rr yields delayed generalization; and this delay decreases as r→1r\to 1. This matches known behavior on algorithmic tasks (Power et al. 2022; Notsawo Jr et al. 2023).

We can observe that a​c​u¯ac\bar{u} algebras are consistently the easiest to learn (in terms of shorter grokking time and stronger generalization after grokking, measured in terms of test loss), followed by a​c¯​u¯a\bar{c}\bar{u}, with the remaining categories showing almost indistinguishable behavior. This shows that the combination of non-unitality and associativity most strongly facilitates generalization. This finding is consistent with the previous discussion on representation learning. When the algebra is associative but non-unital (a​c¯​u¯a\bar{c}\bar{u} and a​c​u¯ac\bar{u}), it admits two trivial representations44 4 The probing from Section 5.2 on representation learning does not target any specific example of representation. It tests whether the model learns a representation that satisfies the constraints similar to those of Proposition 2.3, up to a linear transformation., the zero representation and left regular representation given by the tensor 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} itself, 𝓡i=𝓒i∗⁣⊤​∀i∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{i}\forall i\in[n] (Proposition B.18). Moreover, the representations constraints admit many solutions: if (𝓡i)i∈[n](\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i})_{i\in[n]} is a representation of dimension mm, then for any p≥mp\geq m and 𝐀∈𝔽p×m\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{F}^{p\times m}, 𝐁∈𝔽m×p\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{F}^{m\times p} with 𝐁𝐀=𝕀m\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}=\mathbb{I}_{m}, (𝐀​𝓡i​𝐁)i∈[n](\mathbf{A}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{B})_{i\in[n]} is also a representation (Proposition B.19). These provide simpler and more accessible solutions for the learning process, effectively lowering the complexity of the optimization landscape. In other words, removing the unit constraint allows the model to exploit “shortcuts” in the representation space, which explains why non-unital associative algebras generalize more quickly and grok earlier.

When the algebra is unital, the additional constraint ∑iλi​𝓡i=𝕀m\sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{m} must be satisfied by its representations (Proposition 2.3). This requirement adds equations without adding degrees of freedom, drastically shrinking the feasible set and eliminating many representations, and this typically delays convergence. In fact, it significantly restricts the solution space, since it forces the representation to encode an identity element across all transformations, thereby reducing the flexibility of optimization and leading to slower convergence. In representation theory, such unit constraints are well known to eliminate many otherwise valid low-dimensional representations, leaving only more rigid (and more complex to approximate) ones.

Among the two non-unital regimes (a​c​u¯ac\bar{u} and a​c¯​u¯a\bar{c}\bar{u}), commutativity makes a​c​u¯ac\bar{u} even easier from representation learning perspective because it reduces the number of equations in  (3) from n2n^{2} to n⁡(n+1)/2n(n+1)/2, because 𝓡i​𝓡j=∑k𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\sum_{k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k} and 𝓡j​𝓡i=∑k𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\sum_{k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k} represent the same equation under commutativity, for all i,ji,j. Another way to see this is to observe that the models have the form y⁡(𝐮,𝐯)=φ⁡(ϕ⁡(𝐮,𝐯))y(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=\varphi(\phi(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})), so that when ϕ\phi learns a representation ρ\rho of the FDA, i.e. ϕ⁡(𝐮,𝐯)=ρ⁡(𝐮×𝐯)​∀(𝐮,𝐯)\phi(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=\rho(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\ \forall(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}), then whenever 𝐮×𝐯=𝐮′×𝐯′\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u}^{\prime}\times\mathbf{v}^{\prime} we have identical predictions y⁡(𝐮,𝐯)=y⁡(𝐮′,𝐯′)y(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=y(\mathbf{u}^{\prime},\mathbf{v}^{\prime}). In a commutative FDA, 𝐮×𝐯=𝐯×𝐮\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}\times\mathbf{u}, so each product has two presentations (𝐮,𝐯)(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) and (𝐯,𝐮)(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{u}). Once the classifier predicts one ordering correctly, it also predicts the swapped one, effectively reducing the number of distinct outputs it must separate. This symmetry makes a​c​u¯ac\bar{u} easier than a​c¯​u¯a\bar{c}\bar{u} and yields earlier transitions.

5.4 The Properties of the Structure Tensor on Generalization

We focused in this section on the direct properties of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} that influence generalization. Indeed, while the algebraic constraints on the entries of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} required to ensure properties such as associativity are well understood, there are other structural characteristics of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} whose connection to the underlying algebra remains unclear, especially over finite fields. Here, we examined two such properties: the sparsity ss of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} and the rank r(3)r^{(3)} of the mode-3 unfolding 𝓒(3)∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}_{(3)}, motivated by our earlier discussion in the real-valued setting.

Our experiments show that both the test loss and the time to generalize increase with r(3)r^{(3)} and ss (Figure 6), indicating that higher complexity in these dimensions hinders efficient generalization. This is also true for other mode-unfolding (Figure 13). Note that the rank is basis-invariant (Corollary B.4) and reflects the intrinsic multilinear complexity of the operation, which we claim is why increasing rank leads to longer grokking delays. Sparsity, on the other hand, is not basis-invariant. It reflects a genuine “privileged basis” problem familiar in mechanistic interpretability (Olsson et al. 2022), as the neural network sees raw coordinates, and these coordinates implicitly privilege certain representations. Our experiments, therefore, treat sparsity as a task-dependent difficulty parameter, naturally associated with each algebraic example, in the canonical basis. Our empirical claim is therefore conditional on the canonical basis used.

6 Discussion and Limitations

In the case of the Transformer Encoder (Figure 2), 𝒜rep(ℓ)\mathcal{A}_{\text{rep}}^{(\ell)} does not change with 𝒜test\mathcal{A}_{\text{test}} for layer ℓ=0\ell=0, the embedding layer. At first glance, this result contradicts previous work on group operations (Power et al. 2022; Liu et al. 2022), for which an emergence of structure is observed in the model’s embedding layer as it groks. We believe this difference is due to the embedding and unembedding layers being shared. More specifically, for layer 0, we seek 𝓦\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}} such that 𝐟(𝐮×𝐯)=𝓦×1𝐟(𝐮)×2𝐟(𝐯)=𝓦(3)(𝐟(𝐯)⊗𝐟(𝐮))\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})\times_{2}\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}_{(3)}\big(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{v})\otimes\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})\big) for all 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔄\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{A}, where f:𝔄→ℝm2f:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}} is the embedding layer. The fact that 𝒜rep(0)\mathcal{A}_{\text{rep}}^{(0)} remains almost constant simply shows that such a structure does not emerge in our case, without ruling out the possibility that another structure might emerge, such as the emergence of low-rank embeddings. We leave further investigation for future works.

Also, restricting most experiments to n=2n=2 over 𝔽7\mathbb{F}_{7} limits the scope of the empirical evaluation. The space of possible structure tensors grows rapidly, with |𝔽pn×n×n|=pn3|\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n\times n\times n}|=p^{n^{3}}. As a result, exploring this space becomes computationally challenging even for moderate values of nn and pp. We therefore chose a reasonable (n,p)(n,p) to enable a controlled and systematic study of how algebraic properties affect generalization and grokking behavior. Figure 7 shows additional experiments with a non-trivial generalization delay on two associative, noncommutative, and unital (a​c¯​ua\bar{c}u) algebras: the matrix algebras (which arise when nn is a perfect square) and the upper triangular matrix algebra, which are not captured in the n=2n=2 setup. In fact, the minimum dimension nn to get an a​c¯​ua\bar{c}u algebra over any field 𝔽\mathbb{F} is 33 (Proposition B.7).

Several directions remain open. Theoretically, a tighter link between tensor properties (e.g., rank, coherence) and sample complexity is needed over finite fields. Empirically, scaling to larger algebras and probing real-world tasks with latent algebraic structure could further clarify when and why grokking occurs.

7 Conclusion

We introduced a tensorial framework for studying grokking in finite-dimensional algebras, showing that learning multiplication reduces to analyzing properties of structure tensors. This formulation recovers groups as a special case and extends grokking analysis to non-associative, non-commutative, and non-unital algebras. Our experiments demonstrate that algebraic constraints, such as unitality, do not always simplify learning and may even lengthen grokking delays, while structural properties, like sparsity or low rank, often accelerate generalization. We observe that test performance improves only once model layers align with the algebraic multiplication, reinforcing the view of grokking as a representational phase transition. These findings bridge classical algebra with modern learning theory: over real fields, FDA learning connects to low-rank matrix recovery, while over finite fields, grokking arises from the need to form internal representations.

Appendix A Notations and Useful Identities

We used the following standard notations.

  • •

    For n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, [n]:={1,…,n}[n]:=\{1,\dots,n\}. For m,n∈ℕm,n\in\mathbb{N} with m≥nm\geq n, ⟦n,m⟧:={n,n+1,⋯,m}\llbracket n,m\rrbracket:=\{n,n+1,\cdots,m\}.

  • •

    Scalars are denoted by lowercase letters, e.g., aa; vectors are denoted by boldface lowercase letters, e.g., 𝐚=[𝐚i]i\mathbf{a}=[\mathbf{a}_{i}]_{i}; matrices are denoted by boldface capital letters, e.g., 𝐀=[𝐀i,j]i,j\mathbf{A}=[\mathbf{A}_{i,j}]_{i,j}; higher-order tensors (order three or higher) are denoted by boldface Euler script letters, e.g., 𝓐=[𝓐i1,i2,i3,…]i1,i2,i3,…\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}=[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}_{i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},\dots}]_{i_{1},i_{2},i_{3},\dots}.

  • •

    The it​hi^{th} row (resp. column) of a matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} will be denoted by 𝐀i,:\mathbf{A}_{i,:} or simply 𝐀i\mathbf{A}_{i} (resp. 𝐀:,i\mathbf{A}_{:,i}). This notation is extended to slices of a tensor straightforwardly. Commas in subscripts may occasionally be omitted whenever no ambiguity arises, e.g., 𝐀=[𝐀i​j]i​j\mathbf{A}=[\mathbf{A}_{ij}]_{ij} and 𝐀i:\mathbf{A}_{i:}. Unless otherwise stated, indices of vectors, matrices, and tensors will start at 11. When 00-based indexing is used, it will be explicitly mentioned.

  • •

    For a given dimension n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, 𝐞(k)∈ℝn\mathbf{e}^{(k)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is the kt​hk^{th} vector of the canonical basis of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, 𝐞l(k)=δk​l​∀l∈[n]\mathbf{e}^{(k)}_{l}=\delta_{kl}\forall l\in[n]. Here, δ\delta is the Kronecker delta function.

  • •

    For a vector 𝐱∈ℝn\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, ‖𝐱‖0=|{i∈[n],𝐱i≠0}|\|\mathbf{x}\|_{0}=|\{i\in[n],\mathbf{x}_{i}\neq 0\}|, ‖𝐱‖p=(∑i=1n|𝐱i|p)1p​∀p∈(0,∞)\|\mathbf{x}\|_{p}=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}|\mathbf{x}_{i}|^{p}\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}\forall p\in(0,\infty) and ‖𝐱‖∞=maxi∈[n]⁡|𝐱i|\|\mathbf{x}\|_{\infty}=\max_{i\in[n]}|\mathbf{x}_{i}|.

  • •

    For a matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×n\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}, the operator vec⁡(𝐀)∈ℝm​n\vect(\mathbf{A})\in\mathbb{R}^{mn} stacks the column of 𝐀\mathbf{A} in a vector, i.e. (vec⁡(𝐀))(j−1)​m+i=𝐀i​j(\vect(\mathbf{A}))_{(j-1)m+i}=\mathbf{A}_{ij} for all (i,j)∈[m]×[n](i,j)\in[m]\times[n]. We have ‖𝐀‖F:=‖vec⁡(𝐀)‖2\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\text{F}}:=\|\vect(\mathbf{A})\|_{2}.

  • •

    For the operations on vectors and matrices, we denote by ⊙\odot the Hadamard product, ⊗\otimes the Kronecker product, ⋆\star the Khatri-Rao product, ∙\bullet the face-splitting product, and ∘\circ the outer product. For nn vectors 𝐚(i)∈ℝmi​∀i∈[n]\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{i}}\ \forall i\in[n], (𝐚(1)∘⋯∘𝐚(n))i1,⋯,in=𝐚i1(1)⋯𝐚in(n)∀(i1,⋯,in)∈[m1]×⋯×[mn]\left(\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\circ\cdots\circ\mathbf{a}^{(n)}\right)_{i_{1},\cdots,i_{n}}=\mathbf{a}^{(1)}_{i_{1}}\cdots\mathbf{a}^{(n)}_{i_{n}}\ \forall(i_{1},\cdots,i_{n})\in[m_{1}]\times\cdots\times[m_{n}].

Let 𝓣∈ℝd1×d2×d3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times d_{3}}.

  • •

    For a vector 𝐚∈ℝd1\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}, the matrix 𝐀=𝓣×1𝐚∈ℝd2×d3\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times d_{3}} is such that 𝐀j​k=∑i=1d1𝓣i​j​k𝐚i=𝓣:,j,k⊤𝐚∀(j,k)∈[d2]×[d3]\mathbf{A}_{jk}=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{1}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{a}_{i}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,j,k}^{\top}\mathbf{a}\ \forall(j,k)\in[d_{2}]\times[d_{3}], that is 𝐀=∑i=1d1𝐚i𝓣i,:,:\mathbf{A}=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{1}}\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{i,:,:}. The matrices 𝓣×2𝐚∈ℝd1×d3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{3}} and 𝓣×3𝐚∈ℝd1×d2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{3}\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}} are define similarly, for 𝐚∈ℝd2\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}} and 𝐚∈ℝd3\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{3}} respectively: 𝓣×2𝐚=∑j=1d2𝓣:,j,:𝐚j\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{a}=\sum_{j=1}^{d_{2}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,j,:}\mathbf{a}_{j} and 𝓣×3𝐚=∑k=1d3𝓣:,:,k𝐚k\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{3}\mathbf{a}=\sum_{k=1}^{d_{3}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,:,k}\mathbf{a}_{k}.

    So, for 𝐚∈ℝd1\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}} and 𝐛∈ℝd2\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}, the vector 𝐜=𝓣×1𝐚×2𝐛=𝐀×2𝐛=𝐀⊤𝐛∈ℝd3\mathbf{c}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{a}\times_{2}\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{A}\times_{2}\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{3}}, with 𝐀=𝓣×1𝐚∈ℝd2×d3\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times d_{3}}, is such that 𝐜k=𝐚⊤𝓣:,:,k𝐛=𝐀:,k⊤𝐛∀k∈[d3]\mathbf{c}_{k}=\mathbf{a}^{\top}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,:,k}\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{A}_{:,k}^{\top}\mathbf{b}\ \forall k\in[d_{3}], i.e. 𝐜=∑i=1d1∑j=1d2𝐚i𝐛j𝓣i,j,:=∑j=1d2𝐛j𝐀j,:\mathbf{c}=\sum_{i=1}^{d_{1}}\sum_{j=1}^{d_{2}}\mathbf{a}_{i}\mathbf{b}_{j}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{i,j,:}=\sum_{j=1}^{d_{2}}\mathbf{b}_{j}\mathbf{A}_{j,:}.

    As a special case, identifying matrices with tensors in ℝd1×d2×1\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times 1} gives

    {𝐀×1𝐚=𝐀⊤​𝐚∈ℝd2𝐀×2𝐛=𝐀𝐛∈ℝd1​∀𝐀∈ℝd1×d2,𝐚∈ℝd1,𝐛∈ℝd2\begin{split}\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll}\mathbf{A}\times_{1}\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}\\ \mathbf{A}\times_{2}\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}\end{array}\right.\forall\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}},\mathbf{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}},\mathbf{b}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}}\end{split} (5)
  • •

    For a matrix 𝐀∈ℝm×d1\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{1}}, the tensor 𝓐=𝓣×1𝐀∈ℝm×d2×d3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{2}\times d_{3}} is such that 𝓐i​j​k=∑l=1d1𝐀i​l​𝓣l​j​k​∀(i,j,k)∈[m]×[d2]×[d3]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}_{ijk}=\sum_{l=1}^{d_{1}}\mathbf{A}_{il}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{ljk}\ \forall(i,j,k)\in[m]\times[d_{2}]\times[d_{3}]; or equivalently, 𝓐i,:,:=∑l=1d1𝐀i​l𝓣l,:,:∈ℝd2×d3∀i∈[m]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}_{i,:,:}=\sum_{l=1}^{d_{1}}\mathbf{A}_{il}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{l,:,:}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times d_{3}}\ \forall i\in[m].

    Similarly, for 𝐀∈ℝm×d2\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{2}}, 𝓐=𝓣×2𝐀∈ℝd1×m×d3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{2}\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times m\times d_{3}} is such that 𝓐i​j​k=∑l=1d2𝐀j​l​𝓣i​l​k​∀(i,j,k)∈[d1]×[m]×[d3]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}_{ijk}=\sum_{l=1}^{d_{2}}\mathbf{A}_{jl}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{ilk}\ \forall(i,j,k)\in[d_{1}]\times[m]\times[d_{3}]; or equivalently, 𝓐:j:=∑l=1d2𝐀j​l𝓣:,l,:∈ℝd1×d3∀j∈[m]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}_{:j:}=\sum_{l=1}^{d_{2}}\mathbf{A}_{jl}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,l,:}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{3}}\ \forall j\in[m];

    In the same way, for 𝐀∈ℝm×d3\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{3}}, the tensor 𝓐=𝓣×3𝐀∈ℝd1×d2×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{3}\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}\times m} is such that 𝓐i​j​k=∑l=1d3𝐀k​l​𝓣i​j​l​∀(i,j,k)∈[d1]×[d2]×[m]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}_{ijk}=\sum_{l=1}^{d_{3}}\mathbf{A}_{kl}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{ijl}\ \forall(i,j,k)\in[d_{1}]\times[d_{2}]\times[m]; or equivalently, 𝓐:,:,k=∑l=1d3𝐀k​l𝓣:,:,l∈ℝd1×d2∀k∈[m]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}_{:,:,k}=\sum_{l=1}^{d_{3}}\mathbf{A}_{kl}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,:,l}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}}\ \forall k\in[m].

    So, for 𝐀(ℓ)∈ℝmℓ×dℓ​∀ℓ∈[3]\mathbf{A}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{\ell}\times d_{\ell}}\ \forall\ell\in[3], the tensor 𝓐=𝓣×1𝐀(1)×2𝐀(2)×3𝐀(3)∈ℝm1×m2×m3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{A}^{(1)}\times_{2}\mathbf{A}^{(2)}\times_{3}\mathbf{A}^{(3)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{1}\times m_{2}\times m_{3}} is such that

    𝓐i​j​k=∑l=1d1∑r=1d2∑s=1d3𝓣l​r​s𝐀(1)i​l𝐀(2)j​r𝐀(3)k​s∀i,j,k⟺𝓐=∑l=1d1∑r=1d2∑s=1d3𝓣l​r​s𝐀(1):,l∘𝐀(2):,r∘𝐀(3):s\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}_{ijk}=\sum_{l=1}^{d_{1}}\sum_{r=1}^{d_{2}}\sum_{s=1}^{d_{3}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{lrs}\mathbf{A}^{(1)}_{il}\mathbf{A}^{(2)}_{jr}\mathbf{A}^{(3)}_{ks}\forall i,j,k\Longleftrightarrow\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{A}}}=\sum_{l=1}^{d_{1}}\sum_{r=1}^{d_{2}}\sum_{s=1}^{d_{3}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{lrs}\mathbf{A}^{(1)}_{:,l}\circ\mathbf{A}^{(2)}_{:,r}\circ\mathbf{A}^{(3)}_{:s} (6)
  • •

    We denoted by 𝓣(1)∈ℝd1×d2​d3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}d_{3}}, 𝓣(2)∈ℝd2×d1​d3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{(2)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times d_{1}d_{3}} and 𝓣(3)∈ℝd3×d1​d2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{(3)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{3}\times d_{1}d_{2}} the mode-1,2,3 unfolding of 𝓣\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}, respectively. They are defined by (𝓣(1))i,(j−1)​d3+k=(𝓣(2))j,(k−1)​d1+i=(𝓣(3))k,(j−1)​d1+i=𝓣i​j​k​∀(i,j,k)∈[d1]×[d2]×[d3]\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{(1)}\right)_{i,(j-1)d_{3}+k}=\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{(2)}\right)_{j,(k-1)d_{1}+i}=\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{(3)}\right)_{k,(j-1)d_{1}+i}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{ijk}\ \forall(i,j,k)\in[d_{1}]\times[d_{2}]\times[d_{3}], or equivalently:

    𝓣(1)=[−vec(𝓣1,:,:⊤)−−vec(𝓣2,:,:⊤)−−⋯−−vec(𝓣d1,:,:⊤)−]𝓣(2)=[−vec(𝓣:,1,:)−−vec(𝓣:,2,:)−−⋯−−vec(𝓣:,d2,:)−]𝓣(3)=[−vec(𝓣:,:,1)−−vec(𝓣:,:,2)−−⋯−−vec(𝓣:,:,d3)−]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{(1)}=\begin{bmatrix}-\ \vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{1,:,:}^{\top})\ -\\ -\ \vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{2,:,:}^{\top})\ -\\ -\ \ \quad\cdots\quad\quad-\\ -\vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{d_{1},:,:}^{\top})-\end{bmatrix}\quad\quad\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{(2)}=\begin{bmatrix}-\ \vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,1,:})\ -\\ -\ \vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,2,:})\ -\\ -\ \ \quad\cdots\quad\quad-\\ -\vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,d_{2},:})-\end{bmatrix}\quad\quad\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{(3)}=\begin{bmatrix}-\ \vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,:,1})\ -\\ -\ \vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,:,2})\ -\\ -\ \ \quad\cdots\quad\quad-\\ -\vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{:,:,d_{3}})-\end{bmatrix} (7)

    The following identities follow from these definitions using standard tensor and Kronecker-product manipulations.

    • –

      For all ℓ∈[3]\ell\in[3], we have

      𝐀​𝓣(ℓ)=(𝓣×ℓ𝐀)(ℓ)​∀𝐀∈ℝm×dℓ\mathbf{A}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}_{(\ell)}=(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{T}}}\times_{\ell}\mathbf{A})_{(\ell)}\ \forall\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d_{\ell}} (8)
