Appendix B Finite-Dimensional Algebra (FDA)

We intentionally adopt a relatively broad and self-contained exposition in this section in order to make the paper accessible to a wider audience. Readers already familiar with the underlying algebraic background may safely skip most of the introductory material and proceed directly to the proofs of the propositions (many of which rely on standard or straightforward arguments), or move directly to the next section.

B.1 Definitions

A monoid is a set equipped with a binary operation that combines any two elements to form a third element of that set. Specifically, a monoid (M,⋅)(M,\cdot) must satisfy a⋅b∈M​∀a,b∈Ma\cdot b\in M\ \forall a,b\in M (closure), (a⋅b)⋅c=a⋅(b⋅c)∀a,b,c∈M(a\cdot b)\cdot c=a\cdot(b\cdot c)\ \forall a,b,c\in M (associativity), and ∃e∈M,e⋅a=a⋅e=a​∀a∈M\exists e\in M,\ e\cdot a=a\cdot e=a\ \forall a\in M (identity element).

A group is a monoid in which every element admits an inverse. More precisely, a group (G,⋅)(G,\cdot) is a monoid such that ∀a∈G,∃b∈G,a⋅b=b⋅a=e\forall a\in G,\exists b\in G,\ a\cdot b=b\cdot a=e, where ee denotes the identity element of GG. The element bb is called the inverse of aa and is usually denoted by a−1a^{-1}. A group GG is said to be abelian or commutative if a⋅b=b⋅a∀a,b∈Ga\cdot b=b\cdot a\ \forall a,b\in G. An additive group is a group where the group operation is typically thought of as addition. This terminology is most commonly used when the group elements are intuitively additive in nature, such as numbers or functions. The group operation is denoted by ++, the identity element by 00, and the inverse of an element aa is denoted by −a-a. A multiplicative group is a group in which the group operation is typically understood as multiplication. This terminology is used especially when dealing with elements that naturally support a multiplicative structure, such as non-zero numbers, invertible matrices, and permutations. The group operation is denoted by ∗* or simply by juxtaposition (a​bab), the identity element by 11, and the inverse of an element aa by a−1a^{-1}.

A ring (R,+,∗)(R,+,*) is a structure consisting of a set equipped with two binary operations: addition (++) and multiplication (∗*), such that (R,+)(R,+) is an abelian (additive) group, (R,∗)(R,*) is a (multiplicative) monoid, and multiplication is distributive over addition (a∗(b+c)=a∗b+a∗ca*(b+c)=a*b+a*c and (a+b)∗c=a∗c+b∗c(a+b)*c=a*c+b*c, corresponding to the left and right distributivity respectively). A ring is commutative if (R,∗)(R,*) is a commutative monoid: a∗b=b∗aa*b=b*a for all a,b∈Ra,b\in R.

Example B.1.

For m∈ℕ∗m\in\mathbb{N}^{*}, let ℳm​(𝔽)\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) denote the set of m×mm\times m matrices with entries in 𝔽\mathbb{F}. Equipped with matrix multiplication, ℳm​(𝔽)\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) forms a monoid. The subset GLm​(𝔽)⊂ℳm​(𝔽)\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{F})\subset\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) of invertible matrices forms a group under matrix multiplication, the general linear group of degree mm over 𝔽\mathbb{F}. Moreover, endowed with the usual matrix addition and multiplication, ℳm​(𝔽)\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) forms a non-commutative ring.

A field (𝔽,+,∗)(\mathbb{F},+,*) is a commutative ring in which every non-zero element has a multiplicative inverse, making (𝔽∖{0},∗)(\mathbb{F}\setminus\{0\},*) an abelian group as well.

Example B.2.

For a prime integer pp, 𝔽p=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}_{p}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} endowed with modular arithmetic forms a finite field, the prime field of order pp (also known as the Galois field of order pp). In general, for any integer qq, a finite field of order qq exists if and only if qq is a prime power (i.e., q=pkq=p^{k} where pp is a prime number and kk is a positive integer). In this case, all fields of order qq are isomorphic to each other. In 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, the multiplicative inverse of an element α\alpha is the element β\beta (denoted α−1\alpha^{-1}) such that (α​β)%​p=1(\alpha\beta)\%p=1, and can be computed using the extended Euclidean Algorithm. The result of α/β\alpha/\beta is (α​β−1)%​p(\alpha\beta^{-1})\%p.

A vector space over a field (𝔽,+,∗)(\mathbb{F},+,*) is a set VV equipped with two operations, vector addition (V×V→VV\times V\rightarrow V) and scalar multiplication (𝔽×V→V\mathbb{F}\times V\rightarrow V), such that VV with vector addition forms an abelian group (with identity 00 and inverses −𝐯-\mathbf{v}) and scalar multiplication is associative and distributive over vector addition, i.e. for all a,b∈𝔽a,b\in\mathbb{F} and 𝐮,𝐯∈V\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in V: a⁡(𝐮+𝐯)=a​𝐮+a​𝐯,(a+b)​𝐮=a​𝐮+b​𝐮,(a​b)​𝐮=a⁡(b​𝐮), 1𝔽​𝐮=𝐮a(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=a\mathbf{u}+a\mathbf{v},\ (a+b)\mathbf{u}=a\mathbf{u}+b\mathbf{u},\ (ab)\mathbf{u}=a(b\mathbf{u}),\ 1_{\mathbb{F}}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}.

A module over a ring RR generalizes vector spaces by allowing the scalars to come from a ring, not necessarily a field. The key differences are the absence of scalar inverses generally and the fact that the ring does not need to be commutative.

An algebra 𝔄\mathfrak{A} over a field (resp. ring) (𝔽,+,∗)(\mathbb{F},+,*) is a vector space (resp. module) equipped with a 𝔽\mathbb{F}-bilinear product55 5 i.e. a map that is linear in each argument separately: (α​𝐮+β​𝐯)⋅𝐰=α⁡(𝐮⋅𝐯)+β⁡(𝐮⋅𝐰)(\alpha\mathbf{u}+\beta\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{w}=\alpha(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})+\beta(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}) and 𝐰⋅(α​𝐮+β​𝐯)=α⁡(𝐰⋅𝐮)+β⁡(𝐰⋅𝐯)\mathbf{w}\cdot(\alpha\mathbf{u}+\beta\mathbf{v})=\alpha(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{u})+\beta(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{v}) for all 𝐮,𝐯,𝐰∈𝔄\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{A}, α,β∈𝔽\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}. ⋅:𝔄×𝔄→𝔄\cdot:\mathfrak{A}\times\mathfrak{A}\to\mathfrak{A} such that (𝐮+𝐯)⋅𝐰=𝐮⋅𝐰+𝐯⋅𝐰(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w} (right distributivity), 𝐰⋅(𝐮+𝐯)=𝐰⋅𝐮+𝐰⋅𝐯\mathbf{w}\cdot(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{v} (left distributivity) and (α​𝐮)⋅(β​𝐯)=(α∗β)​(𝐮⋅𝐯)(\alpha\mathbf{u})\cdot(\beta\mathbf{v})=(\alpha*\beta)(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}) (compatibility with scalars) for all 𝐮,𝐯,𝐰∈𝔄\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{A} and α,β∈𝔽\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}. When ⋅\cdot is associative (resp. commutative), the algebra is said to be associative (resp. commutative). When the multiplicative identity exists, i.e., there exists an element 1𝔄∈𝔄1_{\mathfrak{A}}\in\mathfrak{A} such that 1𝔄⋅𝐮=𝐮⋅1𝔄=𝐮​∀𝐮∈𝔄1_{\mathfrak{A}}\cdot\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}\cdot 1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathbf{u}\ \forall\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A}, the algebra is said to be unital. The dimension of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is its dimension as a 𝔽\mathbb{F}-vector space, denoted by dim𝔽​𝔄\text{dim}_{\mathbb{F}}\mathfrak{A}. We say that 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is finite-dimensional if n=dim𝔽​𝔄n=\text{dim}_{\mathbb{F}}\mathfrak{A} is finite. This means that a finite number of elements in the set can be combined linearly to express any element in the algebra, i.e., there exists a finite basis {𝐚(i)}i∈[n]\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} (as a vector space over 𝔽\mathbb{F}) such that for every 𝐮∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A}, 𝐮=∑i=1nαi​𝐚(i)\mathbf{u}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)} with αi∈𝔽​∀i∈[n]\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{F}\ \forall i\in[n].

Let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) and (𝔅,×)(\mathfrak{B},\times) be two 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebras. A homomorphism of 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebras ϕ:𝔄→𝔅\phi:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathfrak{B} is a 𝔽\mathbb{F}-linear map satisfying ϕ⁡(𝐮⋅𝐯)=ϕ⁡(𝐮)×ϕ⁡(𝐯)\phi(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})=\phi(\mathbf{u})\times\phi(\mathbf{v}) for all 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔄\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{A}; and ϕ⁡(1𝔄)=1𝔅\phi(1_{\mathfrak{A}})=1_{\mathfrak{B}} when 𝔄\mathfrak{A} and 𝔅\mathfrak{B} are unitals. The algebra homomorphism ϕ\phi is called an isomorphism if it is bijective, or equivalently, if there exists an algebra homomorphism φ:𝔅→𝔄\varphi:\mathfrak{B}\to\mathfrak{A}, often denoted ϕ−1\phi^{-1}, such that φ⁡(ϕ⁡(𝐮))=𝐮​∀𝐮∈𝔄\varphi(\phi(\mathbf{u}))=\mathbf{u}\ \forall\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A} and ϕ⁡(φ⁡(𝐯))=𝐯​∀𝐯∈𝔅\phi(\varphi(\mathbf{v}))=\mathbf{v}\ \forall\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{B}. If further 𝔅=𝔄\mathfrak{B}=\mathfrak{A}, the isomorphism ϕ\phi is called an automorphism of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}.

Two 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebras 𝔄\mathfrak{A} and 𝔅\mathfrak{B} are isomorphic (or, informally, similar) if there exists an algebra isomorphism ϕ:𝔄→𝔅\phi:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathfrak{B} between them. In other words, 𝔄\mathfrak{A} and 𝔅\mathfrak{B} may look different at the level of their elements or chosen bases, but they share exactly the same algebraic structure: the operations in one correspond perfectly to the operations in the other under ϕ\phi.

B.2 Structure Constants of FDA

Let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) be an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA and B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} a basis of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} (as a vector space over 𝔽\mathbb{F}). Then the structure of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in BB is entirely captured by the tensor 𝓒(B)∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} defined by

𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j)=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k(B)​𝐚(k)\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}^{(B)}\mathbf{a}^{(k)} (12)

The elements of 𝓒(B)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)} are called structure coefficients/constants of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in BB. We will call the tensor 𝓒(B)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)} the structure tensor of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in the basis BB, and when the context is clear, we will omit BB from the notation. That said, we have for all 𝐮=∑i=1n𝐮i​𝐚(i)\mathbf{u}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)} and 𝐯=∑i=1n𝐯i​𝐚(i)\mathbf{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{v}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)} in 𝔄\mathfrak{A},

𝐮⋅𝐯=∑i=1n∑j=1n𝐮i𝐯j(𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j))=∑k=1n(∑i=1n∑j=1n𝓒i​j​k𝐮i𝐯j)𝐚(k)=∑k=1n(𝓒×1𝐮×2𝐯)k𝐚(k)\begin{split}\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}&=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}(\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)})=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\right)\mathbf{a}^{(k)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}\right)_{k}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\end{split} (13)

Using (𝐮,𝐯)=(𝐚(i),𝐚(j))(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=(\mathbf{a}^{(i)},\mathbf{a}^{(j)}), we obtain 𝓒i​j​k=𝐚(i)⊤𝓒::k𝐚(j)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=\mathbf{a}^{(i)\top}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{::k}\mathbf{a}^{(j)} for all i,j,k∈[n]i,j,k\in[n]. Note that (see Equation (11))

𝓒×1𝐮×2𝐯=𝓒(3)(𝐯⊗𝐮)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(3)}\left(\mathbf{v}\otimes\mathbf{u}\right) (14)

with (Equation (7))

𝓒(3)⊤:=[|||vec(𝓒::1)vec(𝓒::2)⋯vec(𝓒::n)|||]∈𝔽n2×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(3)}^{\top}:=\begin{bmatrix}|&|&&|\\ \vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{::1})&\vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{::2})&\cdots&\vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{::n})\\ |&|&&|\\ \end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{F}^{n^{2}\times n} (15)

The Proposition 2.1 states that for all 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n}, there exists an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA whose structure tensor is 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} is some basis BB; and that all n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA that have 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} as a structure tensor in one of their bases are isomorphic to each other. The proof of the first part is given by Lemma B.1 and the proof of the second part is given by Lemma B.2.

Lemma B.1.

For a ring 𝔽\mathbb{F} (which can be a field), let 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n}, and ×:𝔽n×𝔽n→𝔽n\times:\mathbb{F}^{n}\times\mathbb{F}^{n}\to\mathbb{F}^{n} defined by 𝐮×𝐯=𝓒×1𝐮×2𝐯\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}. Then (𝔽n,×)(\mathbb{F}^{n},\times) is an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA, and 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} its structure tensor in its canonical basis {𝐞(i)}i∈[n]\{\mathbf{e}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}.

Proof.

It is easy to check that this structure forms an algebra over 𝔽\mathbb{F}. For the structure tensor, observe that (𝐮×𝐯)k=(𝓒×1𝐮×2𝐯)k=∑=1n∑j=1n𝓒i​j​k𝐮i𝐯j(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})_{k}=(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v})_{k}=\sum_{=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j} for all 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔽n\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{F}^{n}. So (𝐞(i)×𝐞(j))k=𝓒i​j​k​∀i,j,k∈[n](\mathbf{e}^{(i)}\times\mathbf{e}^{(j)})_{k}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\ \forall i,j,k\in[n]. ∎

Lemma B.2.

Let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) be an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA with structure tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} in a basis B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}, and {𝐞(i)}i∈[n]\{\mathbf{e}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} be the canonical basis of 𝔽n\mathbb{F}^{n}. The linear map ϕ:𝔽n→𝔄\phi:\mathbb{F}^{n}\rightarrow\mathfrak{A} defined by ϕ⁡(𝐞(i))=𝐚(i)​∀i∈[n]\phi(\mathbf{e}^{(i)})=\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\ \forall i\in[n] is an isomorphism (of vector spaces), and we have the relation ϕ(𝐮×𝐯)=ϕ(𝐮)⋅ϕ(𝐯)∀𝐮,𝐯∈𝔽n\phi(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})=\phi(\mathbf{u})\cdot\phi(\mathbf{v})\ \forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{F}^{n}. As a consequence, by defining the product 𝐮×𝐯=𝓒×1𝐮×2𝐯\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v} on 𝔽n\mathbb{F}^{n}, ϕ\phi becomes an algebra isomorphism between (𝔽n,×)(\mathbb{F}^{n},\times) and (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot).

Proof.

It is easy to see that ϕ\phi is an isomorphism of vector spaces. We also have for all 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔽n\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{F}^{n}:

ϕ⁡(𝐮×𝐯)=∑k=1n(𝓒×1𝐮×2𝐯)kϕ(𝐞(k))=∑k=1n(∑i=1n∑j=1n𝓒i​j​k𝐮i𝐯j)𝐚(k)=∑i=1n∑j=1n𝐮i​𝐯j​∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝐚(k)=∑i=1n∑j=1n𝐮i​𝐯j​(𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j))=(∑i=1n𝐮i​𝐚(i))⋅(∑j=1n𝐯j​𝐚(j))=(∑i=1n𝐮i​ϕ​(𝐞(i)))⋅(∑j=1n𝐯j​ϕ​(𝐞(j)))=ϕ⁡(∑i=1n𝐮i​𝐞(i))⋅ϕ⁡(∑j=1n𝐯j​𝐞(j))=ϕ⁡(𝐮)⋅ϕ⁡(𝐯)\begin{split}\phi\left(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}\right)&=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}\right)_{k}\phi(\mathbf{e}^{(k)})=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\right)\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}(\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)})=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{v}_{j}\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\right)\\ &=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\phi(\mathbf{e}^{(i)})\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{v}_{j}\phi(\mathbf{e}^{(j)})\right)\\ &=\phi\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{e}^{(i)}\right)\cdot\phi\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\mathbf{v}_{j}\mathbf{e}^{(j)}\right)=\phi\left(\mathbf{u}\right)\cdot\phi\left(\mathbf{v}\right)\end{split} (16)

∎

This shows that learning multiplication ⋅\cdot in (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) is equivalent to learning ×\times in 𝔽⁡[𝓒]:=(𝔽n,×)\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}]:=(\mathbb{F}^{n},\times). If we are working in an arbitrary basis {𝐚(i)}i∈[n]\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} of 𝔽n\mathbb{F}^{n} such that 𝐚(i)=∑k=1n𝐏k​i​𝐞(k)​∀i∈[n]\mathbf{a}^{(i)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{P}_{ki}\mathbf{e}^{(k)}\forall i\in[n], we need to rescale 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} accordingly.

Proposition B.3.

Let 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} and 𝓒~\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}} be the structure tensors of an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA 𝔄\mathfrak{A} with respect to two bases B={𝐚(i))}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)})\}_{i\in[n]} and B~={𝐚~(i)}i∈[n]\tilde{B}=\{\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} respectively. If 𝐏∈𝔽n×n\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n} is the basis change matrix from BB to B~\tilde{B}, i.e. 𝐚~(i)=∑k=1n𝐏k​i​𝐚(k)​∀i∈[n]\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(i)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{P}_{ki}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\ \forall i\in[n], then we have 𝓒~=𝓒×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}, or equivalently, 𝓒~×3𝐏=𝓒×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}. If further BB and B~\tilde{B} are orthogonal basis, then 𝓒~=𝓒×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏⊤\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{\top}.

Proof.

For all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], we have

𝐚~(i)⋅𝐚~(j)=(∑ℓ=1n𝐏ℓ​i​𝐚(ℓ))⋅(∑r=1n𝐏r​j​𝐚(r))=∑ℓ=1n∑r=1n𝐏ℓ​i​𝐏r​j​(𝐚(ℓ)⋅𝐚(r))=∑ℓ=1n∑r=1n𝐏ℓ​i​𝐏r​j​∑s=1n𝓒ℓ​r​s​𝐚(s)=∑ℓ=1n∑r=1n𝐏ℓ​i​𝐏r​j​∑s=1n𝓒ℓ​r​s​∑k=1n(𝐏−1)k​s​𝐚~(k)=∑k=1n(∑ℓ,r,s=1n𝓒ℓ​r​s​(𝐏⊤)i​ℓ​(𝐏⊤)j​r​(𝐏−1)k​s)​𝐚~(k)=∑k=1n(𝓒×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1)i​j​k𝐚~(k) (Equation (6))\begin{split}\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(i)}\cdot\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(j)}&=\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\mathbf{P}_{\ell i}\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\mathbf{P}_{rj}\mathbf{a}^{(r)}\right)\\ &=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\mathbf{P}_{\ell i}\mathbf{P}_{rj}\left(\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(r)}\right)\\ &=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\mathbf{P}_{\ell i}\mathbf{P}_{rj}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{\ell rs}\mathbf{a}^{(s)}\\ &=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\mathbf{P}_{\ell i}\mathbf{P}_{rj}\sum_{s=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{\ell rs}\sum_{k=1}^{n}(\mathbf{P}^{-1})_{ks}\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(k)}\\ &=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{\ell,r,s=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{\ell rs}(\mathbf{P}^{\top})_{i\ell}(\mathbf{P}^{\top})_{jr}({\mathbf{P}^{-1}})_{ks}\right)\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(k)}\\ &=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}\right)_{ijk}\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(k)}\text{ (Equation~\eqref{eq:T_A_A_A})}\end{split} (17)

So 𝓒~=𝓒×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}. We have (see Equation (8)) (𝓒~×3𝐏)(3)=𝐏𝓒~(3)=𝐏(𝓒×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1)(3)=𝐏𝐏−1(𝓒×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤)(3)=(𝓒×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤)(3)(\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}}\times_{3}\mathbf{P})_{(3)}=\mathbf{P}\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}}_{(3)}=\mathbf{P}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1})_{(3)}=\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P}^{-1}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top})_{(3)}=(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top})_{(3)}. So 𝓒~×3𝐏=𝓒×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}. If further BB and B~\tilde{B} are orthogonal basis, then 𝐏−1=𝐏⊤\mathbf{P}^{-1}=\mathbf{P}^{\top}. In fact, let 𝐁=[−𝐚(i)−]i∈[n]⊤∈𝔽n×n\mathbf{B}=[-\mathbf{a}^{(i)}-]_{i\in[n]}^{\top}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n} (𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i} is the it​hi^{th} column of 𝐁\mathbf{B}) and 𝐁~=[−𝐚~(i)−]i∈[n]⊤∈𝔽n×n\tilde{\mathbf{B}}=[-\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(i)}-]_{i\in[n]}^{\top}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n}. We have 𝐁~=𝐁𝐏\tilde{\mathbf{B}}=\mathbf{B}\mathbf{P}. Assuming 𝐁⊤​𝐁=𝕀n\mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{B}=\mathbb{I}_{n}, this give 𝐏=𝐁⊤​𝐁~\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{B}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}, so that 𝐏⊤​𝐏=𝕀n\mathbf{P}^{\top}\mathbf{P}=\mathbb{I}_{n} if 𝐁𝐁⊤=𝐁~⊤​𝐁~=𝕀n\mathbf{B}\mathbf{B}^{\top}=\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}=\mathbb{I}_{n} and 𝐏𝐏⊤=𝕀n\mathbf{P}\mathbf{P}^{\top}=\mathbb{I}_{n} if 𝐁~​𝐁~⊤=𝐁⊤​𝐁=𝕀n\tilde{\mathbf{B}}\tilde{\mathbf{B}}^{\top}=\mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{B}=\mathbb{I}_{n}. ∎

As a consequence of this proposition, we get that the rank of the structure tensor of a FDA is basis-invariant: it is an intrinsic invariant of the algebra.

Corollary B.4.

For all i∈[3]i\in[3], the rank of 𝓒(i)(B)∈𝔽n×n2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{(i)}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n^{2}} is independant from the basis BB.

Proof.

If 𝐏\mathbf{P} is the basis change matrix from an arbitrary basis BB to another basis B~\tilde{B}, then 𝓒(B~)=𝓒(B)×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(\tilde{B})}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1} by Proposition B.3. This implies (see Equations (8) and (9)):

  • •

    𝓒(1)(B~)=(𝓒(B)×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1)(1)=𝐏⊤(𝓒(B)×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1)(1)=𝐏⊤𝓒(1)(B)(𝐏⊤⊗𝐏−1)⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(\tilde{B})}_{(1)}=\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}\right)_{(1)}=\mathbf{P}^{\top}\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}\right)_{(1)}=\mathbf{P}^{\top}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{(1)}(\mathbf{P}^{\top}\otimes\mathbf{P}^{-1})^{\top}

  • •

    𝓒(2)(B~)=(𝓒(B)×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1)(2)=𝐏⊤(𝓒(B)×1𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1)(2)=𝐏⊤𝓒(2)(B)(𝐏−1⊗𝐏⊤)⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(\tilde{B})}_{(2)}=\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}\right)_{(2)}=\mathbf{P}^{\top}\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}\right)_{(2)}=\mathbf{P}^{\top}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{(2)}(\mathbf{P}^{-1}\otimes\mathbf{P}^{\top})^{\top}

  • •

    𝓒(3)(B~)=(𝓒(B)×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1)(3)=𝐏−1(𝓒(B)×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤)(3)=𝐏−1𝓒(3)(B)(𝐏⊗𝐏)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(\tilde{B})}_{(3)}=\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}\right)_{(3)}=\mathbf{P}^{-1}\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\right)_{(3)}=\mathbf{P}^{-1}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{(3)}(\mathbf{P}\otimes\mathbf{P})

In each case, 𝓒(i)(B~)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(\tilde{B})}_{(i)} is obtained from 𝓒(i)(B)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{(i)} by left- and right-multiplication with invertible matrices. Such operations preserve matrix rank, hence rank(𝓒(i)(B~))=rank(𝓒(i)(B))​∀i∈[3]\rank\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(\tilde{B})}_{(i)}\right)=\rank\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{(i)}\right)\ \forall i\in[3]. ∎

Sparsity, on the other hand, is not basis-invariant. But it may be possible to find a basis of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in which 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} is as sparse as possible, making the problem of learning 𝔄\mathfrak{A} simpler to study; 𝓒~∈argmin𝐏≠𝕀n,rank(𝐏)=n‖𝓒×1𝐏⊤×2𝐏⊤×3𝐏−1‖0\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}}\in\arg\min_{\mathbf{P}\neq\mathbb{I}_{n},\rank(\mathbf{P})=n}\left\|\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{2}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}^{-1}\right\|_{0}. For example, if we go from a basis B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} to its orthonormal equivalent Q={𝐪(i)}i∈[n]Q=\{\mathbf{q}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}, then we have 𝐁=𝐐𝐏\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{Q}\mathbf{P} under the QR decomposition, with 𝐁=[−𝐚(i)−]i∈[n]⊤∈𝔽n×n\mathbf{B}=[-\mathbf{a}^{(i)}-]_{i\in[n]}^{\top}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n} (𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i} is the it​hi^{th} column of 𝐁\mathbf{B}), 𝐐=[−𝐪(i)−]i∈[n]⊤∈𝔽n×n\mathbf{Q}=[-\mathbf{q}^{(i)}-]_{i\in[n]}^{\top}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n} orthogonal, and 𝐏∈𝔽n×n\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n} upper triangular. Note that 𝓒i​j​k(Q)=∑ℓ,r,s𝓒ℓ​r​s(B)​𝐏ℓ​i​𝐏r​j​(𝐏−1)k​s\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}^{(Q)}=\sum_{\ell,r,s}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{\ell rs}^{(B)}\mathbf{P}_{\ell i}\mathbf{P}_{rj}(\mathbf{P}^{-1})_{ks}, with 𝐏−1\mathbf{P}^{-1} also upper triangular.

Although any tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} defines an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA, a key question is how the algebraic properties of (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) are reflected in its structure of 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}. The following proposition makes this connection explicit by characterizing associativity, commutativity, and the existence of a unit directly in terms of tensor equations.

Proposition B.5.

Let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) be an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA with structure tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} in B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}. 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is

  • (i)

    associative if and only if ∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓒k​l​m=∑k=1n𝓒i​k​m​𝓒j​l​k​∀i,j,l,m∈[n]\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{klm}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ikm}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{jlk}\ \forall i,j,l,m\in[n];

  • (ii)

    commutative if and only if 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} is symmetric is its first two modes, i.e. 𝓒i​j:=𝓒j​i:∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ij:}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ji:}\ \forall i,j\in[n], or equivalently, 𝓒::k⊤=𝓒::k∀k∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{::k}^{\top}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{::k}\forall k\in[n];

  • (iii)

    unital if and only if there exist λ∈𝔽n\lambda\in\mathbb{F}^{n} such that 𝓒×1λ=𝕀n=𝓒×2λ\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda=\mathbb{I}_{n}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{2}\lambda, that is ∑i=1nλi𝓒i,:,:=𝕀n=∑i=1nλi𝓒:,i,:\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{i,:,:}=\mathbb{I}_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{:,i,:}, or equivalently, 𝓒(1)⊤​λ=vec⁡(𝕀n)=𝓒(2)⊤​λ\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(1)}^{\top}\lambda=\vect(\mathbb{I}_{n})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(2)}^{\top}\lambda. In this case, 1𝔄=∑i=1nλi​𝐚(i)1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}, with λ∈𝔽n\lambda\in\mathbb{F}^{n} the unique solution of the system of equations 𝓒(1)⊤​λ=vec⁡(𝕀n)=𝓒(2)⊤​λ\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(1)}^{\top}\lambda=\vect(\mathbb{I}_{n})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(2)}^{\top}\lambda.

Proof.

(i) For associative FDA, the multiplication must satisfy (𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j))⋅𝐚(l)=𝐚(i)⋅(𝐚(j)⋅𝐚(l))∀i,j,l(\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)})\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(l)}=\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot(\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(l)})\ \forall i,j,l. Expanding this using the structure constants (Equation (12)), we require ∑m=1n(∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓒k​l​m)​𝐚(m)=∑m=1n(∑k=1n𝓒i​k​m​𝓒j​l​k)​𝐚(m)​∀i,j,l∈[n]\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{klm}\right)\mathbf{a}^{(m)}=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ikm}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{jlk}\right)\mathbf{a}^{(m)}\ \forall i,j,l\in[n].

(ii) For commutative FDA, the multiplication must satisfy 𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j)=𝐚(j)⋅𝐚(i)∀i,j∈[n]⟺∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k𝐚(k)=∑k=1n𝓒j​i​k𝐚(k)∀i,j∈[n]⟺𝓒i​j:=𝓒j​i:∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)}=\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\ \forall i,j\in[n]\Longleftrightarrow\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{jik}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\ \forall i,j\in[n]\Longleftrightarrow\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ij:}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ji:}\ \forall i,j\in[n].

(iii) First, consider the algebra (𝔽⁡[𝓒],×)(\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}],\times) generated by 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}. Suppose (𝔽⁡[𝓒],×)(\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}],\times) is unital, i.e. there exists λ∈𝔽n\lambda\in\mathbb{F}^{n} such that 𝐮×λ=𝐮=λ×𝐮\mathbf{u}\times\lambda=\mathbf{u}=\lambda\times\mathbf{u} for all 𝐮∈𝔽n\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{F}^{n}. Then, expanding using Equation (13), wet get 𝓒×1𝐮×2λ=𝐮=𝓒×1λ×2𝐮∀𝐮∈𝔽n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\lambda=\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda\times_{2}\mathbf{u}\ \forall\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{F}^{n}, which is equivalent to 𝓒×2λ=𝕀n=𝓒×1λ\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{2}\lambda=\mathbb{I}_{n}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda. The direction ⟸\Longleftarrow of this equivalence is obvious, considering the fact that 𝕀n×1𝐮=𝕀n⊤​𝐮=𝐮\mathbb{I}_{n}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}=\mathbb{I}_{n}^{\top}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u} and 𝕀n×2𝐮=𝕀n​𝐮=𝐮\mathbb{I}_{n}\times_{2}\mathbf{u}=\mathbb{I}_{n}\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u} for all 𝐮∈𝔽n\mathbf{u}\in\mathbb{F}^{n} (Equation (5)). The direction ⟹\Longrightarrow follows by taking 𝐮\mathbf{u} as a kthk^{\text{th}} canonical vector of 𝔽n\mathbb{F}^{n}, for all k∈[n]k\in[n]. We also have

𝓒×1λ=𝕀n=𝓒×2λ⟺(𝓒×1λ)⊤=𝕀n=𝓒×2λ⟺vec⁡((𝓒×1λ)⊤)=vec⁡(𝕀n)=vec⁡(𝓒×2λ)⟺𝓒(1)⊤​λ=vec⁡(𝕀n)=𝓒(2)⊤​λ​ (Equation (10))\begin{split}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda=\mathbb{I}_{n}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{2}\lambda&\Longleftrightarrow(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda)^{\top}=\mathbb{I}_{n}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{2}\lambda\\ &\Longleftrightarrow\vect\left((\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda)^{\top}\right)=\vect(\mathbb{I}_{n})=\vect(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{2}\lambda)\\ &\Longleftrightarrow\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(1)}^{\top}\lambda=\vect(\mathbb{I}_{n})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(2)}^{\top}\lambda\text{ (Equation~\eqref{eq:vect_Ta})}\end{split} (18)

Now, suppose there exist λ,λ~∈𝔽n\lambda,\tilde{\lambda}\in\mathbb{F}^{n} such that 𝓒×1λ=𝕀n=𝓒×2λ\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda=\mathbb{I}_{n}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{2}\lambda and 𝓒×1λ~=𝕀n=𝓒×2λ~\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\tilde{\lambda}=\mathbb{I}_{n}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{2}\tilde{\lambda}. From 𝓒×1λ=𝕀n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda=\mathbb{I}_{n}, we get 𝓒×1λ×2λ~=𝕀n×2λ~=λ~\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda\times_{2}\tilde{\lambda}=\mathbb{I}_{n}\times_{2}\tilde{\lambda}=\tilde{\lambda}; and from 𝕀n=𝓒×2λ~\mathbb{I}_{n}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{2}\tilde{\lambda}, we get λ=𝕀n×1λ=𝓒×2λ~×1λ\lambda=\mathbb{I}_{n}\times_{1}\lambda=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{2}\tilde{\lambda}\times_{1}\lambda. So λ=𝓒×1λ×2λ~=λ~\lambda=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda\times_{2}\tilde{\lambda}=\tilde{\lambda}. Therefore, when a solution λ\lambda to 𝓒(1)⊤​λ=vec⁡(𝕀n)=𝓒(2)⊤​λ\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(1)}^{\top}\lambda=\vect(\mathbb{I}_{n})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(2)}^{\top}\lambda exists, it is unique, and thus equals 1𝔽⁡[𝓒]1_{\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}]}. Finally, since (𝔽⁡[𝓒],×)(\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}],\times) and (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) are isomorphic by the linear map ϕ:𝔽n→𝔄\phi:\mathbb{F}^{n}\rightarrow\mathfrak{A} defined by ϕ⁡(𝐞(i))=𝐚(i)​∀i∈[n]\phi(\mathbf{e}^{(i)})=\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\ \forall i\in[n] (Lemma B.2), if (𝔽⁡[𝓒],×)(\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}],\times) is unital with 1𝔽⁡[𝓒]=∑i=1nλi​𝐞(i)1_{\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}]}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{e}^{(i)}, then (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) is also unital with 1𝔄=ϕ⁡(1𝔽⁡[𝓒])=∑i=1nλi​ϕ​(𝐞(i))=∑i=1nλi​𝐚(i)1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\phi(1_{\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}]})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\phi(\mathbf{e}^{(i)})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}. ∎

The corollary of (iii) in this proposition tells us how we can get the unit element of (𝔽⁡[𝓒],×)(\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}],\times) in B={𝐞(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{e}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} when we only have access to 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} and the condition of its existence.

Corollary B.6.

Let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) be an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA with structure tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} in B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}. Let 𝐀:=[𝓒(1),𝓒(2)]⊤∈𝔽2​n2×n\mathbf{A}:=\left[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(1)},\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(2)}\right]^{\top}\in\mathbb{F}^{2n^{2}\times n} and 𝐛:=[vec⁡(𝕀n),vec⁡(𝕀n)]⊤∈𝔽2​n2\mathbf{b}:=\left[\vect(\mathbb{I}_{n}),\vect(\mathbb{I}_{n})\right]^{\top}\in\mathbb{F}^{2n^{2}}. 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is unital if and only if rank𝔽(𝐀)=rank𝔽([𝐀|𝐛])\rank_{\mathbb{F}}(\mathbf{A})=\rank_{\mathbb{F}}\left(\left[\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{b}\right]\right), where [𝐀|𝐛]∈𝔽2​n2×(n+1)\left[\mathbf{A}|\mathbf{b}\right]\in\mathbb{F}^{2n^{2}\times(n+1)} is the augmented matrix of 𝐀\mathbf{A} with 𝐛\mathbf{b} added as a column. In this case, 1𝔄=∑i=1nλi​𝐚(i)1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}, with λ\lambda the unique solution to 𝐀​λ=𝐛\mathbf{A}\lambda=\mathbf{b}.

Proof.

We need to check that there exists a joint solution to the two λ\lambda linear equations 𝓒(k)⊤​λ=vec⁡(𝕀n)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(k)}^{\top}\lambda=\vect(\mathbb{I}_{n}), k∈{1,2}k\in\{1,2\}, that is 𝐀​λ=𝐛\mathbf{A}\lambda=\mathbf{b}. The system has 2​n22n^{2} equations for nn variables, and solutions are cosets of ker⁡(𝐀)\ker(\mathbf{A}). We just need to check the system’s consistency (in 𝔽\mathbb{F}, this precision is important). ∎

We can also solve the system 𝐀​λ=𝐛\mathbf{A}\lambda=\mathbf{b} to find the coordinates of the unit element of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}. It all depends on the field we are in. This can be done quite easily in ℝ\mathbb{R} or ℂ\mathbb{C}. The system 𝐀​λ=𝐛\mathbf{A}\lambda=\mathbf{b} has solutions if and only if 𝐀𝐀†​𝐛=𝐛\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{b}, and the solutions are the vectors λ=𝐀†​𝐛+(𝕀−𝐀†​𝐀)​𝐮\lambda=\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}\mathbf{b}+\left(\mathbb{I}-\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A}\right)\mathbf{u} for an arbitrary conformable vector 𝐮\mathbf{u}. Here, 𝐀†\mathbf{A}^{\dagger} is the pseudo-inverse of 𝐀\mathbf{A} : 𝐀𝐀†​𝐀=𝐀\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{A} and 𝐀†​𝐀𝐀†=𝐀†\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}=\mathbf{A}^{\dagger}.

In a field like 𝔽p\mathbb{F}_{p}, a given solution of the system is not guaranteed to be in 𝔽\mathbb{F}, and solving the system is not easy. In fact, in this field, everything is modulo pp, for example, Equation (13) should be read (∑i𝐮i​𝐚(i))⋅(∑i𝐯i​𝐚(i))=∑k((∑i,j𝓒i​j​k​𝐮i​𝐯j)%​p)​𝐚(k)\left(\sum_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\right)=\sum_{k}\left(\left(\sum_{i,j}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\right)\%p\right)\mathbf{a}^{(k)}, and the system, (𝐀​λ)%​p=𝐛\left(\mathbf{A}\lambda\right)\%p=\mathbf{b}. The multiplicative inverse of an element α\alpha is the element β\beta (denoted α−1\alpha^{-1}) such that (α​β)%​p=1(\alpha\beta)\%p=1, and can be computed using the extended Euclidean Algorithm. The result of α/β\alpha/\beta is (α​β−1)%​p(\alpha\beta^{-1})\%p. So, these details must be considered if we opt for Gaussian Elimination to solve the system.

It should be noted that associative, unital, noncommutative algebras only exist for n≥3n\geq 3 over any field 𝔽\mathbb{F}.

Proposition B.7.

For any field 𝔽\mathbb{F}, the smallest integer n∈ℕ∗n\in\mathbb{N}^{*} for which there exists an associative, unital, noncommutative n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA is n=3n=3. Equivalently, (i) every associative and unital n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA with n≤2n\leq 2 is commutative; (ii) and there exists an associative, unital, noncommutative 3​𝔽3\mathbb{F}-FDA.

Proof.

We split the proof into two parts.

(i) Nonexistence for n≤2n\leq 2.

For n=1n=1, let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) be a unital 1​𝔽1\mathbb{F}-FDA. Since dim𝔽(𝔄)=1\dim_{\mathbb{F}}(\mathfrak{A})=1, the unit element 1𝔄1_{\mathfrak{A}} forms a basis of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}. Therefore 𝔄={λ​1𝔄,λ∈𝔽}\mathfrak{A}=\{\lambda 1_{\mathfrak{A}},\lambda\in\mathbb{F}\}. Hence, for all 𝐮=λ​1𝔄\mathbf{u}=\lambda 1_{\mathfrak{A}} and 𝐯=μ​1𝔄\mathbf{v}=\mu 1_{\mathfrak{A}} in 𝔄\mathfrak{A}, we have

𝐮⋅𝐯=(λ​1𝔄)⋅(μ​1𝔄)=λ​μ​(1𝔄⋅1𝔄)=λ​μ​1𝔄=μ​λ​1𝔄=𝐯⋅𝐮\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=(\lambda 1_{\mathfrak{A}})\cdot(\mu 1_{\mathfrak{A}})=\lambda\mu(1_{\mathfrak{A}}\cdot 1_{\mathfrak{A}})=\lambda\mu 1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\mu\lambda 1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u} (19)

So 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is commutative. Now let n=2n=2, and let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) be an associative and unital 2​𝔽2\mathbb{F}-FDA. Since dim𝔽(𝔄)=2\dim_{\mathbb{F}}(\mathfrak{A})=2 and 1𝔄≠01_{\mathfrak{A}}\neq 0, there exists 𝐞∈𝔄\mathbf{e}\in\mathfrak{A} such that B={1𝔄,𝐞}B=\{1_{\mathfrak{A}},\mathbf{e}\} is a basis of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}. Since 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is closed under multiplication, there exist α,β∈𝔽\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F} such that 𝐞2=α​1𝔄+β​𝐞\mathbf{e}^{2}=\alpha 1_{\mathfrak{A}}+\beta\mathbf{e}. Let 𝐮=a​1𝔄+b​𝐞\mathbf{u}=a1_{\mathfrak{A}}+b\mathbf{e} and 𝐯=c​1𝔄+d​𝐞\mathbf{v}=c1_{\mathfrak{A}}+d\mathbf{e} be two arbitrary elements of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}, with a,b,c,d∈𝔽a,b,c,d\in\mathbb{F}. Then

𝐮⋅𝐯=(a​1𝔄+b​𝐞)⋅(c​1𝔄+d​𝐞)=a​c​1𝔄⋅1𝔄+a​d​1𝔄⋅𝐞+b​c​𝐞⋅1𝔄+b​d​𝐞2=a​c​ 1𝔄+a​d​𝐞+b​c​𝐞+b​d​(α​1𝔄+β​𝐞)=(a​c+α​b​d)​1𝔄+(a​d+b​c+β​b​d)​𝐞\begin{split}\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}&=(a1_{\mathfrak{A}}+b\mathbf{e})\cdot(c1_{\mathfrak{A}}+d\mathbf{e})\\ &=ac1_{\mathfrak{A}}\cdot 1_{\mathfrak{A}}+ad1_{\mathfrak{A}}\cdot\mathbf{e}+bc\mathbf{e}\cdot 1_{\mathfrak{A}}+bd\mathbf{e}^{2}\\ &=ac\,1_{\mathfrak{A}}+ad\mathbf{e}+bc\mathbf{e}+bd(\alpha 1_{\mathfrak{A}}+\beta\mathbf{e})\\ &=(ac+\alpha bd)1_{\mathfrak{A}}+(ad+bc+\beta bd)\mathbf{e}\end{split} (20)

The right-hand side is symmetric in (a,b)(a,b) and (c,d)(c,d), since a​c+α​b​d=c​a+α​d​bac+\alpha bd=ca+\alpha db and a​d+b​c+β​b​d=c​b+d​a+β​d​bad+bc+\beta bd=cb+da+\beta db. Therefore 𝐮⋅𝐯=𝐯⋅𝐮∀𝐮,𝐯∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}\ \forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{A}. So every associative and unital 2​𝔽2\mathbb{F}-FDA is commutative.

(ii) Existence for n=3n=3.

Consider

𝔄=UT2(𝔽):={(ab0c):a,b,c∈𝔽},\mathfrak{A}=\textsc{UT}_{2}(\mathbb{F}):=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ 0&c\end{pmatrix}\ :\ a,b,c\in\mathbb{F}\right\},

equipped with the usual matrix multiplication. This is the algebra of upper triangular 2×22\times 2 matrices over 𝔽\mathbb{F}. We have 𝔄=span𝔽​{𝐚(1),𝐚(2),𝐚(3)}\mathfrak{A}=\text{span}_{\mathbb{F}}\left\{\mathbf{a}^{(1)},\mathbf{a}^{(2)},\mathbf{a}^{(3)}\right\} where

𝐚(1)=(1000),𝐚(2)=(0100),𝐚(3)=(0001)\mathbf{a}^{(1)}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf{a}^{(2)}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ 0&0\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathbf{a}^{(3)}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\ 0&1\end{pmatrix} (21)

These three matrices are linearly independent, so dim𝔽(𝔄)=3\dim_{\mathbb{F}}(\mathfrak{A})=3. Since matrix multiplication is bilinear and associative, (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) is an associative 3​𝔽3\mathbb{F}-FDA. It is also unital, with unit 1𝔄=𝐚(1)+𝐚(3)1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathbf{a}^{(1)}+\mathbf{a}^{(3)}. Finally, 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is not commutative, because 𝐚(1)​𝐚(2)=𝐚(2)≠0=𝐚(2)​𝐚(1)\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\mathbf{a}^{(2)}=\mathbf{a}^{(2)}\neq 0=\mathbf{a}^{(2)}\mathbf{a}^{(1)}. ∎

B.3 Examples of FDA

Examples B.3, B.4 and B.5 are associative, commutative and unital. Example B.6 is associative and unital but not commutative. The algebra of quaternions is associative and unitary but non-commutative. The algebra of octonions is unitary but neither associative nor commutative. Lie algebras (Example B.8) are not associative, not commutative, nor unital.

Example B.3 (Complex Numbers).

𝔽=ℝ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}, n=2n=2 and 𝔄=ℂ=(𝔽2,⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\mathbb{C}=\left(\mathbb{F}^{2},\cdot\right). The product ⋅\cdot is defined as (a+b​𝐢)⋅(c+d​𝐢):=(a​c−b​d)+(a​d+b​c)​𝐢(a+b\mathbf{i})\cdot(c+d\mathbf{i}):=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)\mathbf{i} with 𝐢2=−1\mathbf{i}^{2}=-1. The structure tensor of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in its canonical basis (𝐚(1),𝐚(2))≡(1,𝐢)(\mathbf{a}^{(1)},\mathbf{a}^{(2)})\equiv(1,\mathbf{i}) is

[𝓒111𝓒112𝓒121𝓒122],[𝓒211𝓒212𝓒221𝓒222]=[1001],[01−10]\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{111}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{112}\\ \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{121}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{122}\\ \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{211}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{212}\\ \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{221}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{222}\\ \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\\ \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\\ \end{bmatrix} (22)

since 𝐚(1)⋅𝐚(1)=𝐚(1)⟹𝓒11:=[1,0]\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(1)}=\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\Longrightarrow\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{11:}=[1,0], 𝐚(1)⋅𝐚(2)=𝐚(2)⋅𝐚(1)=𝐚(2)⟹𝓒12:=𝓒21:=[0,1]\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(2)}=\mathbf{a}^{(2)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(1)}=\mathbf{a}^{(2)}\Longrightarrow\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{12:}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{21:}=[0,1], and 𝐚(2)⋅𝐚(2)=−𝐚(1)⟹𝓒22:=[−1,0]\mathbf{a}^{(2)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(2)}=-\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\Longrightarrow\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{22:}=[-1,0]. In the field 𝔽=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} for pp prime, we have 𝐢=(−1)%​p=p−1\mathbf{i}=(-1)\%p=p-1, so 𝓒221=p−1\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{221}=p-1.

In the same way, we can also calculate the structure constants of quaternions (n=4n=4) and octonions (n=8n=8).

Example B.4 (Dual Numbers).

𝔄=(𝔽2,⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\mathbb{F}^{2},\cdot\right) with product ⋅\cdot is defined as (a+b​ε)⋅(c+d​ε):=a​c+(a​d+b​c)​ε(a+b\varepsilon)\cdot(c+d\varepsilon):=ac+(ad+bc)\varepsilon, where ε2=0\varepsilon^{2}=0. The structure tensor of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in its canonical basis (𝐚(1),𝐚(2))≡(1,ε)(\mathbf{a}^{(1)},\mathbf{a}^{(2)})\equiv(1,\varepsilon) is

[𝓒111𝓒112𝓒121𝓒122],[𝓒211𝓒212𝓒221𝓒222]=[1001],[0100]\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{111}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{112}\\ \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{121}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{122}\\ \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{211}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{212}\\ \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{221}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{222}\\ \end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\\ \end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ 0&0\\ \end{bmatrix} (23)
Example B.5 (Polynomials modulo xn−1x^{n}-1).

𝔄=(𝔽n−1​[x],⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\mathbb{F}_{n-1}[x],\cdot\right), with 𝔽n−1​[x]\mathbb{F}_{n-1}[x] the set of polynomial of degree at most n−1n-1 on 𝔽\mathbb{F}. The product ⋅\cdot is defined as (∑i=0n−1ai​xi)⋅(∑i=0n−1bi​xi):=∑i,j=0n−1ai​bi​x(i+j)%​n=∑k=0n−1(∑i,j=0n−1ai​bi​δk,(i+j)%​n)​xk\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}a_{i}x^{i}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}b_{i}x^{i}\right):=\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}a_{i}b_{i}x^{(i+j)\%n}=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(\sum_{i,j=0}^{n-1}a_{i}b_{i}\delta_{k,(i+j)\%n}\right)x^{k}. Equivalently, 𝔄≃𝔽⁡[x]/(xn−1)\mathfrak{A}\simeq\mathbb{F}[x]/(x^{n}-1), with 𝔽⁡[x]\mathbb{F}[x] the polynomial ring in one indeterminate xx over the field 𝔽\mathbb{F}. The structure tensor of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in its canonical basis (𝐚(0),…,𝐚(n−1))≡(x0,⋯,xn−1)(\mathbf{a}^{(0)},\dots,\mathbf{a}^{(n-1)})\equiv(x^{0},\cdots,x^{n-1}) is 𝓒i​j​k=δk,(i+j)%​n∀i,j,k∈⟦0,n−1⟧\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=\delta_{k,(i+j)\%n}\ \forall i,j,k\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket since xi⋅xj=x(i+j)modnx^{i}\cdot x^{j}=x^{(i+j)\bmod n}. Here we adopt 00-based indexing, i.e., indices range from 00 to n−1n-1, for the convenience of notation.

Example B.6 (Square matrices of size nn).

𝔄=(ℳn​(𝔽),⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{F}),\cdot\right), with ℳn​(𝔽)\mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{F}) the set of square matrices of size nn with entries in 𝔽\mathbb{F}. The product ⋅\cdot is defined as (𝐀⋅𝐁)i​j:=∑k=1n𝐀i​k​𝐁k​j\left(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}\right)_{ij}:=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{A}_{ik}\mathbf{B}_{kj}. Let’s consider the canonical basis B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n2]={𝐚((q−1)​n+r)}(q,r)∈[n]2B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n^{2}]}=\{\mathbf{a}^{((q-1)n+r)}\}_{(q,r)\in[n]^{2}} of ℳn​(𝔽)\mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{F}), where each 𝐚((q−1)​n+r)\mathbf{a}^{((q-1)n+r)} has 1𝔽1_{\mathbb{F}} at position (q,r)∈[n]2(q,r)\in[n]^{2} and 0𝔽0_{\mathbb{F}} everywhere. Since 𝐚((q1−1)​n+r1)⋅𝐚((q2−1)​n+r2)=δq2​r1​𝐚((q1−1)​n+r2)\mathbf{a}^{((q_{1}-1)n+r_{1})}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{((q_{2}-1)n+r_{2})}=\delta_{q_{2}r_{1}}\mathbf{a}^{((q_{1}-1)n+r_{2})}, the structure tensor of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in BB is 𝓒(q1−1)​n+r1,(q2−1)​n+r2,(q3−1)​n+r3=δq2​r1​δq1​q3​δr2​r3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(q_{1}-1)n+r_{1},(q_{2}-1)n+r_{2},(q_{3}-1)n+r_{3}}=\delta_{q_{2}r_{1}}\delta_{q_{1}q_{3}}\delta_{r_{2}r_{3}}.

Example B.7 (Upper triangular matrices of size tt).

𝔄=(UTt​(𝔽),⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\textsc{UT}_{t}(\mathbb{F}),\cdot\right), with UTt​(𝔽):={𝐀∈ℳt​(𝔽):𝐀i​j=0𝔽​∀i>j}\textsc{UT}_{t}(\mathbb{F}):=\left\{\mathbf{A}\in\mathcal{M}_{t}(\mathbb{F}):\mathbf{A}_{ij}=0_{\mathbb{F}}\forall i>j\right\} the set of upper triangular square matrices of size mm with entries in 𝔽\mathbb{F}. The product ⋅\cdot is defined as the usual matrix multiplication. The dimension of UTt​(𝔽)\textsc{UT}_{t}(\mathbb{F}) is n=t⁡(t+1)2n=\frac{t(t+1)}{2}, since the free entries are exactly those on and above the diagonal.

Example B.8.

A Lie algebra (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) is an algebra whose binary operation ⋅\cdot (generally denoted by [⋅,⋅][\cdot,\cdot] and called the Lie bracket) satisfies the alternating property (or antisymmetry) 𝐮⋅𝐮=0​∀𝐮∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}=0\ \forall\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A}, and the Jacobi identity (𝐮⋅𝐯)⋅𝐰+(𝐯⋅𝐰)⋅𝐮+(𝐰⋅𝐮)⋅𝐯=0​∀𝐮,𝐯,𝐰∈𝔄(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})\cdot\mathbf{w}+(\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{w})\cdot\mathbf{u}+(\mathbf{w}\cdot\mathbf{u})\cdot\mathbf{v}=0\ \forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{A}.

For any associative algebra (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot), one can define a Lie algebra using [𝐮,𝐯]=𝐮⋅𝐯−𝐯⋅𝐮∀𝐮,𝐯∈𝔄[\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}]=\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{u}\ \forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{A}. For example, if we replace matrix multiplication 𝐀𝐁\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} with the matrix commutator 𝐀⋅𝐁:=𝐀𝐁−𝐁𝐀\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}:=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}, then 𝔄=(ℳn​(𝔽),⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{F}),\cdot\right) becomes a Lie algebra, with 𝓒(q1−1)​n+r1,(q2−1)​n+r2,(q3−1)​n+r3=δq2​r1​δq1​q3​δr2​r3−δq1​r2​δq2​q3​δr1​r3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(q_{1}-1)n+r_{1},(q_{2}-1)n+r_{2},(q_{3}-1)n+r_{3}}=\delta_{q_{2}r_{1}}\delta_{q_{1}q_{3}}\delta_{r_{2}r_{3}}-\delta_{q_{1}r_{2}}\delta_{q_{2}q_{3}}\delta_{r_{1}r_{3}}. In general, we have the following result about the structure tensor of Lie Algebra.

Proposition B.8.

An n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) with structure tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} in the basis B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} is a Lie algebra if and only if

  • (i)

    skew-symmetric:

    𝓒i​j​k=−𝓒j​i​k∀i,j,k∈[n];\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=-\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{jik}\qquad\forall i,j,k\in[n]; (24)
  • (ii)

    Jacobi identity:

    ∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓒k​ℓ​m+∑k=1n𝓒j​ℓ​k​𝓒k​i​m+∑k=1n𝓒ℓ​i​k​𝓒k​j​m=0∀i,j,ℓ,m∈[n]\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{k\ell m}+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{j\ell k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{kim}+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{\ell ik}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{kjm}=0\qquad\forall i,j,\ell,m\in[n] (25)
Proof.

Recall that (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) is a Lie algebra if and only if its product is bilinear, skew-symmetric, and satisfies the Jacobi identity. Since (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) is already an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA, bilinearity is part of the definition. It therefore remains to characterize skew-symmetry and the Jacobi identity in terms of 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}.

(i) We first characterize skew-symmetry. For all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], we have 𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j)=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝐚(k)\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{a}^{(k)} and 𝐚(j)⋅𝐚(i)=∑k=1n𝓒j​i​k​𝐚(k)\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(i)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{jik}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}. Thus,

𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j)=−𝐚(j)⋅𝐚(i)∀i,j∈[n]⟺∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k𝐚(k)=∑k=1n(−𝓒j​i​k)𝐚(k)∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)}=-\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\ \forall i,j\in[n]\Longleftrightarrow\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}(-\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{jik})\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\quad\forall i,j\in[n] (26)

Since B={𝐚(k)}k∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\}_{k\in[n]} is a basis, this holds if and only if Equation (24) holds.

(ii) We now characterize the Jacobi identity. For all i,j,ℓ∈[n]i,j,\ell\in[n], we have

(𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j))⋅𝐚(ℓ)=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​(𝐚(k)⋅𝐚(ℓ))=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​∑m=1n𝓒k​ℓ​m​𝐚(m)=∑m=1n(∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓒k​ℓ​m)​𝐚(m)(\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)})\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\left(\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\sum_{m=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{k\ell m}\mathbf{a}^{(m)}=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{k\ell m}\right)\mathbf{a}^{(m)} (27)

Similarly,

(𝐚(j)⋅𝐚(ℓ))⋅𝐚(i)=∑m=1n(∑k=1n𝓒j​ℓ​k​𝓒k​i​m)​𝐚(m) and (𝐚(ℓ)⋅𝐚(i))⋅𝐚(j)=∑m=1n(∑k=1n𝓒ℓ​i​k​𝓒k​j​m)​𝐚(m)(\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)})\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(i)}=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{j\ell k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{kim}\right)\mathbf{a}^{(m)}\quad\text{ and }\quad(\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(i)})\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)}=\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{\ell ik}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{kjm}\right)\mathbf{a}^{(m)} (28)

Thus, the Jacobi identity

(𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j))⋅𝐚(ℓ)+(𝐚(j)⋅𝐚(ℓ))⋅𝐚(i)+(𝐚(ℓ)⋅𝐚(i))⋅𝐚(j)=0∀i,j,ℓ∈[n](\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)})\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)}+(\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)})\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(i)}+(\mathbf{a}^{(\ell)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(i)})\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)}=0\qquad\forall i,j,\ell\in[n] (29)

is equivalent to

∑m=1n[∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓒k​ℓ​m+∑k=1n𝓒j​ℓ​k​𝓒k​i​m+∑k=1n𝓒ℓ​i​k​𝓒k​j​m]​𝐚(m)=0∀i,j,ℓ∈[n]\sum_{m=1}^{n}\left[\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{k\ell m}+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{j\ell k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{kim}+\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{\ell ik}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{kjm}\right]\mathbf{a}^{(m)}=0\qquad\forall i,j,\ell\in[n] (30)

Since BB is a basis, this holds if and only if Equation (25) holds. ∎

B.4 From Groups to FDA: A Unified View

Definition B.9.

For a group (G,∘)(G,\circ) and a field 𝔽\mathbb{F}, the group algebra of GG over 𝔽\mathbb{F}, denoted (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot), is the set of all linear combinations of elements of GG with coefficients in 𝔽\mathbb{F}. If GG has nn elements {gi}i∈[n]\{g_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}, then 𝔽[G]={∑i=1nαigi∣α1,…,αn∈𝔽}\mathbb{F}[G]=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}g_{i}\ \mid\ \alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{n}\in\mathbb{F}\right\} and (∑i=1nαi​gi)⋅(∑j=1nβj​gj)=∑i,j=1nαi​βi​(gi∘gj)=∑k=1n(∑i,j=1nαi​βj​𝟙​(gi∘gj=gk))​gk\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}g_{i}\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\beta_{j}g_{j}\right)=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}\beta_{i}\left(g_{i}\circ g_{j}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}\beta_{j}\mathbb{1}(g_{i}\circ g_{j}=g_{k})\right)g_{k}, with 𝟙\mathbb{1} the indicator function. We have 1𝔽⁡[G]=e1_{\mathbb{F}[G]}=e, with ee is the identity of GG. The structure tensor of 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G] in {gi}i=1n\{g_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} is 𝓒i​j​k=𝟙⁡(gk=gi∘gj)∈{0,1}​∀i,j,k∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=\mathbb{1}(g_{k}=g_{i}\circ g_{j})\in\{0,1\}\ \forall i,j,k\in[n].

Note that the formal expression ∑i=1nαi​gi\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}g_{i} should not be interpreted as a genuine linear combination inside GG, since a group has no intrinsic compatibility between its operation ∘\circ and the scalar or additive structure of 𝔽\mathbb{F}. As explained in Section 3, this expression acquires meaning once we pass to one-hot encoding. Redefine 𝔽⁡[G]:={∑i=1nαi​𝐚(i)|α∈𝔽n}\mathbb{F}[G]:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\;\big|\;\alpha\in\mathbb{F}^{n}\right\} where 𝐚(i)=Ψ⁡(gi)\mathbf{a}^{(i)}=\Psi(g_{i}) and Ψ:G→{0𝔽,1𝔽}n\Psi:G\to\{0_{\mathbb{F}},1_{\mathbb{F}}\}^{n} is the one-hot encoding of GG over 𝔽\mathbb{F}, given by Ψ⁡(gi):=[𝟙⁡(gk=gi)]k∈[n]\Psi(g_{i}):=\big[\mathbb{1}(g_{k}=g_{i})\big]_{k\in[n]}. Multiplication in 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G], which is a free vector space over GG with multiplication given by linearly extending the group law, is then defined by 𝐮⋅𝐯:=∑i,j𝐮i​𝐯j​Ψ​(gi∘gj)=∑k=1n(∑i,j=1n𝐮i​𝐯j​𝟙​(gi∘gj=gk))​𝐚(k)\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}:=\sum_{i,j}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\Psi(g_{i}\circ g_{j})=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\Big(\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\mathbb{1}(g_{i}\circ g_{j}=g_{k})\Big)\mathbf{a}^{(k)} for all 𝐮=∑i𝐮i​𝐚(i)\mathbf{u}=\sum_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)} and 𝐯=∑j𝐯j​𝐚(j)\mathbf{v}=\sum_{j}\mathbf{v}_{j}\mathbf{a}^{(j)}. In this way, linear combinations of group elements become well-defined elements of the vector space 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G], and the group multiplication naturally extends to an algebra product on 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G]. With this construction, we can show that (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot) is an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA, and that training a model on the group (G,∘)(G,\circ) is equivalent to training it on the multiplication in (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot).

Proposition B.10.

For a finite group (G,∘)(G,\circ) with nn elements {gi}i∈[n]\{g_{i}\}_{i\in[n]} and identity ee, (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot) is an nn-dimensional associative and unital 𝔽\mathbb{F}-FDA with 1𝔽⁡[G]=Ψ⁡(e)1_{\mathbb{F}[G]}=\Psi(e). Also, (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot) is commutative if and only if GG is commutative. Moreover, the structure tensor of 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G] in B={Ψ⁡(gi)}i∈[n]B=\{\Psi(g_{i})\}_{i\in[n]} is given by 𝓒i​j​k=𝟙𝔽​(gi∘gj=gk)​∀i,j,k∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=\mathbb{1}_{\mathbb{F}}(g_{i}\circ g_{j}=g_{k})\ \forall i,j,k\in[n]; and we have Ψ(gi∘gj)=𝓒×1Ψ(gi)×2Ψ(gj)∀i,j∈[n]\Psi(g_{i}\circ g_{j})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\Psi(g_{i})\times_{2}\Psi(g_{j})\ \forall i,j\in[n].

Proof.

It is easy to check that 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G] is a vector space over 𝔽\mathbb{F}, and that ⋅\cdot verifies the axioms of an algebra operation (bilinearity, right and left distributivity, compatibility with scalars). The associativity and unitality conditions follow from the fact that GG is by definition associative and unital. Now, let i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n]. We have Ψ⁡(gi)⋅Ψ⁡(gj)=Ψ⁡(gi∘gj)\Psi(g_{i})\cdot\Psi(g_{j})=\Psi(g_{i}\circ g_{j}), so 𝓒i​j​k=𝟙⁡(gk=gi∘gj)=(Ψ⁡(gi∘gj))k​∀k∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=\mathbb{1}(g_{k}=g_{i}\circ g_{j})=(\Psi(g_{i}\circ g_{j}))_{k}\ \forall k\in[n]. If GG is commutative, then 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G] is commutative by Proposition B.5 since 𝓒i​j​k=𝟙⁡(gi∘gj=gk)=𝟙⁡(gj∘gi=gk)=𝓒j​i​k​∀i,j,k∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=\mathbb{1}(g_{i}\circ g_{j}=g_{k})=\mathbb{1}(g_{j}\circ g_{i}=g_{k})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{jik}\ \forall i,j,k\in[n]. The converse is also true by the same proposition. Finally, we have Ψ(gi∘gj)=𝓒×1Ψ(gi)×2Ψ(gj)\Psi(g_{i}\circ g_{j})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\Psi(g_{i})\times_{2}\Psi(g_{j}) for all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n] since

(𝓒×1Ψ(gi)×2Ψ(gj))k=∑l,r=1n𝓒l​r​k(Ψ(gi))l(Ψ(gj))r=∑l,r=1n𝓒l​r​kδl​iδr​j=𝓒i​j​k=(Ψ(gi∘gj))k∀k∈[n]\begin{split}\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\Psi(g_{i})\times_{2}\Psi(g_{j})\right)_{k}=\sum_{l,r=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{lrk}(\Psi(g_{i}))_{l}(\Psi(g_{j}))_{r}=\sum_{l,r=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{lrk}\delta_{li}\delta_{rj}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=(\Psi(g_{i}\circ g_{j}))_{k}\ \forall k\in[n]\end{split} (31)

∎

Remark B.11.

Given a group G={gi}i∈[n]G=\{g_{i}\}_{i\in[n]}, the structure tensor of 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G] in B={Ψ⁡(gi)}i∈[n]B=\{\Psi(g_{i})\}_{i\in[n]} is the same for all 𝔽=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}, p>1p>1. For all i,j,k∈[n]i,j,k\in[n], we have 𝓒i​j​k=1\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=1 if gi∘gj=gkg_{i}\circ g_{j}=g_{k} and 00 otherwise. So for groups and finite fields, we can always choose p=2p=2 without loss of generality.

Remark B.12.

The assignment sending a group GG to its group algebra 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G] is a functor from the category of groups to the category of 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebras. Indeed, to every group homomorphism ϕ:G→H\phi:G\to H one can associate the algebra homomorphism 𝔽⁡[ϕ]:𝔽⁡[G]→𝔽⁡[H]\mathbb{F}[\phi]:\mathbb{F}[G]\to\mathbb{F}[H] defined by 𝔽⁡[ϕ]​(∑g∈Gαg​g):=∑g∈Gαg​ϕ​(g)=∑h∈H(∑g∈G,ϕ⁡(g)=hαg)​h\mathbb{F}[\phi]\left(\sum_{g\in G}\alpha_{g}g\right):=\sum_{g\in G}\alpha_{g}\phi(g)=\sum_{h\in H}\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}g\in G,\ \phi(g)=h\end{subarray}}\alpha_{g}\right)h. This construction preserves identities (𝔽⁡[idG]=id𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[\mathrm{id}_{G}]=\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{F}[G]} with idG\mathrm{id}_{G} the identity map on the group GG, and id𝔽⁡[G]\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb{F}[G]} the identity map on the algebra 𝔽⁡[G]\mathbb{F}[G]) and composition (𝔽⁡[ψ∘ϕ]=𝔽⁡[ψ]∘𝔽⁡[ϕ]\mathbb{F}[\psi\circ\phi]=\mathbb{F}[\psi]\circ\mathbb{F}[\phi] for all ϕ:G→H\phi:G\to H and ψ:H→K\psi:H\to K). Hence, it defines a functor. As a consequence, 𝔽⁡[Ψ]\mathbb{F}[\Psi] is an isomorphism between (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot) and (𝔽⁡[𝓒],×)(\mathbb{F}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}],\times) in Proposition B.10.

(32)
Example B.9 (Group algebra of the additive group ℤ/n​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z} over 𝔽\mathbb{F}).

𝔄=(𝔽⁡[ℤ/n​ℤ],⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\mathbb{F}[\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}],\cdot\right), with ℤ/nℤ={gi}i∈⟦0,n−1⟧≡⟦0,n−1⟧\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}=\left\{g_{i}\right\}_{i\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket}\equiv\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket and gi∘gj=(i+j)modn=g(i+j)modn∀i,j∈⟦0,n−1⟧g_{i}\circ g_{j}=(i+j)\mod n=g_{(i+j)\mod n}\ \forall i,j\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket. So 𝓒i​j​k=𝟙(gk=gi∘gj)=δk,(i+j)%​n∀i,j,k∈⟦0,n−1⟧\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=\mathbb{1}(g_{k}=g_{i}\circ g_{j})=\delta_{k,(i+j)\%n}\ \forall i,j,k\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket. This is the structure tensor of 𝔽n−1​[x]=𝔽⁡[x]/(xn−1)\mathbb{F}_{n-1}[x]=\mathbb{F}[x]/(x^{n}-1) in its canonical basis (Example B.5), so 𝔽⁡[ℤ/n​ℤ]≅𝔽n−1​[x]\mathbb{F}[\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}]\cong\mathbb{F}_{n-1}[x]. Here we adopt 00-based indexing for the convenience of notation.

Example B.10 (Group algebra of the Dihedral group DtD_{t} over 𝔽\mathbb{F}).

𝔄=(𝔽⁡[Dt],⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\mathbb{F}[D_{t}],\cdot\right), with Dt=(r0,…,rt−1,s0,…,st−1)D_{t}=(r_{0},\dots,r_{t-1},s_{0},\dots,s_{t-1}) the group of symmetries of a regular tt-gon, where each rir_{i} denotes the rotation of angle 2​π​i/t2\pi i/t and each sis_{i} the reflection across the axis passing through vertex ii (the axis at angle π​i/t\pi i/t). The group composition is given by

ri∘rj=r(i+j)%​t,ri∘sj=s(i+j)%​t,si∘rj=s(i−j)%​t,si∘sj=r(i−j)%​t∀i,j∈⟦0,t−1⟧r_{i}\circ r_{j}=r_{(i+j)\%t},\quad r_{i}\circ s_{j}=s_{(i+j)\%t},\quad s_{i}\circ r_{j}=s_{(i-j)\%t},\quad s_{i}\circ s_{j}=r_{(i-j)\%t}\quad\forall i,j\in\llbracket 0,t-1\rrbracket (33)

We have n=dim𝔽​𝔄=|Dt|=2​tn=\mathrm{dim}_{\mathbb{F}}\mathfrak{A}=|D_{t}|=2t. Let us index the elements of Dt={gi}i∈⟦0,n−1⟧D_{t}=\{g_{i}\}_{i\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket} by gi=rig_{i}=r_{i} for i∈⟦0,t−1⟧i\in\llbracket 0,t-1\rrbracket and gi=si−tg_{i}=s_{i-t} for i∈⟦t,n−1⟧i\in\llbracket t,n-1\rrbracket. Then, for all i,j,k∈⟦0,n−1⟧i,j,k\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket, the structure tensor of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in its canonical basis {gi}i∈⟦0,n−1⟧\{g_{i}\}_{i\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket} is given by

𝓒i​j​k={δk,(i+j)%​tif ​0≤i,j<tsince ​gi∘gj=rj∘ri=r(i+j)%​t=g(i+j)%​tδk,t+(i+j−t)%​tif ​0≤i<t,t≤j<2​tsince ​gi∘gj=ri∘sj−t=s(i+j−t)%​t=gt+(i+j−t)%​tδk,t+(i−t−j)%​tif ​t≤i<2​t,0≤j<tsince ​gi∘gj=si−t∘rj=s(i−t−j)%​t=gt+(i−t−j)%​tδk,((i−t)−(j−t))%​tif ​t≤i,j<2​tsince ​gi∘gj=si−t∘sj−t=r(i−t−j+t)%​t=g(i−t−j+t)%​t\begin{split}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}&=\left\{\begin{array}[]{llll}\delta_{k,(i+j)\%t}&\mbox{if }0\leq i,j<t&\mbox{since }g_{i}\circ g_{j}=r_{j}\circ r_{i}=r_{(i+j)\%t}=g_{(i+j)\%t}\\[5.69054pt] \delta_{k,t+(i+j-t)\%t}&\mbox{if }0\leq i<t,\ t\leq j<2t&\mbox{since }g_{i}\circ g_{j}=r_{i}\circ s_{j-t}=s_{(i+j-t)\%t}=g_{t+(i+j-t)\%t}\\[5.69054pt] \delta_{k,t+(i-t-j)\%t}&\mbox{if }t\leq i<2t,0\leq j<t&\mbox{since }g_{i}\circ g_{j}=s_{i-t}\circ r_{j}=s_{(i-t-j)\%t}=g_{t+(i-t-j)\%t}\\[5.69054pt] \delta_{k,((i-t)-(j-t))\%t}&\mbox{if }t\leq i,j<2t&\mbox{since }g_{i}\circ g_{j}=s_{i-t}\circ s_{j-t}=r_{(i-t-j+t)\%t}=g_{(i-t-j+t)\%t}\end{array}\right.\end{split}
Example B.11 (Group algebra of the symmetric group StS_{t} over 𝔽\mathbb{F}).

𝔄=(𝔽⁡[St],⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\mathbb{F}[S_{t}],\cdot\right). The elements of 𝔽⁡[St]\mathbb{F}[S_{t}] can be seen as endomorphisms of 𝔽t\mathbb{F}^{t} and can be written 𝐮=∑σ∈St𝐮σ​σ\mathbf{u}=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{t}}\mathbf{u}_{\sigma}\sigma, i.e. 𝐮\mathbf{u} takes an element of 𝔽t\mathbb{F}^{t}, applies all the permutations of StS_{t} to it, then makes a linear combination of these permutations with coefficients (𝐮σ)σ∈St(\mathbf{u}_{\sigma})_{\sigma\in S_{t}} in 𝔽\mathbb{F}. The product ⋅\cdot is define as (∑σ∈St𝐮σ​σ)⋅(∑π∈St𝐯π​π)=∑σ,π∈St𝐮σ​𝐯π​(σ∘π)=∑γ∈St(∑σ∘π=γ𝐮σ​𝐯π)​γ\left(\sum_{\sigma\in S_{t}}\mathbf{u}_{\sigma}\sigma\right)\cdot\left(\sum_{\pi\in S_{t}}\mathbf{v}_{\pi}\pi\right)=\sum_{\sigma,\pi\in S_{t}}\mathbf{u}_{\sigma}\mathbf{v}_{\pi}\left(\sigma\circ\pi\right)=\sum_{\gamma\in S_{t}}\left(\sum_{\sigma\circ\pi=\gamma}\mathbf{u}_{\sigma}\mathbf{v}_{\pi}\right)\gamma, where ∘\circ is the composition of permutations. We have n=dim𝔽​𝔄=|St|=t!n=\text{dim}_{\mathbb{F}}\mathfrak{A}=|S_{t}|=t!.

B.5 Representation of FDA

Structure-like groups have representations with respect to their elements and the operators acting on them.

Definition B.13.

A representation of a group (G,∘)(G,\circ) over a field 𝔽\mathbb{F} is a group homomorphism ρ:G→GLm​(𝔽)\rho:G\to\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) such that ρ⁡(g∘h)=ρ⁡(g)​ρ​(h)​∀g,h∈G\rho(g\circ h)=\rho(g)\rho(h)\ \forall g,h\in G and ρ⁡(e)=𝕀m\rho(e)=\mathbb{I}_{m}, where ee is the identity of GG.

For example, any cyclic group of order pp generated by gg has the following 2-dimensional irreducible representation:

ρ(gk)=(cos⁡(2​π​kp)−sin⁡(2​π​kp)sin⁡(2​π​kp)cos⁡(2​π​kp))∀k∈⟦0,p⟧\rho(g^{k})=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k}{p}\right)&-\sin\left(\frac{2\pi k}{p}\right)\\ \sin\left(\frac{2\pi k}{p}\right)&\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k}{p}\right)\end{pmatrix}\ \forall k\in\llbracket 0,p\rrbracket (34)

Each element gkg^{k} is represented by the angle rotation 2​π​k/p2\pi k/p. An example of a finite cyclic group of order pp is the additive group (𝔽p,+)(\mathbb{F}_{p},+) for pp a prime integer.

Definition B.14.

The representation of an 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebra (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) involves a homomorphism ρ\rho from 𝔄\mathfrak{A} to the algebra of matrices (Example B.6), preserving both the linear and the multiplicative structures, i.e. ρ⁡(α​𝐮+β​𝐯)=α​ρ​(𝐮)+β​ρ​(𝐯)\rho(\alpha\mathbf{u}+\beta\mathbf{v})=\alpha\rho(\mathbf{u})+\beta\rho(\mathbf{v}) and ρ⁡(𝐮⋅𝐯)=ρ⁡(𝐮)​ρ​(𝐯)\rho(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})=\rho(\mathbf{u})\rho(\mathbf{v}) for all 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔄\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{A} and α,β∈𝔽\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}. When 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is unital, it is also required that ρ⁡(1𝔄)=𝕀\rho(1_{\mathfrak{A}})=\mathbb{I}, the identity matrix.

This notion of algebra representation is central to the interpretation of the results of this paper. However, the theory of algebra representations is somewhat more abstract than that of groups, involving concepts such as (right or left) modules of algebra, semi-simplicity, and others. Nevertheless, the picture becomes less abstract (though still difficult) if we work directly with the structure tensor of the algebra. Let us consider the representations of an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) over 𝔽\mathbb{F} itself, of dimension m∈ℕ∗m\in\mathbb{N}^{*}. From the Definition B.14, we see that it is necessary and sufficient (Proposition B.15) to find a representation 𝓡i:=ρ⁡(𝐚(i))∈𝔽m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}:=\rho(\mathbf{a}^{(i)})\in\mathbb{F}^{m\times m} of the elements of a basis B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} in order to represent all other elements using

ρ⁡(∑k=1nαk​𝐚(k))=∑k=1nαk​𝓡k​∀(α1,⋯,αn)∈𝔽n\rho\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\ \forall(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{n})\in\mathbb{F}^{n} (35)

In this way, we always have ρ⁡(α​𝐮+β​𝐯)=α​ρ​(𝐮)+β​ρ​(𝐯)\rho(\alpha\mathbf{u}+\beta\mathbf{v})=\alpha\rho(\mathbf{u})+\beta\rho(\mathbf{v}) for all 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔄\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{A} and α,β∈𝔽\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{F}. To also ensure that ρ⁡(𝐮⋅𝐯)=ρ⁡(𝐮)​ρ​(𝐯)​∀𝐮,𝐯∈𝔄\rho(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})=\rho(\mathbf{u})\rho(\mathbf{v})\ \forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathfrak{A}, it is necessary and sufficient (Propositon B.16) that

Pi,j​(𝓡):=𝓡i​𝓡j−∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k(B)​𝓡k=0​∀i,j∈[n]P_{i,j}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}):=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}-\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}=0\ \forall i,j\in[n] (36)

That is,

Pi,jl,r(𝓡):=∑s=1m𝓡i​l​s𝓡j​s​r−∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k(B)𝓡k​l​r=0∀i,j∈[n];l,r∈[m]P_{i,j}^{l,r}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}):=\sum_{s=1}^{m}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{ils}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{jsr}-\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{klr}=0\ \forall i,j\in[n];\;l,r\in[m] (37)
Proposition B.15.

Let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) be an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA. For all representation ρ\rho and all basis B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}, we have ρ⁡(∑k=1nαk​𝐚(k))=∑k=1nαk​ρ​(𝐚(k))​∀(α1,⋯,αn)∈𝔽n\rho\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}\rho\left(\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right)\ \forall(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{n})\in\mathbb{F}^{n} and ρ⁡(𝐚(i))​ρ​(𝐚(j))=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k(B)​ρ​(𝐚(k))​∀i,j∈[n]\rho\left(\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\right)\rho\left(\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{ijk}\rho\left(\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right)\ \forall i,j\in[n].

Proof.

ρ⁡(∑k=1nαk​𝐚(k))=∑k=1nαk​ρ​(𝐚(k))​∀α∈𝔽n\rho\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}\rho\left(\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right)\ \forall\alpha\in\mathbb{F}^{n} since ρ\rho is an algebra homomorphism. For all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n] :

ρ⁡(𝐚(i))​ρ​(𝐚(j))=ρ⁡(𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j))​ since ρ is an algebra homomorphism=ρ⁡(∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k(B)​𝐚(k))​ by the definition of 𝓒(B)=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k(B)​ρ​(𝐚(k))\begin{split}\rho\left(\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\right)\rho\left(\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\right)&=\rho\left(\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\right)\text{ since $\rho$ is an algebra homomorphism}\\ &=\rho\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{ijk}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right)\text{ by the definition of $\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}$}\\ &=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{ijk}\rho\left(\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right)\end{split} (38)

∎

Proposition B.16.

Let (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) be an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA with structure tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} in B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}. Fix m∈ℕ∗m\in\mathbb{N}^{*} and 𝓡∈𝔽n×m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times m\times m}. Set 𝓡k=𝓡k,:,:∈𝔽m×m∀k∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k,:,:}\in\mathbb{F}^{m\times m}\ \forall k\in[n], and define the linear map ρ:𝔄→ℳm​(𝔽)\rho:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) by

ρ⁡(∑k=1nαk​𝐚(k)):=∑k=1nαk​𝓡k​∀(α1,⋯,αn)∈𝔽n\rho\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right):=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\alpha_{k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\ \forall(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{n})\in\mathbb{F}^{n} (39)

Then ρ\rho is an algebra homomorphism if and only if

𝓡i​𝓡j=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\quad\forall i,j\in[n] (40)

If 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is unital with 1𝔄=∑i=1nλi​𝐚(i)1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}, then the additional condition ρ⁡(1𝔄)=𝕀m\rho(1_{\mathfrak{A}})=\mathbb{I}_{m} is equivalent to

∑i=1nλi​𝓡i=𝕀m\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{m} (41)
Proof.

(⟹\Longrightarrow) Suppose ρ\rho is an algebra homomorphism. Then, we have for all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n] :

𝓡i​𝓡j=ρ⁡(𝐚(i))​ρ​(𝐚(j))​ by the definition of ρ=ρ⁡(𝐚(i)⋅𝐚(j))​ since ρ is an algebra homomorphism=ρ⁡(∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝐚(k))​ by the definition of 𝓒 (Equation (12))=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k​ by the definition of ρ\begin{split}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}&=\rho(\mathbf{a}^{(i)})\rho(\mathbf{a}^{(j)})\text{ by the definition of $\rho$}\\ &=\rho\left(\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\cdot\mathbf{a}^{(j)}\right)\text{ since $\rho$ is an algebra homomorphism}\\ &=\rho\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right)\text{ by the definition of $\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}$ (Equation~\eqref{eq:structure_tensor})}\\ &=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\text{ by the definition of $\rho$}\end{split} (42)

(⟸\Longleftarrow) Assume (40) holds. For all 𝐮=∑i=1n𝐮i​𝐚(i)\mathbf{u}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)} and 𝐯=∑i=1n𝐯i​𝐚(i)\mathbf{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{v}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}, we have

ρ⁡(𝐮)​ρ​(𝐯)=(∑i=1n𝐮i​𝓡i)​(∑i=1n𝐯i​𝓡i)​ by the definition of ρ=∑i,j=1n𝐮i​𝐯j​𝓡i​𝓡j=∑i,j=1n𝐮i​𝐯j​∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k​ (Equation (40))=∑k=1n(∑i,j=1n𝐮i​𝐯j​𝓒i​j​k)​𝓡k=ρ⁡(∑k=1n(∑i,j=1n𝐮i​𝐯j​𝓒i​j​k)​𝐚(k))​ by the definition of ρ=ρ⁡(𝐮⋅𝐯)​ (Equation (13))\begin{split}\rho(\mathbf{u})\rho(\mathbf{v})&=\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbf{v}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\right)\text{ by the definition of $\rho$}\\ &=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}\\ &=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\text{ (Equation~\eqref{eq:R_iR_j=C_kR_k})}\\ &=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\right)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\\ &=\rho\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\right)\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\right)\text{ by the definition of $\rho$}\\ &=\rho\left(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}\right)\text{ (Equation~\eqref{eq:uv=Cuv})}\end{split} (43)

Therefore, ρ\rho is multiplicative. Since it is a 𝔽\mathbb{F}-linear map, this proves that it is a homomorphism of 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebras. ∎

From this proposition, it follows that we can find a solution 𝓡∈𝔽n×m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times m\times m} to

Pi,j​(𝓡):=𝓡i​𝓡j−∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k(B)​𝓡k=0​∀i,j∈[n]∑i=1nλi(B)​𝓡i=𝕀m​ if 𝔄 is unital with 1𝔄=∑i=1nλi(B)​𝐚(i)\begin{split}&P_{i,j}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}):=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}-\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{(B)}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}=0\ \forall i,j\in[n]\\ &\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda^{(B)}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{m}\text{ if $\mathfrak{A}$ is unital with $1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda^{(B)}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}$}\end{split} (44)

in order to obtain a representation of size mm of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} over 𝔽\mathbb{F}, or more generally over any field into which 𝔽\mathbb{F} embeds. In particular, even if 𝔽=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}, one may regard its elements as integer representatives and solve the same equations over ℝ\mathbb{R} or ℂ\mathbb{C}, so that real (or complex) matrix representations remain valid.

It should be noted that if we switch from the basis BB to another basis B~\tilde{B}, then a solution 𝓡\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}} in BB to the above system of equations becomes 𝓡×1𝐏⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top} in B~\tilde{B}, with 𝐏∈𝔽n×n\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n} the basis change matrix from BB to B~\tilde{B}.

Proposition B.17.

Let 𝓒\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}} and 𝓒~\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}} be the structure tensors of an n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA 𝔄\mathfrak{A} with respect to two bases B={𝐚(i))}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)})\}_{i\in[n]} and B~={𝐚~(i)}i∈[n]\tilde{B}=\{\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} respectively. Let 𝐏∈𝔽n×n\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n} be the basis change matrix from BB to B~\tilde{B}, i.e. 𝐚~(i)=∑k=1n𝐏k​i​𝐚(k)​∀i∈[n]\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(i)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{P}_{ki}\mathbf{a}^{(k)}\ \forall i\in[n]. For all 𝓡∈𝔽n×m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times m\times m}, by defining 𝓡~:=𝓡×1𝐏⊤\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}:=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}, which is equivalent to 𝓡=𝓡~×1𝐏−1⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}=\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}\times_{1}{\mathbf{P}^{-1}}^{\top}, we have:

    𝓡i​𝓡j=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k​∀i,j∈[n]⇔𝓡~i​𝓡~j=∑k=1n𝓒~i​j​k​𝓡~k​∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\ \forall i,j\in[n]\iff\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}}_{ijk}\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}_{k}\ \forall i,j\in[n];

    ∑i=1nλi​𝓡i=𝕀m⇔∑i=1nλ~i​𝓡~i=𝕀m\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{m}\iff\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{\lambda}_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{m} if further 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is unital with 1𝔄=∑i=1nλi​𝐚(i)=∑i=1nλ~i​𝐚~(i)1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\tilde{\lambda}_{i}\tilde{\mathbf{a}}^{(i)}.

Proof.

Let 𝓡∈𝔽n×m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times m\times m}. Set 𝓡~=𝓡×1𝐏⊤\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}. First, note that this is equivalent to 𝓡=𝓡~×1𝐏−1⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}=\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}\times_{1}{\mathbf{P}^{-1}}^{\top} since (𝓡×1𝐏⊤×1𝐏−1⊤)(1)=𝐏−1⊤(𝓡×1𝐏⊤)(1)=𝐏−1⊤𝐏⊤𝓡(1)=𝓡(1)(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\times_{1}{\mathbf{P}^{-1}}^{\top})_{(1)}={\mathbf{P}^{-1}}^{\top}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top})_{(1)}={\mathbf{P}^{-1}}^{\top}\mathbf{P}^{\top}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{(1)}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{(1)} and (𝓡~×1𝐏−1⊤×1𝐏⊤)(1)=𝐏⊤𝐏−1⊤𝓡~(1)=𝓡~(1)(\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}\times_{1}{\mathbf{P}^{-1}}^{\top}\times_{1}\mathbf{P}^{\top})_{(1)}=\mathbf{P}^{\top}{\mathbf{P}^{-1}}^{\top}\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}_{(1)}=\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}_{(1)} (Equation (8)).

Assume 𝓡i​𝓡j=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k​∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\ \forall i,j\in[n]. Then, for all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], we have:
