Then, for all i,j∈[n]i,j\in[n], we have (the derivation steps are similar to those above) 𝓡i𝓡j=∑k=1n(𝓒~×1𝐏−1⊤×2𝐏−1⊤×3𝐏)i​j​k𝓡k=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k𝓡k\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}}\times_{1}{\mathbf{P}^{-1}}^{\top}\times_{2}{\mathbf{P}^{-1}}^{\top}\times_{3}\mathbf{P}\right)_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}. ∎

We have a system of n2​m2n^{2}m^{2} (for a non-unital 𝔄\mathfrak{A}) or (n2+1)​m2(n^{2}+1)m^{2} (for a unital 𝔄\mathfrak{A}) non-linear equations in n​m2nm^{2} variables, so in general, overdetermined. Solutions form an algebraic variety. For a non-unital 𝔄\mathfrak{A}, the trivial solution is 𝓡=0n×m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}=0_{n\times m\times m}, the zero tensor. For a unital 𝔄\mathfrak{A}, there is no trivial solution. It is worth asking what is the smallest mm (or the values of mm) for which this system admits a non-trivial solution., i.e., a solution to

P⁡(𝓡)=∑i,j‖Pi,j​(𝓡)‖F2=∑i,j∑l,r(Pi,jl,r​(𝓡))2=0subject to∑i=1n‖𝓡i‖F2≠0∑i=1nλi(B)​𝓡i=𝕀m​ if 𝔄 is unital with 1𝔄=∑i=1nλi(B)​𝐚(i)\begin{split}&P(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}})=\sum_{i,j}\|P_{i,j}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}})\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}=\sum_{i,j}\sum_{l,r}\left(P_{i,j}^{l,r}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}})\right)^{2}=0\qquad\text{subject to}\qquad\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\|_{\mathrm{F}}^{2}\neq 0\\ &\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda^{(B)}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{m}\text{ if $\mathfrak{A}$ is unital with $1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda^{(B)}_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}$}\end{split} (47)

For associatives n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA, the smallest mm is less than or equal to nn, since the tensor 𝓡∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} defined by 𝓡i=𝓒i⊤​∀i∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}^{\top}\forall i\in[n] is solution to (44) (Proposition B.18). For non-unital FDA, if there is a solution for a certain mm, then there is one for all p≥mp\geq m. In fact, if 𝓡∈𝔽n×m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times m\times m} is solution to Equation (44), then for all 𝐀∈𝔽p×m\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{F}^{p\times m} and 𝐁∈𝔽m×p\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{F}^{m\times p} such that 𝐁𝐀=𝕀m\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}=\mathbb{I}_{m}, 𝓡~=[𝐀​𝓡i​𝐁]i∈[n]∈𝔽n×p×p\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}=\left[\mathbf{A}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{B}\right]_{i\in[n]}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times p\times p} is also solution to Equation (44) (Proposition B.19). But this is false for unital FDA in general. If ∑i=1nλi​𝓡i=𝕀m\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{m}, then we have ∑i=1nλi​𝐀​𝓡i​𝐁=𝐀⁡(∑i=1nλi​𝓡i)​𝐁=𝐀𝐁\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{A}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{A}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\right)\mathbf{B}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}. For this to equals 𝕀p\mathbb{I}_{p}, we need p=mp=m. Describing the solution set of (44) in full generality is challenging. A basic invariance is simultaneous conjugation: if 𝓡=[𝓡1,…,𝓡n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}=[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{n}] solves (44) for all i,ji,j, then so does [𝐒​𝓡1​𝐒−1,…,𝐒​𝓡n​𝐒−1][\mathbf{S}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}\mathbf{S}^{-1},\dots,\mathbf{S}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{n}\mathbf{S}^{-1}] for any 𝐒∈GLm​(𝔽)\mathbf{S}\in\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) (Corollary B.20).

Proposition B.18 (Left-regular representation).

If (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) is an associative n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA with structure tensor 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} in B={𝐚(i)}i∈[n]B=\{\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]}, then the tensor 𝓡∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} defined by 𝓡i:=𝓒i⊤​∀i∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}:=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}^{\top}\forall i\in[n] satisfies

𝓡i𝓡j=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k𝓡k=0∀i,j∈[n], and ∑i=1nλi𝓡i=𝕀n if 𝔄 is unital with 1𝔄=∑i=1nλi​𝐚(i)\begin{split}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}=0\ \forall i,j\in[n],\quad\text{ and }\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{n}\text{ if $\mathfrak{A}$ is unital with $1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{a}^{(i)}$}\end{split} (48)
Proof.

Assume (𝔄,⋅)(\mathfrak{A},\cdot) is an associative n​𝔽n\mathbb{F}-FDA. That is (Proposition B.5)

∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓒k​l​m=∑k=1n𝓒i​k​m​𝓒j​l​k​∀i,j,l,m∈[n]⟺∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​(𝓒k⊤)m​l=(𝓒i⊤​𝓒j⊤)m​l​∀i,j,l,m∈[n]⟺∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓒k⊤=𝓒i⊤​𝓒j⊤​∀i,j∈[n]⟺∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k=𝓡i​𝓡j​∀i,j∈[n]\begin{split}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{klm}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ikm}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{jlk}\ \forall i,j,l,m\in[n]&\Longleftrightarrow\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{k}^{\top})_{ml}=(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{j}^{\top})_{ml}\ \forall i,j,l,m\in[n]\\ &\Longleftrightarrow\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{k}^{\top}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{j}^{\top}\ \forall i,j\in[n]\\ &\Longleftrightarrow\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}\ \forall i,j\in[n]\end{split} (49)

If further 𝔄\mathfrak{A} is unital, then 𝓒×1λ=∑i=1nλi​𝓒i=𝕀n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\lambda=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{n} (Proposition B.5), which is equivalent to ∑i=1nλi​𝓡i=𝕀n\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{n}. ∎

Proposition B.19 (Invariance of the solution set).

Let 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n}. For all 𝓡∈𝔽n×m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times m\times m}, if 𝓡i​𝓡j=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k​∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\ \forall i,j\in[n], then (𝐀​𝓡i​𝐁)​(𝐀​𝓡j​𝐁)=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​(𝐀​𝓡k​𝐁)​∀i,j∈[n]\left(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{B}\right)\left(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}\mathbf{B}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\mathbf{B})\ \forall i,j\in[n] for all for all 𝐀∈𝔽p×m\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{F}^{p\times m} and 𝐁∈𝔽m×p\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{F}^{m\times p} such that 𝐁𝐀=𝕀m\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}=\mathbb{I}_{m}.

Corollary B.20 (Conjugacy invariance of the solution set).

Let 𝓒∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n}. For all 𝓡∈𝔽n×m×m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times m\times m}, if 𝓡i​𝓡j=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝓡k​∀i,j∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\ \forall i,j\in[n], then (𝐒​𝓡i​𝐒−1)​(𝐒​𝓡j​𝐒−1)=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​(𝐒​𝓡k​𝐒−1)​∀i,j∈[n]\left(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{S}^{-1}\right)\left(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}\mathbf{S}^{-1}\right)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{k}\mathbf{S}^{-1})\ \forall i,j\in[n] for all 𝐒∈GLm​(𝔽)\mathbf{S}\in\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{F}). If further ∑i=1nλi​𝓡i=𝕀m\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbb{I}_{m}, then ∑i=1nλi​𝐒​𝓡i​𝐒−1=𝕀m\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{S}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{S}^{-1}=\mathbb{I}_{m}.

It is therefore natural to work up to the equivalence relation defined on 𝔽n×m×m\mathbb{F}^{n\times m\times m} by the following equation, i.e., to consider orbits under simultaneous conjugation.

𝓡∼𝓡~⟺∃𝐒∈GLm(𝔽)such that𝓡~i=𝐒𝓡i𝐒−1∀i∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}\sim\tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists\mathbf{S}\in\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{F})\ \text{such that}\ \tilde{\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}}_{i}=\mathbf{S}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{S}^{-1}\ \ \forall i\in[n] (50)

One might hope this allows choosing a diagonal normal form. However, this would require a single change of basis that diagonalizes all 𝓡i\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i} at once. In general the 𝓡i\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i} need not commute or be simultaneously diagonalizable, so this reduction is not available without additional assumptions. Nevertheless, let us imagine we restrict ourselves to diagonal solutions. In that case, writing 𝓡i=diag⁡(𝐫i(1),…,𝐫i(m))\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbf{r}_{i}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{r}_{i}^{(m)}) for all i∈[n]i\in[n], the defining system (Equation (44)) decouples coordinate-wise. For each t∈[m]t\in[m], the scalars (𝐫1(t),…,𝐫n(t))(\mathbf{r}_{1}^{(t)},\dots,\mathbf{r}_{n}^{(t)}) must satisfy

𝐫i(t)​𝐫j(t)=∑k=1n𝓒i​j​k​𝐫k(t)∀i,j∈[n],∑i=1nλi​𝐫i(t)=1​ if ​𝔄​ is unital\begin{split}&\mathbf{r}_{i}^{(t)}\mathbf{r}_{j}^{(t)}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{r}_{k}^{(t)}\quad\forall i,j\in[n],\quad\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{r}_{i}^{(t)}=1\text{ if }\mathfrak{A}\text{ is unital}\end{split} (51)

Thus, the diagonal ansatz reduces the matrix problem to a family of scalar problems, one for each diagonal entry. A diagonal solution of size mm is obtained by picking mm points in

𝒮⁡(𝓒):={𝐫∈𝔽n:𝐫i​𝐫j=∑k𝓒i​j​k​𝐫k​∀(i,j)∈[n]2​and​∑iλi​𝐫i=1​if unitality holds}\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}):=\left\{\mathbf{r}\in\mathbb{F}^{n}:\mathbf{r}_{i}\mathbf{r}_{j}=\sum_{k}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}\mathbf{r}_{k}\ \forall(i,j)\in[n]^{2}\ \text{and}\ \sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\mathbf{r}_{i}=1\ \text{if unitality holds}\right\} (52)

and placing them on the diagonal (conjugation by permutation matrices only reorders the diagonal). Thus, diagonal solutions correspond to 𝒮​(𝓒)m/Sm\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}})^{m}/S_{m}66 6 The quotient /Sm/S_{m} indicates that two mm-tuples which differ only by a permutation of their coordinates correspond to the same diagonal solution.. In particular, a nontrivial diagonal solution exists if and only if 𝒮⁡(𝓒)∖{0}≠∅\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}})\setminus\{0\}\neq\emptyset. Hence, the minimal matrix size for a diagonal solution is m=1m=1 whenever 𝒮⁡(𝓒)\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}) contains a nonzero point; otherwise, no diagonal solution exists for any mm.

While the defining equations for representations are explicit (see (44) and the diagonal reduction (51)), a general description of their solution set (e.g., orbit structure, invariances, dimensions, and stratification) would require tools from algebraic geometry, invariant theory, or representation theory. For this reason, we now provide a few examples of representation for the algebras of Section B.3 and proceed to the next section, which addresses the problem of learning algebras using deep learning models.

Example B.12 (Complex Numbers).

For the algebra of complex numbers (Example B.3) with 𝔽=ℝ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R} and {𝐚(1),𝐚(2)}={1,𝐢}\{\mathbf{a}^{(1)},\mathbf{a}^{(2)}\}=\{1,\mathbf{i}\}, the relations are

𝓡12=𝓡1,𝓡1​𝓡2=𝓡2​𝓡1=𝓡2,𝓡22=−𝓡1,𝓡1=𝕀m​ since ​1𝔄=𝐚(1)\begin{split}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}^{2}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1},\ \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2},\ \mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}^{2}=-\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1},\quad\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}=\mathbb{I}_{m}\text{ since }1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathbf{a}^{(1)}\end{split} (53)

Therefore 𝓡1=𝕀m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}=\mathbb{I}_{m} (representation of multiplication by 11 in ℂ\mathbb{C} for m=2m=2) and 𝓡22=−𝕀m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}^{2}=-\mathbb{I}_{m}. This requires mm to be even, because over ℝ\mathbb{R} there is no odd-dimensional m×mm\times m real matrix squaring to −𝕀m-\mathbb{I}_{m}. The minimal case is m=2m=2 with 𝓡2=𝓒2⊤=[[0−1],[10]]=−𝓒2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}^{\top}=\begin{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0&-1\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}1&0\end{bmatrix}\end{bmatrix}=-\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{2} (Equation (2)), which is the standard real representation of multiplication by 𝐢\mathbf{i}. Writing m=2​km=2k, the general solution is 𝓡2=𝐒⁡(𝕀k⊗𝓒2⊤)​𝐒−1\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}=\mathbf{S}(\mathbb{I}_{k}\otimes\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}^{\top})\mathbf{S}^{-1} for an arbitrary invertible real matrix 𝐒∈GLm​(ℝ)\mathbf{S}\in\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{R}). Equivalently, 𝓡2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2} is any real matrix with minimal polynomial x2+1x^{2}+1. If one requires 𝓡2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2} to be orthogonal, then 𝓡2=𝐐⁡(𝕀k⊗𝓒2⊤)​𝐐⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}=\mathbf{Q}(\mathbb{I}_{k}\otimes\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{2}^{\top})\mathbf{Q}^{\top} for any 𝐐∈O⁡(m)\mathbf{Q}\in O(m), with O⁡(m)O(m) the general orthogonal group.

With 𝔽=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} for pp prime, we have 𝓒221=(−1)%​p=p−1\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{221}=(-1)\%p=p-1, so the relation 𝓡22=−𝓡1=−𝕀m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}^{2}=-\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}=-\mathbb{I}_{m} over ℝ\mathbb{R} becomes 𝓡22=(p−1)​𝕀m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}^{2}=(p-1)\,\mathbb{I}_{m}. Since p−1>0p-1>0, the polynomial x2−(p−1)=(x−p−1)​(x+p−1)x^{2}-(p-1)=(x-\sqrt{p-1})(x+\sqrt{p-1}) has distinct real roots, hence any real solution 𝓡2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2} is diagonalizable over ℝ\mathbb{R} with eigenvalues in {±p−1}\{\pm\sqrt{p-1}\}. Equivalently, 𝓡2=(p−1)1/2​𝐉\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}=(p-1)^{1/2}\mathbf{J} with 𝐉2=𝕀m\mathbf{J}^{2}=\mathbb{I}_{m} i.e., 𝓡2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2} is p−1\sqrt{p-1} times an involution. There is no parity restriction on mm (unlike the 𝔽=ℝ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R} case). A convenient normal form is 𝓡2=(p−1)1/2​𝐒​diag⁡(ϵ)​𝐒−1\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}=(p-1)^{1/2}\mathbf{S}\diag\big(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\big)\mathbf{S}^{-1} for any 𝐒∈GLm​(ℝ)\mathbf{S}\in\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{R}) and signs ϵ∈{±1}m\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\in\{\pm 1\}^{m}. If one also requires 𝓡2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2} to be symmetric (hence orthogonally diagonalizable), then 𝓡2=(p−1)1/2​𝐐​diag⁡(ϵ)​𝐐⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}=(p-1)^{1/2}\mathbf{Q}\diag\left(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\right)\mathbf{Q}^{\top} for any 𝐐∈O⁡(m)\mathbf{Q}\in O(m).

Example B.13 (Dual Numbers).

For the algebra of dual numbers (Example B.4) with {𝐚(1),𝐚(2)}={1,ε}\{\mathbf{a}^{(1)},\mathbf{a}^{(2)}\}=\{1,\varepsilon\}, 𝓡1=𝕀m\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}=\mathbb{I}_{m} and 𝓡22=0\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{2}^{2}=0 (corresponding to the dual number ε\varepsilon). Example B.14 (Polynomials modulo xnx^{n}).

𝔄=(𝔽n−1​[x],⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\mathbb{F}_{n-1}[x],\cdot\right) with basis 𝐚(i)=xi∀i∈⟦0,n−1⟧\mathbf{a}^{(i)}=x^{i}\ \forall i\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket and product xi⋅xj=x(i+j)modnx^{i}\cdot x^{j}=x^{(i+j)\bmod n} (Example B.5). 𝓡i𝓡j=𝓡(i+j)%​n∀i,j∈⟦0,n−1⟧,𝓡0=𝕀m since 1𝔄=𝐚(0)\begin{split}&\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{(i+j)\%n}\ \forall i,j\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket,\quad\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{0}=\mathbb{I}_{m}\text{ since }1_{\mathfrak{A}}=\mathbf{a}^{(0)}\end{split} (54)

Setting 𝐀:=𝓡1\mathbf{A}:=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{1}, (54) yields 𝓡i+1=𝐀​𝓡i\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i+1}=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i} and hence 𝓡i=𝐀i\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbf{A}^{i} for all ii. In particular, 𝐀n=𝓡n=𝓡0=𝕀m\mathbf{A}^{n}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{n}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{0}=\mathbb{I}_{m}. Conversely, for any 𝐀∈ℳm​(𝔽)\mathbf{A}\in\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) with 𝐀n=𝕀m\mathbf{A}^{n}=\mathbb{I}_{m}, the assignment 𝓡i:=𝐀i∀i∈⟦0,n−1⟧\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}:=\mathbf{A}^{i}\ \forall i\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket solves (54). In fact, since 𝐀n=𝕀m\mathbf{A}^{n}=\mathbb{I}_{m}, we have for all k=q​n+rk=qn+r with q≥0q\geq 0 and r=k%n∈⟦0,n−1⟧r=k\%n\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket (Euclidean division), 𝐀k=𝐀q​n+r=(𝐀n)q​𝐀r=(𝕀m)q​𝐀r=𝐀r=𝐀k%​n\mathbf{A}^{k}=\mathbf{A}^{qn+r}=(\mathbf{A}^{n})^{q}\mathbf{A}^{r}=(\mathbb{I}_{m})^{q}\mathbf{A}^{r}=\mathbf{A}^{r}=\mathbf{A}^{k\%n}. Therefore, size-mm solutions are in bijection with matrices 𝐀\mathbf{A} satisfying 𝐀n=𝕀m\mathbf{A}^{n}=\mathbb{I}_{m}, via 𝐀↦(𝓡i=𝐀i)i=0n−1\mathbf{A}\mapsto(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{i}=\mathbf{A}^{i})_{i=0}^{n-1}.

Over ℝ\mathbb{R}, a faithful (i.e. injective) size-nn representation is obtained by choosing 𝐀\mathbf{A} to be the n×nn\times n cyclic shift matrix

𝐀=(00⋯0110⋯0001⋱⋱⋱000⋯010)\mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&\cdots&0&1\\ 1&0&\cdots&0&0\\ 0&1&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ \vdots&\ddots&\ddots&0&0\\ 0&\cdots&0&1&0\end{pmatrix} (55)

Since 𝐀𝐞(k)=𝐞(k+1)​∀k∈[n−1]\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}^{(k)}=\mathbf{e}^{(k+1)}\ \forall k\in[n-1] and 𝐀𝐞(n)=𝐞(1)\mathbf{A}\mathbf{e}^{(n)}=\mathbf{e}^{(1)}, we have 𝐀nn​𝐞(k)=𝐞(k)​∀k∈[n]\mathbf{A}_{n}^{n}\mathbf{e}^{(k)}=\mathbf{e}^{(k)}\ \forall k\in[n]. Therefore 𝐀n=𝕀n\mathbf{A}^{n}=\mathbb{I}_{n}. Define ρ(xi)=𝐀i∀i∈⟦0,n−1⟧\rho(x^{i})=\mathbf{A}^{i}\ \forall i\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket. Then for all i,j∈⟦0,n−1⟧i,j\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket, ρ⁡(xi)​ρ​(xj)=𝐀i​𝐀j=𝐀i+j=𝐀(i+j)%​n=ρ⁡(x(i+j)%​n)\rho(x^{i})\rho(x^{j})=\mathbf{A}^{i}\mathbf{A}^{j}=\mathbf{A}^{i+j}=\mathbf{A}^{(i+j)\%n}=\rho\big(x^{(i+j)\%n}\big). So ρ\rho is an algebra homomorphism. This is the regular (cyclic) real representation. More generally, any real solution arises from some 𝐀∈𝔽m×m\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{F}^{m\times m} with 𝐀n=𝕀m\mathbf{A}^{n}=\mathbb{I}_{m} by 𝓡j=𝐀j\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{j}=\mathbf{A}^{j}. Over ℝ\mathbb{R} such 𝐀\mathbf{A} is real-similar to a block diagonal matrix with 1×11\times 1 blocks at ±1\pm 1 (when nn is even) and 2×22\times 2 rotation blocks corresponding to conjugate pairs e±2π𝐢k/ne^{\pm 2\pi\mathbf{i}k/n} (Equation (34)). If fact, if 𝐀∈ℝm×m\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} satisfies 𝐀n=𝕀m\mathbf{A}^{n}=\mathbb{I}_{m}, then every eigenvalue λ\lambda of 𝐀\mathbf{A} solves λn=1\lambda^{n}=1, i.e. λ=e2​π​i​k/n\lambda=e^{2\pi\mathrm{i}k/n} for some k∈⟦0,n−1⟧k\in\llbracket 0,n-1\rrbracket. The real roots among these are λ=1\lambda=1 (always) and, when nn is even, λ=−1\lambda=-1; these give 1×11\times 1 Jordan blocks [1][1] and (if nn is even) [−1][-1]. All remaining roots occur in complex-conjugate pairs e±i​θe^{\pm\mathrm{i}\theta} with θ=2​π​k/n\theta=2\pi k/n. Over ℝ\mathbb{R}, each such conjugate pair corresponds to a 2×22\times 2 real block that acts as a rotation by angle θ\theta.

If we replace matrix multiplication 𝐀𝐁\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B} in 𝔄=(ℳn​(𝔽),⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\mathcal{M}_{n}(\mathbb{F}),\cdot\right) with the matrix commutator [𝐀,𝐁]=𝐀𝐁−𝐁𝐀[\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}]=\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B}-\mathbf{B}\mathbf{A}, then 𝓒(q1−1)​n+r1,(q2−1)​n+r2,(q3−1)​n+r3=δq2​r1​δq1​q3​δr2​r3−δq1​r2​δq2​q3​δr1​r3\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(q_{1}-1)n+r_{1},(q_{2}-1)n+r_{2},(q_{3}-1)n+r_{3}}=\delta_{q_{2}r_{1}}\delta_{q_{1}q_{3}}\delta_{r_{2}r_{3}}-\delta_{q_{1}r_{2}}\delta_{q_{2}q_{3}}\delta_{r_{1}r_{3}} (Example B.8). and

δq2​r1​𝓡(q1−1)​n+r2−δq1​r2​𝓡(q2−1)​n+r1=δq2​r1​δq1​r2​𝐍−δq1​r2​δq2​r1​𝐍=0\delta_{q_{2}r_{1}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{(q_{1}-1)n+r_{2}}-\delta_{q_{1}r_{2}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{(q_{2}-1)n+r_{1}}=\delta_{q_{2}r_{1}}\delta_{q_{1}r_{2}}\mathbf{N}-\delta_{q_{1}r_{2}}\delta_{q_{2}r_{1}}\mathbf{N}=0 (61)

So 𝓡\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}} satisfies the system (59). This yields nontrivial solutions whenever m≥2m\geq 2, since square-zero (nilpotent) matrices exist, e.g. 𝐍=𝐮𝐯⊤∈𝔽m×m\mathbf{N}=\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^{\top}\in\mathbb{F}^{m\times m} for any 𝐮,𝐯∈𝔽m\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{F}^{m} such that 𝐮⊤​𝐯=0\mathbf{u}^{\top}\mathbf{v}=0. Any simultaneous conjugate 𝐒​𝓡(q−1)​n+r​𝐒−1\mathbf{S}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{(q-1)n+r}\mathbf{S}^{-1} for 𝐒∈GLm​(𝔽)\mathbf{S}\in\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) is again a solution, so replacing 𝐍\mathbf{N} by any conjugate 𝐒𝐍𝐒−1\mathbf{S}\mathbf{N}\mathbf{S}^{-1} with (𝐒𝐍𝐒−1)2=0(\mathbf{S}\mathbf{N}\mathbf{S}^{-1})^{2}=0 also works. If m=1m=1 over a field of characteristic ≠2\neq 2 (e.g. ℝ\mathbb{R}), the only solution is trivial: the equations force all scalars to be 00. Hence, the minimal mm for a nontrivial solution is m=2m=2.

Proposition B.21.

Let ρG:G→GLm​(𝔽)\rho_{G}:G\to\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) be a representation of a goup (G,∘)(G,\circ). Define the linear map

ρ:𝔽⁡[G]→ℳm​(𝔽),ρ⁡(∑i=1nαi​gi):=∑i=1nαi​ρG​(gi)\rho:\mathbb{F}[G]\to\mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{F}),\ \rho\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}g_{i}\right):=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}\,\rho_{G}(g_{i}) (62)

Then ρ\rho is an 𝔽\mathbb{F}-algebra homomorphism, and hence a representation of (𝔽⁡[G],⋅)(\mathbb{F}[G],\cdot).

Proof.

ρ\rho is linear by definition. For all 𝐮=∑i𝐮i​gi\mathbf{u}=\sum_{i}\mathbf{u}_{i}g_{i} and 𝐯=∑j𝐯j​gj\mathbf{v}=\sum_{j}\mathbf{v}_{j}g_{j}, ρ⁡(𝐮⋅𝐯)=ρ⁡(∑i,j𝐮i​𝐯j​(gi∘gj))=∑i,j𝐮i​𝐯j​ρG​(gi∘gj)=∑i,j𝐮i​𝐯j​ρG​(gi)​ρG​(gj)=ρ⁡(𝐮)​ρ​(𝐯)\rho(\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v})=\rho\left(\sum_{i,j}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}(g_{i}\circ g_{j})\right)=\sum_{i,j}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\rho_{G}(g_{i}\circ g_{j})=\sum_{i,j}\mathbf{u}_{i}\mathbf{v}_{j}\rho_{G}(g_{i})\rho_{G}(g_{j})=\rho(\mathbf{u})\rho(\mathbf{v}). Finaly, ρ⁡(1𝔽⁡[G])=ρ⁡(e)=𝕀m\rho(1_{\mathbb{F}[G]})=\rho(e)=\mathbb{I}_{m} since ρG​(e)=𝕀m\rho_{G}(e)=\mathbb{I}_{m}. ∎

Example B.17 (Group algebra of the symmetric group StS_{t} over 𝔽\mathbb{F}).

Write n=t!n=t!. The structure tensor of 𝔄=(𝔽⁡[St],⋅)\mathfrak{A}=\left(\mathbb{F}[S_{t}],\cdot\right) in its canonical basis (𝐚(1),…,𝐚(n))≡(σ)σ∈St(\mathbf{a}^{(1)},\dots,\mathbf{a}^{(n)})\equiv(\sigma)_{\sigma\in S_{t}} is 𝓒i​j​k=𝟙⁡(𝐚(k)=𝐚(i)∘𝐚(j))​∀i,j,k∈[n]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{ijk}=\mathbb{1}(\mathbf{a}^{(k)}=\mathbf{a}^{(i)}\circ\mathbf{a}^{(j)})\ \forall i,j,k\in[n] (Example B.11), so the representation equations read (by abuse of notations)

𝓡σi​𝓡σj=𝓡σi∘σj​∀σi,σj∈St\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma_{i}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma_{j}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma_{i}\circ\sigma_{j}}\ \forall\sigma_{i},\sigma_{j}\in S_{t} (63)

Take m=tm=t and define 𝓡σ=𝐏σ∈𝔽m×m​∀σ∈St\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma}=\mathbf{P}_{\sigma}\in\mathbb{F}^{m\times m}\ \forall\sigma\in S_{t}, where 𝐏σ\mathbf{P}_{\sigma} is the permutation matrix associated to σ\sigma, i.e. (𝐏σ)a​b=1(\mathbf{P}_{\sigma})_{ab}=1 if σ⁡(b)=a\sigma(b)=a and 00 otherwise (under cycle notation for permutations). Then 𝓡σi​𝓡σj=𝐏σi​𝐏σj=𝐏σi∘σj=𝓡σi∘σj\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma_{i}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma_{j}}=\mathbf{P}_{\sigma_{i}}\mathbf{P}_{\sigma_{j}}=\mathbf{P}_{\sigma_{i}\circ\sigma_{j}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma_{i}\circ\sigma_{j}}, so (63) is satisfied. This is the standard permutation representation of StS_{t} on 𝔽t\mathbb{F}^{t}. More generally, let m=nm=n and for each σ∈St\sigma\in S_{t} set 𝓡σ:=matrix of left multiplication by σ on 𝔽⁡[St]\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma}:=\text{matrix of left multiplication by $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{F}[S_{t}]$}. Explicitly, (𝓡σ)π,γ=𝟙⁡(γ=σ∘π)​∀π,γ∈St(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma})_{\pi,\gamma}=\mathbb{1}(\gamma=\sigma\circ\pi)\ \forall\pi,\gamma\in S_{t}. Then 𝓡σi​𝓡σj=𝓡σi∘σj\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma_{i}}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma_{j}}=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma_{i}\circ\sigma_{j}}, so (63) holds. This is the left regular representation (Proposition B.18). In general, for any m≥1m\geq 1, any group representation ρ:St→GLm​(𝔽)\rho:S_{t}\to\mathrm{GL}_{m}(\mathbb{F}) gives a solution of (63) by setting 𝓡σ:=ρ⁡(σ)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{R}}}_{\sigma}:=\rho(\sigma) (Proposition B.21). Conversely, any solution of (63) defines a group representation of StS_{t}. Thus, the solutions of the FDA system for 𝔽⁡[St]\mathbb{F}[S_{t}] are in bijection with group representations of StS_{t}.

Appendix C Learning Finite-Dimensional Algebra

C.1 A Linear Inverse View for 𝔽=ℝ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}

In 𝔽=ℝ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{R}, the problem of learning a FDA with structure tensor 𝓒∗∈𝔽n×n×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}\in\mathbb{F}^{n\times n\times n} is similar to a matrix factorization problem with matrix 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤∈𝔽n2×n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)}\in\mathbb{F}^{n^{2}\times n} (Equation (4)). Giving the measures 𝐔,𝐕∈𝔽N×n\mathbf{U},\mathbf{V}\in\mathbb{F}^{N\times n}, let 𝐗:=𝐕∙𝐔=[−𝐕s⊗𝐔s−]s∈[N]∈𝔽N×n2\mathbf{X}:=\mathbf{V}\bullet\mathbf{U}=\left[-\mathbf{V}_{s}\otimes\mathbf{U}_{s}-\right]_{s\in[N]}\in\mathbb{F}^{N\times n^{2}}. The training loss is

ℒ⁡(𝓒)=∑s∈[N]‖(𝓒−𝓒∗)×1𝐔s×2𝐕s‖22=∑s∈[N]‖(𝓒(3)−𝓒∗(3))𝐗s‖22=‖𝐗(𝓒(3)−𝓒∗(3))⊤‖F2\begin{split}\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}})&=\sum_{s\in[N]}\left\|\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}-\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}\right)\times_{1}\mathbf{U}_{s}\times_{2}\mathbf{V}_{s}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\sum_{s\in[N]}\left\|\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(3)}-\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}_{(3)}\right)\mathbf{X}_{s}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\left\|\mathbf{X}\left(\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(3)}-\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}_{(3)}\right)^{\top}\right\|_{\text{F}}^{2}\end{split} (64)

By writing 𝓒∗=⟦𝐀∗,𝐁∗,𝐂∗⟧:=∑ℓ=1R𝐀:,ℓ∗∘𝐁:,ℓ∗∘𝐂:,ℓ∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}=\llbracket\mathbf{A}^{*},\mathbf{B}^{*},\mathbf{C}^{*}\rrbracket:=\sum_{\ell=1}^{R}\mathbf{A}^{*}_{:,\ell}\circ\mathbf{B}^{*}_{:,\ell}\circ\mathbf{C}^{*}_{:,\ell} as the CP decomposition of rank RR of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}, we can use a parametrization 𝓒=⟦𝐀,𝐁,𝐂⟧\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}=\llbracket\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}\rrbracket, so that 𝓒(3)=𝐂​(𝐁⋆𝐀)⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(3)}=\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{B}\star\mathbf{A})^{\top}. In that case, if we are interested in the global structure of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}, we can try to evaluate the effect of the properties of the algebra 𝔄\mathfrak{A} generated by 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} on the CP rank RR of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}, and thus classify which properties of this algebra increase its CP rank (and therefore make it more difficult to learn). Note that 𝓒=⟦𝐀,𝐁,𝐂⟧\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}=\llbracket\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{C}\rrbracket implies 𝓒(3)=𝐂​(𝐁⋆𝐀)⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(3)}=\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{B}\star\mathbf{A})^{\top} and 𝓒×1𝐮×2𝐯=𝐂((𝐀⊤𝐮)⊙(𝐁⊤𝐯))∀𝐮,𝐯∈𝔽n\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{u}\times_{2}\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{C}\left((\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{u})\odot(\mathbf{B}^{\top}\mathbf{v})\right)\ \forall\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}\in\mathbb{F}^{n}, so that 𝐗​𝓒(3)⊤=(𝐕∙𝐔)​(𝐁⋆𝐀)​𝐂⊤=((𝐕𝐁)⊙(𝐔𝐀))​𝐂⊤\mathbf{X}\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}_{(3)}^{\top}=\left(\mathbf{V}\bullet\mathbf{U}\right)(\mathbf{B}\star\mathbf{A})\mathbf{C}^{\top}=\left((\mathbf{V}\mathbf{B})\odot(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{A})\right)\mathbf{C}^{\top}. We recall that ⊙\odot is the Hadamard product, ⋆\star the Khatri-Rao product, ∙\bullet the face-splitting product, and ∘\circ the outer product.

Another way to make things simple, is to just analyze the rank rr of 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)} to characterize the solvability of the problem using a parameterization 𝓒⊤(3)=𝐖(L)⋯𝐖(1)\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{\top}_{(3)}=\mathbf{W}^{(L)}\cdots\mathbf{W}^{(1)}, with 𝐖(L)∈ℝn2×d\mathbf{W}^{(L)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n^{2}\times d}, 𝐖(i)∈ℝd×d\mathbf{W}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} for 1<i<L1<i<L, and 𝐖(1)∈ℝd×n\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n}. This corresponds to a linear network with LL layers. That said, if we are interested in the global structure of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}, we can try to evaluate the effect of the properties of the algebra 𝔄\mathfrak{A} generated by 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} on the rank rr of 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)}, and thus classify which properties of this algebra increase its rank (and therefore make it more difficult to learn). For example, if 𝓒∗=⟦𝐀∗,𝐁∗,𝐂∗⟧\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}=\llbracket\mathbf{A}^{*},\mathbf{B}^{*},\mathbf{C}^{*}\rrbracket, then 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤=(𝐁∗⋆𝐀∗)​𝐂∗⁣⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)}=(\mathbf{B}^{*}\star\mathbf{A}^{*})\mathbf{C}^{*\top}, so that77 7 rank(𝐀)+rank(𝐁)−d2≤rank(𝐀𝐁)≤min⁡(rank(𝐀),rank(𝐁))\rank(\mathbf{A})+\rank(\mathbf{B})-d_{2}\leq\rank(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{B})\leq\min\left(\rank(\mathbf{A}),\rank(\mathbf{B})\right) for all 𝐀∈ℝd1×d2\mathbf{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}\times d_{2}} and 𝐁∈ℝd2×d3\mathbf{B}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{2}\times d_{3}}. rank(𝐁∗⋆𝐀∗)+rank(𝐂∗)−R≤r≤min⁡(rank(𝐁∗⋆𝐀∗),rank(𝐂∗))\rank(\mathbf{B}^{*}\star\mathbf{A}^{*})+\rank(\mathbf{C}^{*})-R\leq r\leq\min\left(\rank(\mathbf{B}^{*}\star\mathbf{A}^{*}),\rank(\mathbf{C}^{*})\right). By “making things simple,” we mean that this is a well-studied problem in the matrix setting. With L=1L=1, there is a need for ℓ∗\ell_{*} (nuclear norm) regularization (or any other form of appropriate regularization88 8 For example, if 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)} is extremely sparse so that the notion of sparsity prevails over the notion of rank, then ℓ1\ell_{1} is needed for generalization under gradient descent optimization (Notsawo et al. 2025).) to recover 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)} when NN is large enough (Candès & Tao 2010; Candes & Recht 2012; Notsawo et al. 2025). But when L≥2L\geq 2 (and the initialization scale is small), there is no need for ℓ∗\ell_{*} (or any other form of regularization) to recover 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)} (Gunasekar et al. 2017; Arora et al. 2018; Arora et al. 2019; Gidel et al. 2019; Gissin et al. 2019; Razin & Cohen 2020; Li et al. 2020). Increasing LL implicitly biases 𝓒(3)⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{\top}_{(3)} toward a low-rank solution, which oftentimes leads to more accurate recovery for sufficiently large NN.

The rank is not the only thing to take into account if we treat the problem as a matrix factorization problem. To see this, consider the matrix 𝐞(k)​𝐞(l)⊤\mathbf{e}^{(k)}\mathbf{e}^{(l)\top} for k,l∈[n]k,l\in[n]. Even if the rank of this matrix is 11, it has only zeros everywhere except 11 at position (k,l)(k,l), so we have very little chance of reconstructing it in high dimension by observing a portion of its inputs uniformly at random. The only way to guarantee observation of the input at position (k,l)(k,l) is to choose measurements coherently with its singular basis 𝐞(k)⊗𝐞(l)\mathbf{e}^{(k)}\otimes\mathbf{e}^{(l)}. This idea is formulated more generally below.

Definition C.1.

Let UU be a subspace of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} of dimension rr and 𝐏U\mathbf{P}_{U} be the orthogonal projection onto UU. Then, the coherence of UU vis-a-vis a basis {𝐮(i)}i∈[n]\{\mathbf{u}^{(i)}\}_{i\in[n]} is defined by μ⁡(U)=nr​maxi​‖𝐏U​𝐮(i)‖2\mu(U)=\frac{n}{r}\max_{i}\|\mathbf{P}_{U}\mathbf{u}^{(i)}\|^{2}.

For a matrix 𝐀=𝐔​Σ​𝐕⊤∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\Sigma\mathbf{V}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} under the compact SVD, the projection on the left singular value is 𝐱→𝐔𝐔⊤​𝐱\mathbf{x}\to\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{x}, and ‖𝐔𝐔⊤​𝐱‖22=‖𝐔⊤​𝐱‖22\|\mathbf{U}\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{x}\|^{2}_{2}=\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{x}\|^{2}_{2} for all 𝐱\mathbf{x} (similarly for the right singular value). We have the following definition of coherence, which considers each matrix entry.

Definition C.2 (Local coherence & Leverage score).

Let 𝐀=𝐔​Σ​𝐕⊤∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{U}\Sigma\mathbf{V}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} be the compact SVD of a matrix 𝐀\mathbf{A} of rank rr. The local coherences of 𝐀\mathbf{A} are defined by

μi(𝐀)=n1r∥𝐔⊤𝐞(i)∥2=n1r∥𝐔i,:∥2∀i∈[n1]νj(𝐀)=n2r∥𝐕⊤𝐞(j)∥2=n2r∥𝐕j,:∥2∀j∈[n2]\begin{split}&\mu_{i}(\mathbf{A})=\frac{n_{1}}{r}\|\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{e}^{(i)}\|^{2}=\frac{n_{1}}{r}\|\mathbf{U}_{i,:}\|^{2}\quad\forall i\in[n_{1}]\\ &\nu_{j}(\mathbf{A})=\frac{n_{2}}{r}\|\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{e}^{(j)}\|^{2}=\frac{n_{2}}{r}\|\mathbf{V}_{j,:}\|^{2}\quad\forall j\in[n_{2}]\end{split} (65)

with μi\mu_{i} for row ii and νj\nu_{j} for row jj. In 𝐔⊤​𝐞(i)\mathbf{U}^{\top}\mathbf{e}^{(i)}, 𝐞(i)∈ℝn1\mathbf{e}^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}}, and in 𝐕⊤​𝐞(j)\mathbf{V}^{\top}\mathbf{e}^{(j)}, 𝐞(j)∈ℝn2\mathbf{e}^{(j)}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{2}}. We did not distinguish them explicitly for simplicity’s sake.

The analysis of recovery guarantees for matrix factorization hinges on local coherence of a target matrix 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*}. The local coherence measures (μi,νj)(i,j)∈[n1]×[n2](\mu_{i},\nu_{j})_{(i,j)\in[n_{1}]\times[n_{2}]} of 𝐀∗∈ℝn1×n2\mathbf{A}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n_{1}\times n_{2}} quantify how strongly individual rows and columns align with the top singular vectors. These quantities, also known as leverage scores, indicate the “influence” of each row ii or column jj on the low-rank structure. A row/column with a high leverage score projects strongly onto the span of the singular vectors, meaning that a relatively small number of its entries capture much of the matrix’s structure. Uniformly low coherence (μi\mu_{i} and νi\nu_{i} close to 11) implies that the matrix’s information is well-distributed across rows and columns, thereby reducing the number of samples needed for exact recovery. For example, Chen et al. 2014 show in the context of matrix completion that sampling the training inputs at position (i,j)(i,j) with probability pi​jp_{ij} proportional to μi+νj\mu_{i}+\nu_{j} allows for perfect recovery of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} with fewer samples than uniform sampling, and called such sampling strategies local coherence sampling (see Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.3 in (Chen et al. 2014)). The minimal number of observations required for perfect recovery also depends on the coherence measures (Candès & Tao 2010; Candes & Recht 2012). Let μ(0)\mu^{(0)} and μ(1)\mu^{(1)} be two constants such that μ(0)≥max⁡(maxi⁡μi,maxi⁡νi)\mu^{(0)}\geq\max\left(\max_{i}\mu_{i},\max_{i}\nu_{i}\right) and maxi,j⁡[𝐔∗​𝐕∗⁣⊤]i​j≤μ(1)​r/(n1​n2)\max_{i,j}[\mathbf{U}^{*}\mathbf{V}^{*\top}]_{ij}\leq\mu^{(1)}\sqrt{r/(n_{1}n_{2})}99 9 Since |[𝐔∗𝐕∗⁣⊤]i​j|=|∑k𝐔i,k∗𝐕j,k∗|≤∑k𝐔i,k∗2∑k𝐕j,k∗2=∥𝐔i,:∗∥2∥𝐕j,:∗∥2=rn1​n2μi​νj≤rn1​n2μ0\left|[\mathbf{U}^{*}\mathbf{V}^{*\top}]_{ij}\right|=\left|\sum_{k}\mathbf{U}^{*}_{i,k}\mathbf{V}^{*}_{j,k}\right|\leq\sqrt{\sum_{k}\mathbf{U}^{*2}_{i,k}}\sqrt{\sum_{k}\mathbf{V}^{*2}_{j,k}}=\|\mathbf{U}^{*}_{i,:}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{V}^{*}_{j,:}\|_{2}=\frac{r}{\sqrt{n_{1}n_{2}}}\sqrt{\mu_{i}\nu_{j}}\leq\frac{r}{\sqrt{n_{1}n_{2}}}\mu_{0} for all i,ji,j; we can take any μ(1)≥μ(0)​r\mu^{(1)}\geq\mu^{(0)}\sqrt{r}.. Candes & Recht 2012 show that if μ0\mu_{0} and μ1\mu_{1} are low, few samples are required to recover 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*}. More precisely, put n=max⁡(n1,n2)n=\max(n_{1},n_{2}). Suppose we observe NN entries of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} with locations sampled uniformly at random. There are numerical constants CC and cc such that if N≥C​max⁡(μ12,μ012​μ1,μ0​n14)​n​r​β​log⁡(n)N\geq C\max\left(\mu_{1}^{2},\mu_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}}\mu_{1},\mu_{0}n^{\frac{1}{4}}\right)nr\beta\log\left(n\right) for some β>2\beta>2, then perfect recovery of 𝐀∗\mathbf{A}^{*} is possible from this NN observations with probability at least 1−c/n31-c/n^{3}. In addition, if r≤n1/5/μ0r\leq n^{1/5}/\mu_{0}, then the recovery is exact with probability at least 1−c/n31-c/n^{3} provided that N≥C​μ0​n6/5​r​β​log⁡(n)N\geq C\mu_{0}n^{6/5}r\beta\log\left(n\right) (see Theorem 1.3 in (Candes & Recht 2012))

The research question here can be therefore to know which natural properties of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} affects the rank and the local coherences of 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)}; or more generally, how do the properties of 𝔄\mathfrak{A} affect the rank and the local coherences of 𝓒(3)∗⁣⊤\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*\top}_{(3)}. We leave these questions for future work.

C.2 Finite Fields 𝔽=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z} and Representation-Centric Modeling

For a finite-field FDA (𝔽=𝔽p=ℤ/p​ℤ\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_{p}=\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}, pp prime), we treat 𝔄\mathfrak{A} as a vocabulary, index each element 𝐮∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A} by ⟨𝐮⟩∈[q]\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle\in[q] with q=|𝔄|=pnq=|\mathfrak{A}|=p^{n}, and learn an embedding matrix 𝐄∈ℝq×d\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times d} so that 𝐄⟨𝐮⟩\mathbf{E}_{\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle} is the trainable vector attached to 𝐮\mathbf{u}. We hypothesize that grokking corresponds to the point at which 𝐄\mathbf{E} and the downstream layers collectively represent the algebra, so a simple linear readout recovers the correct output token. To verify this hypothesis: (i) we vary algebraic properties of 𝔽p​[𝓒∗]\mathbb{F}_{p}[\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*}] and measure their effect on grokking delay and generalization; (ii) we study how structural features of 𝓒∗\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{C}}}^{*} shape learning dynamics; and (iii) we probe whether models learn algebraic representations during training. This finite-field setting provides the cleanest laboratory for observing how algebraic structure governs grokking.

Appendix D Experiment Setup

D.1 Task Description and Model Architecture

From now on we work over the finite field 𝔽=𝔽p\mathbb{F}=\mathbb{F}_{p} (prime pp). Identify 𝔄≡𝔽pn\mathfrak{A}\equiv\mathbb{F}_{p}^{n} and set q:=|𝔄|=pnq:=|\mathfrak{A}|=p^{n}. Each element 𝐮∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A} is treated as a vocabulary symbol with index ⟨𝐮⟩∈[q]\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle\in[q]. The models we use will associate to each of these symbols a trainable vector 𝐄⟨𝐮⟩∈ℝd\mathbf{E}_{\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. 𝐄∈ℝV×d\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d}, with V≥qV\geq q the vocabulary size, which include the set special tokens 𝒮\mathcal{S} (see section below). Let Ψ:𝔄→{0,1}V\Psi:\mathfrak{A}\to\{0,1\}^{V} be the one-hot encoding defined the vocabulary 𝒱=𝔄∪𝒮\mathcal{V}=\mathfrak{A}\cup\mathcal{S}, Ψ⁡(𝐚):=[𝟙⁡(𝐯=𝐮)]𝐯∈𝒱​∀𝐮∈𝒱\Psi(\mathbf{a}):=\left[\mathbb{1}(\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{u})\right]_{\mathbf{v}\in\mathcal{V}}\ \forall\mathbf{u}\in\mathcal{V}. We have 𝐄⟨𝐮⟩=𝐄⊤​Ψ​(𝐮)\mathbf{E}_{\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle}=\mathbf{E}^{\top}\Psi(\mathbf{u}).

D.2 Representation Learning

D.2.1 Proof of Propositon 5.1

Proposition D.1.

Assume that (𝔄,×)(\mathfrak{A},\times) has a group structure (of size qq), and denote the inverse of an element 𝐮∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A} by 𝐮−1\mathbf{u}^{-1}. Let ρ:𝔄→ℝm×m\rho:\mathfrak{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{m\times m} be a faithful matrix representation of 𝔄\mathfrak{A}. Suppose a model yθ​(𝐱)=𝐖​ϕ​(𝐱)∈ℝqy_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{W}\phi(\mathbf{x})\in\mathbb{R}^{q} encodes pairs 𝐱=(𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔄2\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathfrak{A}^{2} as ϕ⁡(𝐮,𝐯)=ρ⁡(𝐮×𝐯)\phi(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})=\rho(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}) and decodes with a linear classifier parameterized by weights 𝐖∈ℝq×m2\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times m^{2}} containing ρ⁡(𝐰−1)\rho(\mathbf{w}^{-1}) for each 𝐰∈𝔄\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{A}. Then the predicted label satisfies arg​maxi∈[q]⁡yθ​(𝐱)​[i]=𝐮×𝐯\argmax_{i\in[q]}y_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})[i]=\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}. As a consequence, the classifier linearly separates all qq outputs.

Proof.

Consider the linear classifier yθ​(𝐱)=𝐖​ϕ​(𝐮,𝐯)y_{\theta}(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{W}\phi(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v}) acting on ϕ⁡(𝐮,𝐯)∈ℝm2\phi(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}}, that is yθ​(𝐮,𝐯)​[i]=⟨𝐖i,ϕ⁡(𝐮,𝐯)⟩y_{\theta}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})[i]=\langle\mathbf{W}_{i},\phi(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\rangle where the inner product is the Frobenius product on ℝm×m\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}. Write 𝐖i=ρ⁡(𝐰−1)\mathbf{W}_{i}=\rho(\mathbf{w}^{-1}) for some 𝐰∈𝔄\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{A}, so that

yθ​(𝐮,𝐯)​[i]=⟨ρ⁡(𝐮×𝐯),ρ⁡(𝐰−1)⟩=tr⁡(ρ⁡(𝐮×𝐯)​ρ​(𝐰−1)⊤)y_{\theta}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})[i]=\langle\rho(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}),\rho(\mathbf{w}^{-1})\rangle=\tr\left(\rho(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\rho(\mathbf{w}^{-1})^{\top}\right) (75)

Since ρ​(𝐰−1)⊤=ρ⁡(𝐰−1)\rho(\mathbf{w}^{-1})^{\top}=\rho(\mathbf{w}^{-1}) for an orthogonal (unitary) representation, this reduces to

yθ​(𝐮,𝐯)​[i]=tr⁡(ρ⁡(𝐮×𝐯)​ρ​(𝐰−1))=χρ​((𝐮×𝐯)×𝐰−1)y_{\theta}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})[i]=\tr\left(\rho(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\rho(\mathbf{w}^{-1})\right)=\chi_{\rho}\left((\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\times\mathbf{w}^{-1}\right) (76)

where χρ\chi_{\rho} is the character of ρ\rho. Now, recall that χρ\chi_{\rho} uniquely distinguishes group elements whenever ρ\rho is faithful. In particular, max𝐰∈𝔄⁡χρ​((𝐮×𝐯)​𝐰−1)\max_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{A}}\chi_{\rho}\left((\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\mathbf{w}^{-1}\right) is attained uniquely at 𝐰=𝐮×𝐯\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}. Therefore,

arg​maxi∈[q]⁡yθ​(𝐮,𝐯)​[i]=arg​max𝐰∈𝔄⁡χρ​((𝐮×𝐯)×𝐰−1)=𝐮×𝐯\argmax_{i\in[q]}y_{\theta}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})[i]=\argmax_{\mathbf{w}\in\mathfrak{A}}\chi_{\rho}\left((\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\times\mathbf{w}^{-1}\right)=\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v} (77)

∎

D.2.2 Representation Quality

Let 𝐟(ℓ)​(𝐮)∈ℝm12\mathbf{f}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{u})\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{1}^{2}} and 𝐟(r)​(𝐮)∈ℝm12\mathbf{f}^{(r)}(\mathbf{u})\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{1}^{2}} denote the feature vectors produced by the model for 𝐮∈𝔄\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A} when 𝐮\mathbf{u} appears on the left or on the right of an equation, respectively; and let 𝐟⁡(𝐮)∈ℝm2\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u})\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}} denote the feature vector of 𝐮\mathbf{u} produced by the unembedding layer (the classifier). For the first layer of the model (the embedding), we have 𝐟(ℓ)​(𝐮)=𝐟(r)​(𝐮)=𝐄⟨𝐮⟩\mathbf{f}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{f}^{(r)}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{E}_{\langle\mathbf{u}\rangle} and thus m12=dm_{1}^{2}=d. For Transformer, m12=dm_{1}^{2}=d for all layers, but for LSTM (resp. MLP), m12m_{1}^{2} is the hidden dimension (resp. number of hidden units in the considered layer), which can differ from the embedding size dd. We want to determine whether there exists 𝓦∈ℝm12×m12×m2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{1}^{2}\times m_{1}^{2}\times m^{2}} such that

𝐟(𝐮×𝐯)=𝐟^(𝐮×𝐯):=𝓦×1𝐟(ℓ)(𝐮)×2𝐟(r)(𝐯)=𝓦(3)(𝐟(r)(𝐯)⊗𝐟(ℓ)(𝐮))∀(𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔄2\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})=\hat{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}):=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}\times_{1}\mathbf{f}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{u})\times_{2}\mathbf{f}^{(r)}(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}_{(3)}\big(\mathbf{f}^{(r)}(\mathbf{v})\otimes\mathbf{f}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{u})\big)\quad\forall(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathfrak{A}^{2} (78)

with 𝓦(3)∈ℝm2×m14\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}_{(3)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}\times m_{1}^{4}}. Here, we are seeking a linear transformation from ℝm14\mathbb{R}^{m_{1}^{4}} to ℝm2\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}}, with m14≈m4m_{1}^{4}\approx m^{4} (since mm and m1m_{1} are of similar order). Because N=|𝔄2|=q2N=|\mathfrak{A}^{2}|=q^{2} is not very large, the problem may become trivial if the dimension is too high1010 10 In fact, if m14≫Nm_{1}^{4}\gg N, then the system is overparameterized and admits near-perfect solutions regardless of whether the features encode algebraic structure.. To avoid this, we first project 𝐟(ℓ)​(𝐮)\mathbf{f}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{u}) and 𝐟(r)​(𝐯)\mathbf{f}^{(r)}(\mathbf{v}) into a lower-dimensional space of size m22≤mm_{2}^{2}\leq m. Formally, we want 𝓦∈ℝm22×m22×m2\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{2}^{2}\times m_{2}^{2}\times m^{2}}, 𝐏(ℓ)∈ℝm22×m12\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{2}^{2}\times m_{1}^{2}} and 𝐏(r)∈ℝm22×m12\mathbf{P}^{(r)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{2}^{2}\times m_{1}^{2}} such that

𝐟⁡(𝐮×𝐯)=𝐟^​(𝐮×𝐯):=𝓦(3)​((𝐏(r)​𝐟(r)​(𝐯))⊗(𝐏(ℓ)​𝐟(ℓ)​(𝐮)))=𝓦(3)​𝐏​(𝐟(r)​(𝐯)⊗𝐟(ℓ)​(𝐮))∀(𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔄2\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})=\hat{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}):=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}_{(3)}\Big(\big(\mathbf{P}^{(r)}\mathbf{f}^{(r)}(\mathbf{v})\big)\otimes\big(\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)}\mathbf{f}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{u})\big)\Big)=\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}_{(3)}\,\mathbf{P}\,\big(\mathbf{f}^{(r)}(\mathbf{v})\otimes\mathbf{f}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{u})\big)\quad\forall(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathfrak{A}^{2} (79)

with 𝓦(3)∈ℝm2×m24\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}_{(3)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}\times m_{2}^{4}} and 𝐏=𝐏(r)⊗𝐏(ℓ)∈ℝm24×m14\mathbf{P}=\mathbf{P}^{(r)}\otimes\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{2}^{4}\times m_{1}^{4}}. We do not learn 𝐏(ℓ),𝐏(r)\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{P}^{(r)} jointly with 𝓦\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}, since this would give 𝓦\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}} too much flexibility and risk overfitting (the decomposition (79) could still hold trivially without revealing whether algebra-like structure emerges in the model’s features). Instead, we fix 𝐏(ℓ),𝐏(r)\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{P}^{(r)} in advance, either by drawing them at random or by using a PCA-based construction. We use the mean squared error ℒrep\mathcal{L}_{\text{rep}} and the cosine similarity 𝒜rep\mathcal{A}_{\text{rep}} associated with solving this problem (i.e. finding 𝓦\mathbf{\boldsymbol{\mathcal{W}}}) as measures of how algebra-like structure emerges in the model’s feature space.

ℒrep\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{rep}} =1|𝔄2|​1∑(𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔄2‖𝐟⁡(𝐮×𝐯)‖22​∑(𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔄2‖𝐟⁡(𝐮×𝐯)−𝐟^​(𝐮,𝐯)‖22\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathfrak{A}^{2}|}\frac{1}{\sum_{(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathfrak{A}^{2}}\left\|\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\right\|_{2}^{2}}\sum_{(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathfrak{A}^{2}}\left\|\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})-\hat{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\right\|_{2}^{2} (80)
𝒜rep\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{\text{rep}} =1|𝔄2|​∑(𝐮,𝐯)∈𝔄2⟨𝐟​(𝐮×𝐯),𝐟^​(𝐮,𝐯)⟩‖𝐟⁡(𝐮×𝐯)‖2​‖𝐟^​(𝐮,𝐯)‖2\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathfrak{A}^{2}|}\sum_{(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\in\mathfrak{A}^{2}}\frac{\langle\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v}),\hat{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\rangle}{\|\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{u}\times\mathbf{v})\|_{2}\,\|\hat{\mathbf{f}}(\mathbf{u},\mathbf{v})\|_{2}} (81)
Random projections

A natural choice is to draw 𝐏(ℓ),𝐏(r)\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{P}^{(r)} at random, for example with i.i.d. Gaussian entries followed by row-orthonormalization. Random projections preserve pairwise geometry up to small distortions (Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma (Johnson & Lindenstrauss 1984)) and avoid introducing systematic biases. They are also simple, fast to generate, and hard to overfit since they are fixed across training runs. To pick m2m_{2}, we balance two constraints: (i) avoid the trivial regime where m24≫Nm_{2}^{4}\gg N, and (ii) retain enough information from the features. In practice we set m2≈min⁡(⌊m1/2⌋,⌊(N/κ)1/4⌋)m_{2}\approx\min\big(\lfloor m^{1/2}\rfloor,\ \lfloor(N/\kappa)^{1/4}\rfloor\big) with κ≥1\kappa\geq 1 a safety factor. This ensures m24≲Nm_{2}^{4}\lesssim N while keeping m22m_{2}^{2} on the same scale as mm. To ensure robustness, we repeat the probe with several independent draws of 𝐏\mathbf{P} and report mean ±\pm standard deviation of (ℒrep,𝒜rep)(\mathcal{L}_{\text{rep}},\mathcal{A}_{\text{rep}}).

PCA projections

When the feature distribution is highly anisotropic, random projections may discard important directions. In this case, we compute 𝐏(ℓ)\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)} and 𝐏(r)\mathbf{P}^{(r)} using PCA, fitted separately on {𝐟(ℓ)​(𝐮)}𝐮∈𝔄\{\mathbf{f}^{(\ell)}(\mathbf{u})\}_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A}} and {𝐟(r)​(𝐮)}𝐮∈𝔄\{\mathbf{f}^{(r)}(\mathbf{u})\}_{\mathbf{u}\in\mathfrak{A}}, respectively. We retain the top m22m_{2}^{2} components and whiten them to equalize variances. This choice improves the signal-to-noise ratio by ensuring that the projection focuses on the most informative directions while still enforcing the same dimensionality constraint m24≤m2m_{2}^{4}\leq m^{2}. Thus, PCA projections can complement random projections: the former adapt to data anisotropy, while the latter serve as a neutral and robust baseline.

Appendix E Experimentation Details and Additional Experiments

MLP

For Figures 1,  2 (a),  3 (a),  4,  5,  6,  7,  11, 12, 14 and 13, φ∘ϕ\varphi\circ\phi is implemented as a three-layer MLP with ReLU activations and input, hidden, and output dimensions all set to m2=28m^{2}=2^{8}. More precisely, we define φ⁡(𝐳)=𝐖𝐳∈ℝq,𝐖∈ℝq×m2\varphi(\mathbf{z})=\mathbf{W}\mathbf{z}\in\mathbb{R}^{q},\quad\mathbf{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times m^{2}} and ϕ⁡(𝐳)=g⁡(𝐛(2)+𝐖(2)​g​(𝐛(1)+𝐖(1)​vec⁡(𝐳)))\phi(\mathbf{z})=g\left(\mathbf{b}^{(2)}+\mathbf{W}^{(2)}g\!\left(\mathbf{b}^{(1)}+\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\vect(\mathbf{z})\right)\right) where 𝐖(1)∈ℝm2×2​d\mathbf{W}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}\times 2d}, 𝐛(1)∈ℝ2​d\mathbf{b}^{(1)}\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}, 𝐖(2)∈ℝm2×m2\mathbf{W}^{(2)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}\times m^{2}}, 𝐛(2)∈ℝm2\mathbf{b}^{(2)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m^{2}}, and g⁡(z)=max⁡(0,z)g(z)=\max(0,z). The embedding dimension is therefore d=m2/2d=m^{2}/2. All models are initialized using PyTorch’s default initialization scheme. Training was carried out with the AdamW optimizer, a learning rate of 10−210^{-2}, weight decay of 10−110^{-1}, and a minibatch size of 2102^{10}. Models were optimized on a NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU. For Figure 1, the training data fraction is r=0.5r=0.5.

Transformer

For Figures 2 (b), 3 (b) and  8, ϕ\phi is implemented as a two-layer Transformer Encoder with 22 heads and a hidden/embedding dimension of d=m12=26d=m_{1}^{2}=2^{6}. The models are initialized using PyTorch’s default initialization scheme and trained with the AdamW optimizer, a learning rate of 10−310^{-3}, weight decay of 10−110^{-1}, and a minibatch size of 2102^{10}.

LSTM

For Figures 9 and 10, ϕ\phi is implemented as a three-layer LSTM with hidden dimension m12m_{1}^{2} equal to the embedding dimension d=28d=2^{8}. The models are initialized using PyTorch’s default initialization scheme and trained with the AdamW optimizer, a learning rate of 10−210^{-2}, weight decay of 10−110^{-1}, and a minibatch size of 2102^{10}.

Linear Probing

For the probing experiments (Figures 2, 3 and 10), we apply PCA and retain the top m22=mm_{2}^{2}=m components to construct the projection matrices 𝐏(ℓ),𝐏(r)∈ℝm22×m12\mathbf{P}^{(\ell)},\mathbf{P}^{(r)}\in\mathbb{R}^{m_{2}^{2}\times m_{1}^{2}} with m1=mm_{1}=m. The problem (79) is then solved using ordinary least squares with ℓ2\ell_{2} regularization (10−310^{-3}), implemented via sklearn’s Ridge regression.
